<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{intro:sharp}
There is an absolute constant $C$ such that, for every prime $p$
and every integer $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{intro:eq:sharp}
 p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2}
 \le f(p^m)
 \le p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2+Cm}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
 \log_p f(p^m)=\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2+O(m)
\]
uniformly over all primes.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{intro:domination}
\[
 \lim_{x\longrightarrow\infty}\frac{F_{2,2}(x)}{F(x)}=1.
\]
In particular, almost all finite groups are nilpotent.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{intro:concentration}
There are absolute constants $\varepsilon>0$ and $m_0$ such
that, for every prime $p$ and every $m\ge m_0$,
\[
 f(p^m)-f_{\mathfrak H_p}(p^m)
 \le p^{Q(m)-\varepsilon m^2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 1\le\frac{f(p^m)}{f_{\mathfrak H_p}(p^m)}
 \le1+p^{-\varepsilon m^2}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{intro:uniform-upper}
There is an absolute constant $C$ such that
\[
 f(p^m)\le p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+Cm\log m}
\]
for every prime $p$ and every integer $m\ge1$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{p12:thm:main}
Let $f(p^m)$ denote the number of isomorphism classes of groups of
order $p^m$.  There is an absolute constant $C$ such that, for every
prime $p$ and every positive integer $m$,
\[
 p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2}
 \le f(p^m)
 \le p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+Cm\log m}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{p12:cor:saturated-groups}
Let $p$ be a prime and $m\ge1$.  For every nonabelian group $G$ of
order $p^m$, put $r_2=d(G_2/G_3)$ and let $s=s(G)$ be its Sims rank.
The number of isomorphism classes for which
\[
 r_2>\binom{s-1}{2}
\]
is at most
\[
 p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+O(m\log m)},
\]
with an absolute implied constant.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{p12:cor:nonsaturated-group}
For every fixed $A>0$, there is an integer $m_A$, independent of the
prime $p$, such that the following holds for all $m\ge m_A$.
For every nonabelian group $G$ of order $p^m$, write
\[
 r_2=d(G_2/G_3),\qquad s=s(G),
\]
where $s(G)$ is the Sims rank.  The number of isomorphism classes for
which
\[
 r_2\le\binom{s-1}{2}
\]
is at most
\[
 p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-Am^2}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The abelian groups of order $p^m$ are counted by the partition number
$P(m)\le p^m$.  Every nonabelian group has a well-defined Sims rank
$s$ and second lower-central rank $r_2$, and lies in exactly one of
the two ranges above.  Applying \cref{p12:cor:nonsaturated-group} with
$A=1$, together with \cref{p12:cor:saturated-groups}, gives, for all
sufficiently large $m$,
\[
 f(p^m)
 \le p^m
   +p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+O(m\log m)}
   +p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-m^2}
 \le p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+O(m\log m)},
\]
uniformly in $p$; the factor coming from adding the three terms is
absorbed by the absolute $O(m\log m)$ error.  The finitely many
smaller values $m\ge2$ are covered, uniformly in $p$, by the coarse
Sims presentation count after increasing the absolute constant.
The case $m=1$ follows from $f(p)=1$.
The Frattini-class-$2$ lower bound, recorded in
\cite[Theorem~1.3]{BLQR}, gives, uniformly in $p$,
\[
 f(p^m)\ge
 p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2}.
\]
Combining the two inequalities proves \cref{p12:thm:main}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{p12:rem:comparison-mechanism}
The comparison-$N$-series construction in \cref{p12:thm:first-difference}
and its use in \cref{p12:prop:filtered-fibre,p12:prop:total-relation-bound}
extend the graded three-layer breadth mechanism of
\cite[Proposition~20.16 and Theorem~20.17]{BNV} to deeper
commutator data. The binary endpoint analysis in
Section~\ref{p12:sec:binary-endpoint} supplies the complementary
finite-field estimate needed for the nonsaturated regime.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{p12:rem:BNV-notation}
The symbols at the presentation interface are exactly those of
\cite[Sections~5.3--5.5]{BNV}: $s$ is the Sims rank,
$r_i=d(G_i/G_{i+1})$, $N_p(r_1,r_2,s)$ is the logarithmic map count,
and $d_0,\ldots,d_s$, $a(i,j)$, $b(i,j,u,v)$,
$c(i,j,k,u,v)$, and $g_{ij}$ have their BNV meanings.  Following
\cite[Section~20.4]{BNV}, the associated graded object is
$L=\bigoplus_iL_i$ with $|L_i|=p^{s_i}$.  The symbols $R,M,h$ occur
only as local dummy dimensions inside the self-contained
matrix-space lemmas; they are never group parameters.  In particular,
we use $r_2$ for the second-layer rank to distinguish it from the
total counting exponent $M$ in the proof of \cite[Theorem~5.7]{BNV}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:universal-field}
The following bounds hold with absolute constants, simultaneously for every prime power $q\ge2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item For $0\le k\le n$,
 \begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:uniform-gaussian}
  q^{k(n-k)}\le \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q}
  \le \pi_\infty(2)^{-1}q^{k(n-k)}.
 \end{equation}
 \item For integers $R\ge0$ and $0\le a\le\lfloor R/2\rfloor$, the number of alternating
 forms on a fixed $R$-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-space having rank at most $2a$ is at most
 \begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:uniform-rank-variety}
  2\pi_\infty(2)^{-2}q^{a(2R-2a-1)}.
 \end{equation}
 \item For every integer $d\ge0$, one has $|\operatorname{GL}_d(q)|\le q^{d^2}$.
 If $p$ is prime, $D$ is an abelian $p$-group of order $p^e$, and
 $0\le b\le e$, then the number of its subgroups of order $p^b$ is at most
 \begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:uniform-subgroups}
  p^{b(e-b+1)}.
 \end{equation}
 \item For every prime $p$ and integer $e\ge1$, the number of
 isomorphism types of abelian groups of order $p^e$ is the partition
 number of $e$, and is at most $2^{e-1}\le p^e$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The Gaussian formula is
\[
\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q}=q^{k(n-k)}
 \frac{\pi_n(q)}{\pi_k(q)\pi_{n-k}(q)}.
\]
The ratio is at least one term by term and is at most
$\pi_\infty(2)^{-1}$ by \eqref{p12:eq:uniform-pi}, proving (i).

For each $0\le j\le a$, the number of forms of rank exactly $2j$ is
\[
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{2j}_{q}\frac{|\operatorname{GL}_{2j}(q)|}{|\operatorname{Sp}_{2j}(q)|}
 =
  \frac{\pi_R(q)}{\pi_{R-2j}(q)\pi_j(q^2)}\cdot q^{j(2R-2j-1)}.
\]
See~\cite[Section~5, equation~(24)]{FulmanGoldstein} for this formula
in both odd and even characteristic.
The product factor is at most $\pi_\infty(2)^{-2}$.  The exponent
$E(j)=j(2R-2j-1)$ satisfies
$E(j)-E(j-1)=2R-4j+1\ge1$ for $j\le R/2$.  Thus the largest
power-of-$q$ bound in the range $0\le j\le a$ occurs at $j=a$.
More explicitly, let $N_j$ be the number of forms of rank exactly
$2j$.  For $0\le s\le a$, the consecutive-exponent inequality gives
\[
 E(a-s)\le E(a)-s,
 \qquad
 N_{a-s}\le \pi_\infty(2)^{-2}q^{E(a)-s}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{a}N_j
 =\sum_{s=0}^{a}N_{a-s}
 \le \pi_\infty(2)^{-2}q^{E(a)}
     \sum_{s=0}^{a}q^{-s}
 \le 2\pi_\infty(2)^{-2}q^{E(a)},
\]
where the last inequality follows from $\sum_{s\ge0}q^{-s}=(1-q^{-1})^{-1}\le2$ for $q\ge2$.  This proves (ii).

Part (iii) is immediate for the general linear group from
$|\operatorname{GL}_d(q)|=\prod_{i=0}^{d-1}(q^d-q^i)\le q^{d^2}$.  The subgroup
estimate is \cite[Lemma~20.15]{BNV}; it is the uniform bound used in
Blackburn's breadth argument.  For the classical exact enumeration of
subgroups of prescribed type, see~\cite{Birkhoff}.

Part (iv) follows by encoding a partition by its partial sums.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:saturated-map-estimate}
Let $2\le s\le r_1$ and
$\binom{s-1}{2}<r_2\le\binom{s}{2}$.  Then, for every prime $p$,
\[
 N_p(r_1,r_2,s)=r_2\binom{r_1}{2}+ O(1),
\]
where the implied constant is absolute.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $V=\mathbb F_p^{r_1}$ and $W=\mathbb F_p^{r_2}$.  Fix an $s$-dimensional subspace
$U\le V$.  
        
    
                                           
                                                
    
There are exactly $p^{r_2\binom{r_1}{2}}$ alternating maps
$\wedge^2V\to W$. 

For the lower bound, count the alternating maps
$\lambda:\wedge^2V\to W$
for which $\lambda|_{\wedge^2U}$ is
surjective.  There are
\[
 \prod_{i=0}^{r_2-1}(p^{\binom{s}{2}}-p^i)
 =p^{r_2\binom{s}{2}}
  \prod_{j=\binom{s}{2}-r_2+1}^{\binom{s}{2}}(1-p^{-j})\geq \frac{1}{4} p^{r_2\binom{s}{2}}
\]
choices for the restriction to $\wedge^2U$, where the last inequality uses $\pi_\infty(2)>1/4$ in Eq.~\eqref{p12:eq:uniform-pi}.
There are $p^{r_2(\binom{r_1}{2}-\binom{s}{2})}$ choices for its
extension to $\wedge^2V$, so the total number is at least
$\frac{1}{4}p^{r_2\binom{r_1}{2}}$.

For every map counted above, $\lambda(\wedge^2U)=W$, so its
minimum generating dimension is at most $s$.  On the other hand, no
subspace of dimension $s-1$ can map onto $W$, because
$\dim\wedge^2\mathbb F_p^{s-1}=\binom{s-1}{2}<r_2$.
Indeed, any smaller such subspace could be enlarged to dimension
$s-1$.  The map's minimum generating dimension is therefore exactly
$s$.
Hence
\[
 p^{N_p(r_1,r_2,s)}\ge \frac14p^{r_2\binom{r_1}{2}},
\]
while the ambient count gives the reverse upper bound
$p^{N_p(r_1,r_2,s)}\le p^{r_2\binom{r_1}{2}}$.
Taking base-$p$ logarithms completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:relative-graded}
Let $L=\bigoplus_{i\ge1}L_i$ be a graded abelian group and let
$C_{\mathrm{core}}\le L_1$.  For $\nu\in\{0,1\}$, let
$[-,-]_\nu$ be a graded Lie bracket on $L$ satisfying
\[
 L_2=\bigl\langle[u,v]_\nu:u,v\in C_{\mathrm{core}}\bigr\rangle,
 \qquad
 L_{i+1}=[L_i,C_{\mathrm{core}}]_\nu\quad(i\ge2).
\]
We have the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If the two brackets agree on
$L_1\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$ and
$L_2\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$, then they agree on
$L_2\times L_1$.
\item More generally, if they agree on
$L_i\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$ for every $i\ge1$, then they agree on
$L_a\times L_b$ whenever $\max\{a,b\}\ge2$.
\item If, in addition to the hypothesis of~\textup{(ii)}, they agree
on $L_1\times L_1$, then they agree on $L\times L$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For~\textup{(i)}, let $w\in L_2$ and $x\in L_1$.  By
the generation hypothesis, and because the two brackets agree on
$L_1\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$, we may choose
$u_\alpha,v_\alpha\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$ such that $w=\sum_\alpha[u_\alpha,v_\alpha]_0
  =\sum_\alpha[u_\alpha,v_\alpha]_1$.
For each $\nu\in\{0,1\}$, the Jacobi
identity~\eqref{p12:eq:graded-jacobi-explicit} gives
\[
 [[u_\alpha,v_\alpha]_\nu,x]_\nu
 =-[[v_\alpha,x]_\nu,u_\alpha]_\nu
  -[[x,u_\alpha]_\nu,v_\alpha]_\nu.
\]
The inner brackets on the right are equal for $\nu=0,1$ by the first
common restriction, using alternation, and the outer brackets are equal because the two brackets also agree on $L_2\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$.  Hence
$[w,x]_0=[w,x]_1$, proving~\textup{(i)}.

We follow the induction of
\cite[Lemma~20.13]{BNV} to prove~\textup{(ii)}.  The hypothesis and additivity imply that
the two brackets agree on $L\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$.  We prove by
induction on $j\ge2$ that they agree on $L\times L_j$.  For $j=2$,
let $y\in L_2$ and choose a common core-commutator decomposition of
$y$ as above.  If $x\in L_i$, the same Jacobi calculation uses only
the common restrictions on $L_i\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$ and
$L_{i+1}\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$, so $[x,y]_0=[x,y]_1$.

Now let $j\ge3$ and assume the conclusion for $L\times L_{j-1}$.
The common restriction on $L_{j-1}\times C_{\mathrm{core}}$ and the
generation hypothesis give a common expression
\[
 y=\sum_\alpha[z_\alpha,u_\alpha]_0
  =\sum_\alpha[z_\alpha,u_\alpha]_1,
 \qquad z_\alpha\in L_{j-1},\quad
 u_\alpha\in C_{\mathrm{core}},
\]
and, for $\nu\in\{0,1\}$, the Jacobi identity
\eqref{p12:eq:graded-jacobi-explicit} gives
\[
 [x,[z_\alpha,u_\alpha]_\nu]_\nu
 =[[x,z_\alpha]_\nu,u_\alpha]_\nu
  -[[x,u_\alpha]_\nu,z_\alpha]_\nu.
\]
The first term on the right is equal for $\nu=0,1$ by induction and
then the common core restriction.  The second is equal first by the
common core restriction and then by induction.  Thus the two
brackets agree on $L\times L_j$.  Alternation gives agreement when
the higher-layer input occurs first, proving~\textup{(ii)}.  The only
remaining domain is $L_1\times L_1$, so~\textup{(iii)} follows.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:core_map_fix_breadth}
  Fix a breadth sequence $\mathbf b=(b_i)_{i=2}^{c}$. The number of possible core bracket maps $L_i\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_{i+1}$ for $2\le i\le c-1$ is at most
  $p^{\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}s b_i(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)}$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Fix $2\le i\le c-1$ and a chosen core generator
$u_k=\bar g_{1,k}=g_{1,k}G_2$, where $k\in[s]$.  The slice
$\operatorname{ad}(u_k):L_i\to L_{i+1}$ has image of order at most $p^{b_i}$.
Since $b_i\le s_{i+1}$, a subgroup chain in the finite abelian
$p$-group $L_{i+1}$ extends this image to a subgroup of order exactly
$p^{b_i}$.  By \cref{p12:lem:universal-field}\textup{(iii)}
(cf.~\cite[Lemma~20.15]{BNV}), there are at most
$p^{b_i(s_{i+1}-b_i+1)}$ choices for such a subgroup.  Once it is
chosen, the images of the $r_i$ chosen generators of $L_i$ have at
most $p^{b_i r_i}$ possibilities.  Thus the $u_k$-slice has at most
$p^{b_i(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)}$ possibilities.  The $s$ core generators
determine the whole core bracket map by additivity in the second
variable.  Applying these bounds over all $k\in[s]$ and
$2\le i\le c-1$
gives at most
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:core-bracket-count}
 p^{\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}s b_i(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)}
\end{equation}
possible families of higher core bracket maps.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:count_leading_maps}
Work in a fixed Sims fibre with $c\ge3$, and fix a core bracket map
$L_2\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_3$ with breadth $b_2$ as in
\eqref{p12:eq:core-breadth}. Among valid completions inducing this core
bracket map, the number of possible restrictions
$L_1\times L_1\to L_2$ of the associated graded Lie bracket is at most
\[
 p^{\binom{r_1}{2}s_2-\binom{r_1-s}{2}b_2}.
\]
Here $r_1=d(L_1)$, $s_2=\log_p|L_2|$, and
$C_{\mathrm{core}}=\langle\bar g_{1,1},\ldots,\bar g_{1,s}\rangle$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We first count the restrictions $L_1\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_2$.
It suffices to choose the values on generator pairs
$(\bar g_{1,j},\bar g_{1,k})$ with $1\le j<k\le r_1$ and $j\le s$.
There are $\binom{r_1}{2}-\binom{r_1-s}{2}$ such pairs, and each
value has at most $|L_2|=p^{s_2}$ choices. These values determine the restriction
$L_1\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_2$ by alternation and additivity.

Fix one such restriction arising from a valid completion.
Together with the fixed map $L_2\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_3$,
it determines $L_2\times L_1\to L_3$ by
\cref{p12:lem:relative-graded}\textup{(i)}.
It remains to choose the values on
$(\bar g_{1,j},\bar g_{1,k})$ with $s<j<k\le r_1$;
we call these \emph{outside--outside} pairs.
Choose a maximizing element $h_2^\ast\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$ as in
\eqref{p12:eq:core-breadth}. For each outside--outside pair, the Jacobi
identity~\eqref{p12:eq:graded-jacobi-explicit} gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:elementary-jacobi-model}
 \operatorname{ad}(h_2^\ast)([\bar g_{1,j},\bar g_{1,k}]_L)
 =-[[\bar g_{1,k},h_2^\ast]_L,\bar g_{1,j}]_L-[[h_2^\ast,\bar g_{1,j}]_L,\bar g_{1,k}]_L.
\end{equation}
The inner brackets on the right are fixed by
$L_1\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_2$, and the outer brackets are
fixed by $L_2\times L_1\to L_3$. Thus the right-hand side is fixed.
When nonempty, the set of attainable values of
$[\bar g_{1,j},\bar g_{1,k}]_L$ is therefore contained in a single
coset of $\ker\operatorname{ad}(h_2^\ast)$. By~\eqref{p12:eq:adjoint-kernel-size},
each outside--outside pair has at most $p^{s_2-b_2}$ possible values.
Multiplying this conditional bound over the $\binom{r_1-s}{2}$
outside--outside pairs and then by the number of core restrictions
gives at most
\[
 p^{(\binom{r_1}{2}-\binom{r_1-s}{2})s_2}
 p^{\binom{r_1-s}{2}(s_2-b_2)}
 =p^{\binom{r_1}{2}s_2-\binom{r_1-s}{2}b_2}
\]
possible restrictions $L_1\times L_1\to L_2$.
Further compatibility conditions can only reduce this count.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:total-relation-bound}
Work in a fixed Sims fibre for groups of order $p^m$ with nilpotency
class $c$ and Sims rank $s$, and fix a breadth sequence
$\mathbf b=(b_i)_{i=2}^{c}$ that occurs for a valid completion.  
             
    
                    
                                         
                             
                       
    
          
                                                        
    
                                             
                       
    
     
    
                                           
         
                                                    
    
Then the base-$p$ logarithm of the number of valid completions in the
fibre having breadth sequence $\mathbf b$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:total-relation-bound}
 \binom{r_1}{2}m_{\mathrm{deep}}+sT_{\mathrm{core}}
 +\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}b_i
  \left(s(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)-\binom{r_1-s}{2}\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}
Let $G^{(0)}$ and $G^{(1)}$ be the groups specified by two valid
completions in the same fixed Sims fibre, with Sims generators
$g_{h,a}^{(0)}$ and $g_{h,a}^{(1)}$, respectively.
Fix $\xi\in[c-1]$ and assume that the commutators of every pair of
corresponding Sims generators agree below excess $\xi$: for
$h_1,h_2\in[c]$,
$a\in[r_{h_1}]$, $b\in[r_{h_2}]$, and $0\le e<\xi$ with
$h_1+h_2+e\le c$, $\pi_{h_1+h_2+e}([g_{h_1,a}^{(0)},g_{h_2,b}^{(0)}])
 =\pi_{h_1+h_2+e}([g_{h_1,a}^{(1)},g_{h_2,b}^{(1)}])$.
\medskip

For any $k,u$ with $1\le k\le u\le c$ and $u\le k+\xi$,
the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
 \item There is a unique coordinate-preserving isomorphism $\varphi_{k,u}:G_k^{(0)}/G_{u+1}^{(0)}
  \rightarrow G_k^{(1)}/G_{u+1}^{(1)}$.
 Explicitly, for any integer exponents $0\le e(t,v)<p^{a(t,v)}$ with
 $k\le t\le u$ and $v\in[r_t]$,
 \begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:varphi_action}
  \varphi_{k,u}\left(
    \left(\prod_{t=k}^{u}\prod_{v=1}^{r_t}
      (g_{t,v}^{(0)})^{e(t,v)}\right)G_{u+1}^{(0)}\right)
  =\left(\prod_{t=k}^{u}\prod_{v=1}^{r_t}
      (g_{t,v}^{(1)})^{e(t,v)}\right)G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
 \end{equation}
                                                                
                                                                
                                                                

 \item For any $t\in[c]$, $v\in[r_t]$, and elements
 $g^{(0)}\in G_k^{(0)}$ and $g^{(1)}\in G_k^{(1)}$, suppose that
 \[
  \varphi_{k,u}\bigl(g^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
  =g^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
 \]
 Then
 \begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:sims-conjugation-compatibility}
  \varphi_{k,u}\bigl((g_{t,v}^{(0)})^{-1}g^{(0)}g_{t,v}^{(0)}
  G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
  =(g_{t,v}^{(1)})^{-1}g^{(1)}g_{t,v}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
 \end{equation}
                                                                   
                                                              
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix $k,u$ in the stated range. Throughout this proof, we suppress the indices $k,u$ and write
$\varphi$ for the map being constructed.

We first prove \textup{(i)}. Recall that
if $g\in G_k^{(\nu)}$, $\nu=0,1$, has numerical coordinates
$0\le e(t,v)<p^{a(t,v)}$ as in~\eqref{p12:eq:sims_normal_form}, then the coset $gG_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$ has a unique
Sims normal form
\[
  gG_{u+1}^{(\nu)}=\left(\prod_{t=k}^{u}\prod_{v=1}^{r_t}(g_{t,v}^{(\nu)})^{e(t,v)}\right)G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}.
\]
     
                                                      
                                                                  
                                                            
                                                            
                
For $h_1,h_2\ge k$, $a\in[r_{h_1}]$, $b\in[r_{h_2}]$, and
$h_1+h_2\le t\le u$, we have $\pi_t([g_{h_1,a}^{(0)},g_{h_2,b}^{(0)}])
 =\pi_t([g_{h_1,a}^{(1)},g_{h_2,b}^{(1)}])$ since $0\le t-h_1-h_2\le u-2k\le\xi-k<\xi$.

We construct $\varphi=\varphi_{k,u}$ by adding the generator cosets in decreasing
weight $h=u,\ldots,k$ and, within each weight, in increasing second
index $j=1,\ldots,r_h$.
Before adding $g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$, the cosets
already added generate 
\[
 K^{(\nu)}
 =\bigl\langle
 g_{t,v}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}:h<t\le u,\ v\in[r_t];\
 g_{h,v}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}:1\le v<j
 \bigr\rangle.
\]
Initially $h=u$, $j=1$, and both $K^{(0)}$ and $K^{(1)}$ are trivial.
Suppose that an isomorphism $\varphi:K^{(0)}\to K^{(1)}$
already sends every previously added generator coset to its
 counterpart as in~\eqref{p12:eq:varphi_action}. We extend it to an
 isomorphism
 \[
  \left\langle K^{(0)},g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\right\rangle
  \longrightarrow
  \left\langle K^{(1)},g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}\right\rangle.
 \]

Note that all generators of $G_{h+1}^{(\nu)}/G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$
have already been added, and all generators of $K^{(\nu)}$
have weight at least $h$. Hence
\[
 [K^{(\nu)},g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}]
 \le G_{h+1}^{(\nu)}/G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}
 \le K^{(\nu)}.
\]
Thus conjugation by $g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$ maps
$K^{(\nu)}$ injectively into itself. Since $K^{(\nu)}$ is finite, its
image equals $K^{(\nu)}$, so $K^{(\nu)}$ is normal in
$\langle K^{(\nu)},g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}\rangle$ for $\nu=0,1$.
By item~\textup{(d)} of Section~\ref{p12:sec:sims-counting-strategy},
$p^{a(h,j)}$ is the exact order of $g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$
modulo $K^{(\nu)}$. Consequently,
\[
 \langle K^{(\nu)},g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}\rangle
 =\bigsqcup_{e=0}^{p^{a(h,j)}-1}
       (g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^eK^{(\nu)}.
\]
Every element therefore has a unique expression
$(g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^e z$, with
$0\le e<p^{a(h,j)}$ and $z\in K^{(\nu)}$.

Meanwhile, the fixed power word~\eqref{p12:eq:power_word_normal_form} gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:power_coset}
  (g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{p^{a(h,j)}}
  =\left(\prod_{v=1}^{j-1}
       (g_{h,v}^{(\nu)})^{b(h,j,h,v)}\right)
   \left(\prod_{t=h+1}^{u}\prod_{v=1}^{r_t}
       (g_{t,v}^{(\nu)})^{b(h,j,t,v)}\right)G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}
       \in K^{(\nu)}.
\end{equation}
All generator cosets on the right have already been added, and
the coefficients $b$ are the same in both completions. Hence
\[
 \varphi\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^{p^{a(h,j)}}\bigr)
 =(g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^{p^{a(h,j)}}.
\]

For conjugation, let $g_{t,\ell}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$
be a generator of $K^{(\nu)}$ already added.
If $t+h>u$, the coset of $[g_{t,\ell}^{(\nu)},g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}]$
is trivial. Otherwise, write its Sims normal form as
\[
 [g_{t,\ell}^{(\nu)},g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}]G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}
 =\left(\prod_{w=t+h}^{u}\prod_{v=1}^{r_w}
       (g_{w,v}^{(\nu)})^{e^{(\nu)}(w,v)}\right)G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}.
\]
The commutator components agree through weight $u$, so uniqueness
of the numerical coordinates gives $e^{(0)}(w,v)=e^{(1)}(w,v)$.
Since $w\ge t+h>h$, every generator coset in this word has
already been added. Because these coordinates agree, the induction
hypothesis for the already constructed map gives, in either case,
\[
 \varphi\bigl([g_{t,\ell}^{(0)},g_{h,j}^{(0)}]G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =[g_{t,\ell}^{(1)},g_{h,j}^{(1)}]G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]
Using $g^{-1}hg=h[h,g]$, we obtain
\[
\varphi\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)})^{-1}g_{t,\ell}^{(0)}g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)=\varphi\bigl(g_{t,\ell}^{(0)}[g_{t,\ell}^{(0)},g_{h,j}^{(0)}]G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)=(g_{h,j}^{(1)})^{-1}g_{t,\ell}^{(1)}g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)},
\]
where the homomorphism property of $\varphi$ applies because the
generator coset and the commutator coset both belong to $K^{(0)}$.
The two conjugation maps are homomorphisms and agree on every
generating coset of $K^{(0)}$. Hence, for any $z\in K^{(0)}$,
\[
 \varphi\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^{-1}
       z(g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})\bigr)
 =(g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^{-1}
       \varphi(z)(g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}).
\]
Iterating this identity gives, for $z\in K^{(0)}$ and any integer
$e_2\ge0$,
\[
 \varphi\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^{-e_2}
       z(g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^{e_2}\bigr)
 =(g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^{-e_2}
       \varphi(z)(g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^{e_2}.
\]

Define the extension by
\[
 \widehat\varphi\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^e z\bigr)
 =(g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^e\varphi(z)
\]
for any $z\in K^{(0)}$ and $0\le e<p^{a(h,j)}$.
The unique expressions of elements in $\langle K^{(\nu)},g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}\rangle$ show that $\widehat\varphi$ is well defined
and bijective. Taking $e=0$ shows that it extends $\varphi$;
taking $e=1$, $z=1$ shows that it sends the new generator coset
to its counterpart.

It remains to verify that $\widehat\varphi$ preserves multiplication. Choose
$0\le e_1,e_2<p^{a(h,j)}$ and $z_1^{(0)},z_2^{(0)}\in K^{(0)}$,
and denote $z_a^{(1)}=\varphi(z_a^{(0)})\in K^{(1)}$ for $a=1,2$.
Write $e_1+e_2=dp^{a(h,j)}+e$, where $0\le e<p^{a(h,j)}$.
For $\nu=0,1$,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:multiplication_hat_varphi}
 \begin{split}
 &\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{e_1}z_1^{(\nu)}\bigr)
  \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{e_2}z_2^{(\nu)}\bigr)\\
 ={}&(g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{e_1+e_2}
       \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{-e_2}
             z_1^{(\nu)}(g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{e_2}\bigr)z_2^{(\nu)}\\
 ={}&(g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^e
       \Bigl((g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{dp^{a(h,j)}}
       \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{-e_2}
             z_1^{(\nu)}(g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{e_2}\bigr)z_2^{(\nu)}\Bigr).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Note that 
\[
  (g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{dp^{a(h,j)}}
       \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{-e_2}
             z_1^{(\nu)}(g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)})^{e_2}\bigr)z_2^{(\nu)}\in K^{(\nu)},
\]
since the power term is in $K^{(\nu)}$ by~\eqref{p12:eq:power_coset} and conjugation by $g_{h,j}^{(\nu)}G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$ preserves $K^{(\nu)}$.
Meanwhile, $\varphi$ sends the displayed $\nu=0$ element to its
$\nu=1$ counterpart. Applying the definition of
$\widehat\varphi$ therefore gives
\[
\widehat\varphi\Bigl(
       \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^{e_1}z_1^{(0)}\bigr)
       \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)})^{e_2}z_2^{(0)}\bigr)\Bigr)=\bigl((g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^{e_1}z_1^{(1)}\bigr)
        \bigl((g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)})^{e_2}z_2^{(1)}\bigr).
\]
Thus, $\widehat\varphi$ is an isomorphism from
$\langle K^{(0)},g_{h,j}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\rangle$ to
$\langle K^{(1)},g_{h,j}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}\rangle$. After all
generator cosets of weights $k,\ldots,u$ have been added,
the resulting subgroups are
$G_k^{(\nu)}/G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$. Hence the constructed map is an
isomorphism $\varphi_{k,u}$ between the required quotients. It sends
each generator coset to its counterpart, so applying it to the unique
Sims normal form gives~\eqref{p12:eq:varphi_action}. Conversely,
\eqref{p12:eq:varphi_action} determines the map on every coset and hence
proves uniqueness. This proves~\textup{(i)}.

To prove \textup{(ii)}, fix $t\in[c]$ and $v\in[r_t]$.
Both $G_k^{(\nu)}$ and $G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$ are normal in $G^{(\nu)}$,
so conjugation by $g_{t,v}^{(\nu)}$ induces an automorphism of
$G_k^{(\nu)}/G_{u+1}^{(\nu)}$.
It is enough to show that applying $\varphi$ after conjugation in the
first quotient agrees on every generating coset with applying
conjugation after $\varphi$ in the second quotient.

Let $k\le h\le u$ and $j\in[r_h]$. If $h+t>u$, then the coset of
$[g_{h,j}^{(\nu)},g_{t,v}^{(\nu)}]$ is trivial. If $h+t\le u$, then
for $h+t\le\ell\le u$, $0\le\ell-h-t\le u-k-1<\xi$.
The hypothesis therefore gives equality of all components of the two
commutators through weight $u$. Hence, in either case,
coordinate preservation in~\textup{(i)} gives
\[
 \varphi\bigl([g_{h,j}^{(0)},g_{t,v}^{(0)}]G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =[g_{h,j}^{(1)},g_{t,v}^{(1)}]G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]
Since $g^{-1}hg=h[h,g]$ and $\varphi$ sends each generating coset
to its counterpart, it follows that
\[
\varphi\bigl((g_{t,v}^{(0)})^{-1}g_{h,j}^{(0)}
                 g_{t,v}^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)=(g_{t,v}^{(1)})^{-1}g_{h,j}^{(1)}
                 g_{t,v}^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]
The two compositions are homomorphisms and agree on every generating
coset, so they agree on the whole quotient. This proves
\eqref{p12:eq:sims-conjugation-compatibility}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{p12:cor:sims_collection_multiplication_inverse}
Let $G^{(0)}$, $G^{(1)}$ and $\xi\in[c-1]$ satisfy the hypotheses
of~\cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}; in particular, the commutators
of corresponding Sims generators agree below excess $\xi$.
For $i\in[c]$, $a=1,2$ and $\nu\in\{0,1\}$, let
$g_a^{(\nu)}\in G_i^{(\nu)}$. Suppose that each pair
$(g_a^{(0)},g_a^{(1)})$ is matched below excess $\xi$ in degree $i$.
                                                                                       
                               
Then the componentwise product and inverse pairs, respectively,
\[
 \bigl(g_1^{(0)}g_2^{(0)},g_1^{(1)}g_2^{(1)}\bigr)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \bigl((g_1^{(0)})^{-1},(g_1^{(1)})^{-1}\bigr),
\]
are matched below excess $\xi$ in degree $i$. More precisely,
\[
 \pi_u(g_1^{(0)}g_2^{(0)})=\pi_u(g_1^{(1)}g_2^{(1)}),\qquad
 \pi_u((g_1^{(0)})^{-1})=\pi_u((g_1^{(1)})^{-1})
\]
for any $i\le u\le c$ with $u<i+\xi$. Moreover, when $i+\xi\le c$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \partial_{i,\xi}\bigl(g_1^{(0)}g_2^{(0)},g_1^{(1)}g_2^{(1)}\bigr)
 &=\partial_{i,\xi}\bigl(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)}\bigr)
     +\partial_{i,\xi}\bigl(g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)}\bigr),\\
 \partial_{i,\xi}\bigl((g_1^{(0)})^{-1},(g_1^{(1)})^{-1}\bigr)
 &=-\partial_{i,\xi}\bigl(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Fix $i\in[c]$.  We prove that the product
and inverse pairs are matched below excess $\xi$.
Fix $u$ with $i\le u\le c$ and $u<i+\xi$.
\Cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}\textup{(i)} gives an isomorphism
$\varphi_{i,u}:G_i^{(0)}/G_{u+1}^{(0)}\to
 G_i^{(1)}/G_{u+1}^{(1)}$
that preserves numerical coordinates as in~\eqref{p12:eq:varphi_action}.

The layer matching assumption gives agreement through
weight $u$, so
\[
 \varphi_{i,u}\bigl(g_a^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =g_a^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}
 \qquad(a=1,2).
\]
Since $\varphi_{i,u}$ preserves products and inverses, we have
\[
 \varphi_{i,u}\bigl(g_1^{(0)}g_2^{(0)}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =g_1^{(1)}g_2^{(1)}G_{u+1}^{(1)}~\text{and}~
 \varphi_{i,u}\bigl((g_1^{(0)})^{-1}G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =(g_1^{(1)})^{-1}G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]
By coordinate preservation of $\varphi_{i,u}$, the product and inverse pairs agree
in their $L_u$-components for every $i\le u\le c$ with $u<i+\xi$.

Suppose $i+\xi\le c$. We compute the first differences of the product and inverse pairs
at weight $i+\xi$. Applying~\cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}\textup{(i)}
at this cutoff gives an isomorphism
$\varphi_{i,i+\xi}:G_i^{(0)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(0)}\to
 G_i^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$ that again preserves numerical coordinates.

For $a=1,2$, define the following elements of
$G_i^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$:
\[
 h_a:=\varphi_{i,i+\xi}\bigl(g_a^{(0)}G_{i+\xi+1}^{(0)}\bigr),
 \qquad
 z_a:=h_a^{-1}\bigl(g_a^{(1)}G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}\bigr).
\]
By~\eqref{p12:eq:varphi_action}, $h_a$ is the coset of the corresponding
Sims word in~\eqref{p12:eq:matched-sims-word-decomposition}.
The preceding remainder argument with $k=i$ gives
$z_a\in G_{i+\xi}^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$.
Canceling the common Sims prefix below weight $i+\xi$ leaves
only the quotient of their weight-$(i+\xi)$ blocks, which may differ.

Under the identification of
$G_{i+\xi}^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$ with the additive group
$L_{i+\xi}$, the image of $z_a$ is
\[
 \pi_{i+\xi}(g_a^{(1)})-\pi_{i+\xi}(g_a^{(0)})
 =\partial_{i,\xi}\bigl(g_a^{(0)},g_a^{(1)}\bigr).
\]

Note that $G_{i+\xi}^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$ is central in $G_{i}^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$, since
$[G_{i+\xi}^{(1)},G^{(1)}]\le G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$. Thus products of elements in $G_{i+\xi}^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$ and $G_{i}^{(1)}/G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}$ commute.
We obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 g_1^{(1)}g_2^{(1)}G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}&=h_1z_1h_2z_2
  =h_1h_2z_1z_2=\varphi_{i,i+\xi}(g_1^{(0)}g_2^{(0)}G_{i+\xi+1}^{(0)})z_1z_2,\\
 (g_1^{(1)})^{-1}G_{i+\xi+1}^{(1)}
 &=h_1^{-1}z_1^{-1}=\varphi_{i,i+\xi}((g_1^{(0)})^{-1}G_{i+\xi+1}^{(0)})z_1^{-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The factors $z_1z_2$ and $z_1^{-1}$ change only the weight-$(i+\xi)$
component of the product and the inverse, respectively. Under the
additive identification with $L_{i+\xi}$, the images of $z_1z_2$ and
$z_1^{-1}$ are, respectively, the sum of the images of $z_1,z_2$ and
the negative of the image of $z_1$. Substituting these identified
images proves
the two identities for $\partial_{i,\xi}$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:collection-monotonicity}
Let $G^{(0)}$, $G^{(1)}$ and $\xi\in[c-1]$ satisfy the hypotheses
of~\cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}; in particular, the commutators
of corresponding Sims generators agree below excess $\xi$.
For any $i,j\in[c]$, let $g_1^{(\nu)}\in G_i^{(\nu)}$
and $g_2^{(\nu)}\in G_j^{(\nu)}$ for $\nu=0,1$.
Suppose that $(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)})$ is matched below excess $\xi$
in degree $i$ and $(g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)})$ is matched below excess
$\xi$ in degree $j$.
                                               
                                   
                                               
                               
Then, when $i+j\le c$,
$\bigl([g_1^{(0)},g_2^{(0)}],[g_1^{(1)},g_2^{(1)}]\bigr)$ is matched below excess
$\xi$ in degree $i+j$. More precisely,
\[
 \pi_u([g_1^{(0)},g_2^{(0)}])
 =\pi_u([g_1^{(1)},g_2^{(1)}])
\]
for any $i+j\le u\le c$ with $u<i+j+\xi$. If $i+j>c$, then $[g_1^{(\nu)},g_2^{(\nu)}]=1$ for $\nu=0,1$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If $i+j>c$, then
$[g_1^{(\nu)},g_2^{(\nu)}]\in G_{i+j}^{(\nu)}=1$ for $\nu=0,1$.
Suppose that $i+j\le c$.
                                                                
                                                                
                                                                
                                                         


Apply~\eqref{p12:eq:matched-sims-word-decomposition} first to $(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)})$ with
$k=i$, and then to $(g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)})$ with $k=j$.
Denote the corresponding Sims words by $w_a^{(\nu)}$ and the
remainders by $z_a$ as in~\eqref{p12:eq:matched-sims-word-decomposition}, so
that $g_a^{(0)}=w_a^{(0)}$ and $g_a^{(1)}=w_a^{(1)}z_a$ for $a=1,2$.
Here $w_a^{(0)}$ and $w_a^{(1)}$ use the same generator labels
and numerical coordinates, namely those of $g_a^{(0)}$.

Fix a required weight $u$, so $i+j\le u\le c$ and $u<i+j+\xi$.
Since $z_1\in G_{i+\xi}^{(1)}$ and $z_2\in G_{j+\xi}^{(1)}$, we have 
$[z_1,G_j^{(1)}]\le G_{i+j+\xi}^{(1)}\le G_{u+1}^{(1)}$ and $[G_i^{(1)},z_2]\le G_{i+j+\xi}^{(1)}\le G_{u+1}^{(1)}$.
Thus, modulo $G_{u+1}^{(1)}$, $z_1$ commutes with every element
of $G_j^{(1)}$, and $z_2$ commutes with every element of
$G_i^{(1)}$.  Consequently,
\[
 [g_1^{(1)},g_2^{(1)}]G_{u+1}^{(1)}
 =[w_1^{(1)}z_1,w_2^{(1)}z_2]G_{u+1}^{(1)}
 =[w_1^{(1)},w_2^{(1)}]G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]

Now, it remains to compare $[w_1^{(0)},w_2^{(0)}]$ and
$[w_1^{(1)},w_2^{(1)}]$ through weight $u$.
Expand each positive power in $w_1^{(\nu)}$ and $w_2^{(\nu)}$
into individual generator factors, for $\nu=0,1$.  Apply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [g_1g_2,g_3]=g_2^{-1}[g_1,g_3]g_2\,[g_2,g_3],~\text{and}~[g_1,g_2g_3]=[g_1,g_3]g_3^{-1}[g_1,g_2]g_3
 \end{aligned}
\]
in the same order in both completions. Then $[w_1^{(0)},w_2^{(0)}]$ and
$[w_1^{(1)},w_2^{(1)}]$ are each written as a product of conjugates of generator commutators.
The conjugating words use the same generator labels in the same order in both completions.
We therefore only need to compare the generator commutators and
preserve this comparison under conjugation and multiplication.

For this fixed $u$, apply~\cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}\textup{(i)}
with $k=i+j$
to obtain a coordinate-preserving isomorphism
$\varphi_{i+j,u}:G_{i+j}^{(0)}/G_{u+1}^{(0)}\to
G_{i+j}^{(1)}/G_{u+1}^{(1)}$.
For $h_1\ge i$, $h_2\ge j$ and indices
$a\in[r_{h_1}]$, $b\in[r_{h_2}]$, whenever $h_1+h_2\le t\le u$,
we have
$0\le t-h_1-h_2\le u-i-j<\xi$.
The components below weight $h_1+h_2$ vanish.
The generator-commutator hypothesis and coordinate preservation give
\[
 \varphi_{i+j,u}\bigl([g_{h_1,a}^{(0)},g_{h_2,b}^{(0)}]
                       G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =[g_{h_1,a}^{(1)},g_{h_2,b}^{(1)}]G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]
If $h_1+h_2>u$, both commutator cosets are trivial, so the same
equality holds.

By~\cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}\textup{(ii)},
$\varphi_{i+j,u}$ respects
conjugation by corresponding Sims generators, including those
of weight below $i+j$, and hence by the corresponding words
in the expansion.  It therefore carries each conjugated
generator commutator to its counterpart.  Preservation of
products gives
\[
 \varphi_{i+j,u}\bigl([w_1^{(0)},w_2^{(0)}]G_{u+1}^{(0)}\bigr)
 =[w_1^{(1)},w_2^{(1)}]G_{u+1}^{(1)}.
\]
Coordinate preservation and the removal of the remainders now give
\[
 \pi_u([g_1^{(0)},g_2^{(0)}])=\pi_u([g_1^{(1)},g_2^{(1)}])
\]
for any $u$ with $i+j\le u\le c$ and $u<i+j+\xi$, which proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:sims-lift-comparison}
Assume the hypotheses of \cref{p12:prop:collection-monotonicity} and
use the matched-pair subgroups $\mathcal F_i$ defined above.
For $1\le i\le c-\xi$, there is an isomorphism of abelian groups
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:comparison-graded-identification}
 \mathcal F_i/\mathcal F_{i+1}\cong L_i\oplus L_{i+\xi},
\end{equation}
which sends the class of $(g^{(0)},g^{(1)})$ to
$\bigl(\pi_i(g^{(0)}),\partial_{i,\xi}(g^{(0)},g^{(1)})\bigr)$.

For $1\le i,j\le c$ with $i+j+\xi\le c$, let
$(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)})\in\mathcal F_i$ and
$(g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)})\in\mathcal F_j$. Denote
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:defxyalphaeta}
\begin{aligned}
 x&=\pi_i(g_1^{(0)})=\pi_i(g_1^{(1)}),
 &\alpha&=\partial_{i,\xi}(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)}),\\
 y&=\pi_j(g_2^{(0)})=\pi_j(g_2^{(1)}),
 &\eta&=\partial_{j,\xi}(g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)}).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Then
\[
\partial_{i+j,\xi}\bigl([g_1^{(0)},g_2^{(0)}],
                           [g_1^{(1)},g_2^{(1)}]\bigr)=
 \delta_\xi(x,y)+[x,\eta]_L+[\alpha,y]_L.
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For $1\le i\le c-\xi$, the restriction of $\pi_i$ to $G_i^{(0)}$
is the quotient homomorphism to $L_i$, and
$\partial_{i,\xi}$ is a homomorphism by
\cref{p12:cor:sims_collection_multiplication_inverse}.
Define
\[
 \Psi_i:\mathcal F_i\longrightarrow L_i\oplus L_{i+\xi},
 \qquad
 \Psi_i\bigl(g^{(0)},g^{(1)}\bigr)
 :=\bigl(\pi_i(g^{(0)}),
          \partial_{i,\xi}(g^{(0)},g^{(1)})\bigr).
\]
If a pair $(g^{(0)},g^{(1)})\in\mathcal F_i$ lies in
$\ker\Psi_i$, then $\pi_i(g^{(0)})=0$, so
$g^{(0)}\in G_{i+1}^{(0)}$.  Since the pair is matched at weight
$i$, also $\pi_i(g^{(1)})=0$, and hence
$g^{(1)}\in G_{i+1}^{(1)}$.  The pair already agrees at every
weight $t$ with $i<t<i+\xi$, while
$\partial_{i,\xi}(g^{(0)},g^{(1)})=0$ adds agreement at weight
$i+\xi$.  It therefore belongs to $\mathcal F_{i+1}$.
Conversely, every pair in $\mathcal F_{i+1}$ has zero weight-$i$
components and agrees at weight $i+\xi$, so it lies in
$\ker\Psi_i$. Thus $\ker\Psi_i=\mathcal F_{i+1}$.

The map $\Psi_i$ is also surjective. Indeed, for $x\in L_i$ and
$\alpha\in L_{i+\xi}$, the pairs
$(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})$ and
$(1,\widetilde\alpha^{(1)})$ belong to $\mathcal F_i$. Since
$\Psi_i$ is a homomorphism, their product has image $(x,\alpha)$.
The first isomorphism theorem now proves
\eqref{p12:eq:comparison-graded-identification}.

Since $i+j+\xi\le c$, the identification
\eqref{p12:eq:comparison-graded-identification} applies in degrees $i$,
$j$ and $i+j$.  The two input classes satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:decomposition_g1_g2}
\begin{aligned}
 (g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1}
 &=(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})
   (1,\widetilde\alpha^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},\\
 (g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}
 &=(\widetilde y^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(1)})
   (1,\widetilde\eta^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
because the two sides have the same images under
\eqref{p12:eq:comparison-graded-identification}.

Under~\eqref{p12:eq:comparison-graded-identification} in degree $i+j$,
the first difference on the left-hand side of the asserted formula is
the second component of the bracket class below. By biadditivity of
$[\cdot,\cdot]_{\mathcal F}$ and~\eqref{p12:eq:decomposition_g1_g2},
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl[(g_1^{(0)},g_1^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
       (g_2^{(0)},g_2^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}\\
={}&\bigl[(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
          (\widetilde y^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}+\bigl[(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
          (1,\widetilde\eta^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}\\
 &+\bigl[(1,\widetilde\alpha^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
          (\widetilde y^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}+\bigl[(1,\widetilde\alpha^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
          (1,\widetilde\eta^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}.
\end{aligned}
\]

By the definition of $[\cdot,\cdot]_{\mathcal F}$, we have 
\[
 \bigl[(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
          (\widetilde y^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}=\bigl([\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(0)}],
       [\widetilde x^{(1)},\widetilde y^{(1)}]\bigr)
 \mathcal F_{i+j+1},
\]
whose second component in $L_{i+j}\oplus L_{i+j+\xi}$ is
\[
\partial_{i+j,\xi}
 \bigl([\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(0)}],
       [\widetilde x^{(1)},\widetilde y^{(1)}]\bigr)
 =
 \pi_{i+j+\xi}\bigl([\widetilde x^{(1)},\widetilde y^{(1)}]\bigr)
 -\pi_{i+j+\xi}\bigl([\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(0)}]\bigr).
\]

Meanwhile, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \bigl[(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
          (1,\widetilde\eta^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}
          &=\bigl(1,[\widetilde x^{(1)},\widetilde\eta^{(1)}]\bigr)\mathcal F_{i+j+1}\\
          \bigl[(1,\widetilde\alpha^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
                    (\widetilde y^{(0)},\widetilde y^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}
                    &=\bigl(1,[\widetilde\alpha^{(1)},\widetilde y^{(1)}]\bigr)\mathcal F_{i+j+1}, 
\end{aligned}
\]
whose second components in $L_{i+j}\oplus L_{i+j+\xi}$ are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \partial_{i+j,\xi}\bigl(1,[\widetilde x^{(1)},\widetilde\eta^{(1)}]\bigr)
 &=\pi_{i+j+\xi}\bigl([\widetilde x^{(1)},\widetilde\eta^{(1)}]\bigr)
   =[x,\eta]_L,~\text{and}\\
 \partial_{i+j,\xi}\bigl(1,[\widetilde\alpha^{(1)},\widetilde y^{(1)}]\bigr)
 &=\pi_{i+j+\xi}\bigl([\widetilde\alpha^{(1)},\widetilde y^{(1)}]\bigr)
   =[\alpha,y]_L,
\end{aligned}
\]
respectively. 

Finally,
\[
 \bigl[(1,\widetilde\alpha^{(1)})\mathcal F_{i+1},
       (1,\widetilde\eta^{(1)})\mathcal F_{j+1}\bigr]_{\mathcal F}
 =\bigl(1,[\widetilde\alpha^{(1)},\widetilde\eta^{(1)}]\bigr)
  \mathcal F_{i+j+1}.
\]
Since $[\widetilde\alpha^{(1)},\widetilde\eta^{(1)}]
\in G_{i+j+2\xi}^{(1)}\le G_{i+j+\xi+1}^{(1)}$, the pair belongs to
$\mathcal F_{i+j+1}$, and this bracket is zero in
$\mathcal F_{i+j}/\mathcal F_{i+j+1}$. Adding the four second
components and using~\eqref{p12:eq:sims_lift_commutator_difference}
proves the asserted formula.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{p12:thm:first-difference}
Fix $1\le\xi\le c-2$, and let $G^{(0)}$ and $G^{(1)}$ be the groups specified
by two valid completions in the same fixed Sims fibre that induce the
same graded bracket $[-,-]_L$. Assume that 
$[g_{h_1,a}^{(\nu)},g_{h_2,b}^{(\nu)}]$, for $h_1,h_2\in[c]$,
$a\in[r_{h_1}]$ and $b\in[r_{h_2}]$, have the same
$L_{h_1+h_2+e}$-components for $\nu=0,1$ and for every
$1\le e<\xi$ with $h_1+h_2+e\le c$.
Then the Sims-lift commutator difference defined
in~\eqref{p12:eq:sims_lift_commutator_difference} extends to a well-defined
alternating biadditive map $\delta_\xi:L\times L\rightarrow L$
with $\delta_\xi(L_i,L_j)\subseteq L_{i+j+\xi}$ whenever
$i+j+\xi\le c$.
Moreover, for all homogeneous $x,y,z\in L$, it satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:cocycle}
[x,\delta_\xi(y,z)]_L+[y,\delta_\xi(z,x)]_L
      +[z,\delta_\xi(x,y)]_L=\delta_\xi([x,y]_L,z)+\delta_\xi([y,z]_L,x)+\delta_\xi([z,x]_L,y).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The common graded bracket identifies the excess-zero components of
every pair of corresponding Sims-generator commutators.  Together
with the assumed agreement at excesses $1\le e<\xi$, this verifies
the generator-commutator hypothesis of
\cref{p12:prop:sims-collection-rules}, and hence of
\cref{p12:prop:collection-monotonicity}. We may therefore use the
comparison $N$-series $(\mathcal F_i)$ constructed above.
For each $x\in L_i$,
the Sims lifts $\widetilde x^{(0)}$ and $\widetilde x^{(1)}$ have the
same weight-$i$ numerical coordinates and trivial blocks in all
other weights.  Consequently,
$(\widetilde x^{(0)},\widetilde x^{(1)})\in\mathcal F_i$.

For $i+j+\xi\le c$, apply
\cref{p12:prop:sims-lift-comparison} in degrees $i$, $j$ and $i+j$.
Transporting $[-,-]_{\mathcal F}$ through the identifications
\eqref{p12:eq:comparison-graded-identification} gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:comparison-bracket-formula}
 \bigl[(x,\alpha),(y,\eta)\bigr]_{\mathcal F}
 =\bigl([x,y]_L,
        \delta_\xi(x,y)+[x,\eta]_L+[\alpha,y]_L\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $x\in L_i$, $\alpha\in L_{i+\xi}$, $y\in L_j$ and
$\eta\in L_{j+\xi}$ are defined as in~\eqref{p12:eq:defxyalphaeta}. In particular, $\delta_\xi(x,y)$ is the second
component of $[(x,0),(y,0)]_{\mathcal F}$. The Sims lifts are uniquely
determined, so this map is well-defined. Since $x\mapsto(x,0)$ is
additive, alternation and biadditivity follow from the corresponding properties of
$[-,-]_{\mathcal F}$. Extending over the direct sum, and using the
declared zero value when $i+j+\xi>c$, gives an alternating
biadditive map $\delta_\xi:L\times L\to L$.

Finally, let $x\in L_i$, $y\in L_j$ and $z\in L_k$.
Put $t=i+j+k+\xi$. If $t>c$, the grading rule and the definition
of $\delta_\xi$ make every term in~\eqref{p12:eq:cocycle} zero.
Suppose that $t\le c$, so every term belongs to $L_t$. Apply the Jacobi identity
in $\operatorname{gr}\mathcal F$, in the form of
\eqref{p12:eq:graded-jacobi-explicit}, to $(x,0)$, $(y,0)$ and $(z,0)$.
Formula~\eqref{p12:eq:comparison-bracket-formula} gives
\[
 \bigl[(x,0),(y,0)\bigr]_{\mathcal F}
 =\bigl([x,y]_L,\delta_\xi(x,y)\bigr).
\]
Apply the formula again with inputs
$\bigl([x,y]_L,\delta_\xi(x,y)\bigr)$ and $(z,0)$.  The second
component of their bracket, in $L_t$, is
\[
\delta_\xi([x,y]_L,z)+[[x,y]_L,0]_L
      +[\delta_\xi(x,y),z]_L=\delta_\xi([x,y]_L,z)+[\delta_\xi(x,y),z]_L.
\]
The two cyclic permutations of $(x,y,z)$ give the other two terms.
Consequently, the second component of Jacobi is
\[
0=\delta_\xi([x,y]_L,z)+[\delta_\xi(x,y),z]_L+\delta_\xi([y,z]_L,x)+[\delta_\xi(y,z),x]_L+\delta_\xi([z,x]_L,y)+[\delta_\xi(z,x),y]_L.
\]
Skew-symmetry of $[-,-]_L$ now gives~\eqref{p12:eq:cocycle}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:triangular-second-layer-recovery}
Assume the hypotheses of~\cref{p12:thm:first-difference}. Suppose that
\[
 \delta_\xi(C_{\mathrm{core}},C_{\mathrm{core}})=0,
 \qquad
 \delta_\xi(y_j,u_k)=0
 \quad(k\in[s],\ d_{k-1}<j\le r_2).
\]
Then $\delta_\xi(L_2,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
If $\xi=c-2$, the conclusion holds by definition, since $3+\xi>c$.
Suppose that $\xi\le c-3$.
We prove $\delta_\xi(L_2,u_k)=0$ by induction on $k\in[s]$.
The elements $y_j$ generate $L_2$. For $j>d_{k-1}$,
$\delta_\xi(y_j,u_k)=0$ by assumption; this covers all $j$ when $k=1$, since
$d_0=0$. For $k>1$ and $j\le d_{k-1}$, choose $\ell<k$ with
$d_{\ell-1}<j\le d_\ell$ and put $a=f(j)<\ell$.
By item~\textup{(c)} of Section~\ref{p12:sec:sims-counting-strategy}
and~\eqref{p12:eq:fibre-core-to-layer}, $y_j=[u_a,u_\ell]_L$.
Since $u_a,u_\ell,u_k\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$ and
$\delta_\xi(C_{\mathrm{core}},C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$,
\eqref{p12:eq:cocycle} gives
\[
 \delta_\xi(y_j,u_k)
 =-\delta_\xi([u_\ell,u_k]_L,u_a)
  -\delta_\xi([u_k,u_a]_L,u_\ell)=0.
\]
Here both terms vanish by the induction hypothesis, since
$a,\ell<k$ and $[u_\ell,u_k]_L,[u_k,u_a]_L\in L_2$.
Since the $u_k$ generate $C_{\mathrm{core}}$, biadditivity gives
$\delta_\xi(L_2,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{p12:cor:selected-complete}
Suppose that $G^{(0)}$ and $G^{(1)}$ satisfy the hypotheses
of~\cref{p12:thm:first-difference}. Assume further that their
excess-$\xi$ components agree for every selected relation having a
core input. Then the first-difference map $\delta_\xi$ defined
in~\eqref{p12:eq:sims_lift_commutator_difference} satisfies $\delta_\xi(L_{\ge2},L)=0$ and $\delta_\xi(L,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.
Moreover, $[\delta_\xi(x,y),h]_L=0$ for every
$x,y\in L_1$ and $h\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$.

In particular, among the selected excess-$\xi$ components, the two
completions can differ only in the $L_{\xi+2}$-components of the
first-layer relations $[g_{1,j}^{(\nu)},g_{1,k}^{(\nu)}]$, where $s<j<k\le r_1$ and $\nu=0,1$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For every selected relation having a core input with $i+1+\xi\le c$,
the Sims-lift definition and the assumed component agreement give
\[
\delta_\xi(\bar g_{i,j},\bar g_{1,k})=\pi_{i+1+\xi}\bigl([g_{i,j}^{(1)},g_{1,k}^{(1)}]\bigr)-\pi_{i+1+\xi}\bigl([g_{i,j}^{(0)},g_{1,k}^{(0)}]\bigr)=0.
\]

For $j\in[r_1]$ and $k\in[s]$ with $j\ne k$, the first-layer
relation on these generators is selected after ordering their
indices. Alternation therefore gives
$\delta_\xi(\bar g_{1,j},u_k)=0$, including the case $j=k$.
Since the $\bar g_{1,j}$ generate $L_1$ and the $u_k$ generate
$C_{\mathrm{core}}$, biadditivity gives
$\delta_\xi(L_1,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.
For $3\le i\le c-\xi-1$, all relations corresponding to
$(\bar g_{i,j},u_k)$, with $j\in[r_i]$ and $k\in[s]$, are selected.
The same argument gives $\delta_\xi(L_i,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.
For $i+1+\xi>c$, the same vanishing holds by definition.

If $\xi\le c-3$, the selected source-weight-two relations give $\delta_\xi(y_j,u_k)=0$ for $k\in[s]$ and $d_{k-1}<j\le r_2$.
Together with $\delta_\xi(C_{\mathrm{core}},C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$,
\cref{p12:lem:triangular-second-layer-recovery} gives
$\delta_\xi(L_2,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.
If $\xi=c-2$, this vanishing holds by definition, since $3+\xi>c$.
Thus $\delta_\xi(L_i,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$ for every $i\in[c]$.
Biadditivity and $L=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{c}L_i$ give
$\delta_\xi(L,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.

We next prove $\delta_\xi(w,z)=0$ for every left-normed core Lie word $w$
and homogeneous $z\in L$, by induction on the length of $w$.
For a single core letter, this follows from
$\delta_\xi(L,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$ and alternation.
Write a longer word as $w=[w',h]_L$, with $h\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$.
Applying~\eqref{p12:eq:cocycle} to $w',h,z$ gives
\[
[w',\delta_\xi(h,z)]_L+[h,\delta_\xi(z,w')]_L
       +[z,\delta_\xi(w',h)]_L=\delta_\xi([w',h]_L,z)+\delta_\xi([h,z]_L,w')
       +\delta_\xi([z,w']_L,h).
\]
Since $h\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$ and
$\delta_\xi(L,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$, we have $\delta_\xi(h,z)=-\delta_\xi(z,h)=0$, $\delta_\xi(w',h)=0$, and $\delta_\xi([z,w']_L,h)=0$.
Thus,
\[
 \delta_\xi([w',h]_L,z)
 =[h,\delta_\xi(z,w')]_L-\delta_\xi([h,z]_L,w').
\]
Now $w'$ is a shorter core Lie word. The induction hypothesis applies
to every homogeneous second argument, including $z$ and $[h,z]_L$.
Hence $\delta_\xi(w',z)=0$ and $\delta_\xi(w',[h,z]_L)=0$.
Therefore, we have $\delta_\xi([w',h]_L,z)=0$.

By~\eqref{p12:eq:sims-core-graded-generation}, left-normed core Lie words generate
every $L_i$ with $i\ge2$. Hence
$\delta_\xi(L_i,L)=0$ for $2\le i\le c$.

For any $x,y\in L_1$ and $h\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$,
applying~\eqref{p12:eq:cocycle} to $x,y,h$ gives
\[
[x,\delta_\xi(y,h)]_L
  +[y,\delta_\xi(h,x)]_L
  +[h,\delta_\xi(x,y)]_L= \delta_\xi([x,y]_L,h)
  +\delta_\xi([y,h]_L,x)
  +\delta_\xi([h,x]_L,y).
\]
Since $\delta_\xi(L_1,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$, alternation gives
$\delta_\xi(y,h)=\delta_\xi(h,x)=0$, so the
first two terms on the left vanish. Moreover,
$x,y,h\in L_1$ implies
$[x,y]_L,[y,h]_L,
[h,x]_L\in L_2$. All three terms on the right
therefore vanish by $\delta_\xi(L_{\ge2},L)=0$.
Thus for any $x,y\in L_1$ and $h\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:first_layer_pairs}
 [h,\delta_\xi(x,y)]_L=[\delta_\xi(x,y),h]_L=0.
\end{equation}
Finally, every selected relation other than a first-layer pair with
$s<j<k\le r_1$ has a core input, so its excess-$\xi$ component agrees
by assumption. This proves the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:selected-agreement}
Fix $\xi\in[c-2]$. Let $G^{(0)}$ and $G^{(1)}$ be the groups specified
by two valid completions in the same fixed Sims fibre that induce the
same graded bracket. Assume that the excess-$e$ components agree
for every selected relation and every $1\le e<\xi$. Then the differences
$\delta_e$ defined in~\eqref{p12:eq:sims_lift_commutator_difference} satisfy $\delta_e(L_i,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$ for any $i\in[c]$ and $1\leq e<\xi$.
Furthermore, for any
$x\in L_i$ and $y\in L_j$, the commutators of their corresponding Sims
lifts have identical $L_{i+j+e}$-components whenever
$0\le e<\xi$ and $i+j+e\le c$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We prove both conclusions by induction on the excess $e$. Agreement at
excess zero follows from the common graded bracket. Let $1\le e<\xi$,
and suppose that all Sims-lift commutator components agree at every excess smaller than $e$. In particular, they satisfy the hypotheses of~\cref{p12:thm:first-difference}
at excess $e$. Let $\delta_e$ be the difference defined
in~\eqref{p12:eq:sims_lift_commutator_difference}.

By~\cref{p12:cor:selected-complete} applied at excess $e$,
$\delta_e(L,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$ and $\delta_e(L_{\ge2},L)=0$.

By~\eqref{p12:eq:sims-lift}, each Sims generator is the Sims lift of its
class in the corresponding layer. Agreement of the selected components
at excess $e$ gives $\delta_e(\bar g_{i,j},\bar g_{1,k})=0$
for every selected relation with $i+1+e\le c$.
Since every first-layer relation is selected, alternation and
biadditivity give $\delta_e(L_1,L_1)=0$.
Together with $\delta_e(L_{\ge2},L)=0$, this gives
$\delta_e(L,L)=0$. By its definition, all Sims-lift
commutators therefore agree at excess $e$, completing the induction.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:one-excess}
Work in a fixed Sims fibre, fix one graded Lie bracket with breadth
sequence $\mathbf b=(b_i)_{i=2}^{c}$, and fix $1\le\xi\le c-2$. Recall that
\[
 r_i=d(L_i),\qquad
 s_i=\log_p|L_i|\quad(1\le i\le c),
 \qquad
 b_i=\max_{u\in C_{\mathrm{core}}}\log_p|[L_i,u]_L|
 \quad(2\le i\le c).
\]
Suppose that the layer components of all selected relations have been
fixed at every positive excess $1\le e<\xi$.  Among the valid
completions extending these choices and inducing the fixed bracket,
fix also the excess-$\xi$ components of the first-layer relations
having a core input and of all selected relations of source weight
$2\le i\le c-\xi-1$. Then, for each $[g_{1,j},g_{1,k}]$ with $s<j<k\le r_1$, its
$L_{\xi+2}$-component takes at most
$p^{s_{\xi+2}-b_{\xi+2}}$ values among these completions.
Consequently, before fixing any of the current excess-$\xi$
components, all selected excess-$\xi$ components have at most
\[
 p^{\binom{r_1}{2}s_{\xi+2}
    +s\sum_{i=2}^{c-\xi-1}r_i s_{i+\xi+1}
    -\binom{r_1-s}{2}b_{\xi+2}}
\]
possible choices.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
If no valid completion extends the conditional choices, the assertion
is immediate. Otherwise, let $G^{(0)}$ and $G^{(1)}$ be any two such
completions. By~\cref{p12:prop:selected-agreement}, all corresponding
Sims-generator commutators agree below excess $\xi$, so
\cref{p12:thm:first-difference} applies. By~\cref{p12:cor:selected-complete},
their first-difference map satisfies $\delta_\xi(L_{\ge2},L)=0$ and $\delta_\xi(L_1,C_{\mathrm{core}})=0$.

Choose a maximizing element $h_{\xi+2}^\ast\in C_{\mathrm{core}}$ as
in~\eqref{p12:eq:core-breadth}.  The map
$\operatorname{ad}(h_{\xi+2}^\ast):L_{\xi+2}\to L$ has image of order
$p^{b_{\xi+2}}$; when $\xi=c-2$, it is the zero map as $b_c=0$.
For $x,y\in L_1$,
\eqref{p12:eq:first_layer_pairs} gives
\[
 [h_{\xi+2}^\ast,\delta_\xi(x,y)]_L=[\delta_\xi(x,y),h_{\xi+2}^\ast]_L=0.
\]
Thus, we have $\delta_\xi(x,y)\in\ker\operatorname{ad}(h_{\xi+2}^\ast)$, where,
by~\eqref{p12:eq:adjoint-kernel-size},
 $|\ker\operatorname{ad}(h_{\xi+2}^\ast)|=p^{s_{\xi+2}-b_{\xi+2}}$.


Fix one completion as a reference. For each outside--outside
first-layer relation $[g_{1,j},g_{1,k}]$, with $s<j<k\le r_1$,
$\delta_\xi(\bar g_{1,j},\bar g_{1,k})$ is the difference between
its $L_{\xi+2}$-components in another completion and in the reference
completion. Thus its component lies in a coset of
$\ker\operatorname{ad}(h_{\xi+2}^\ast)$ determined by the reference component for
that pair, and has at most $p^{s_{\xi+2}-b_{\xi+2}}$ possible values.
There are $\binom{r_1-s}{2}$ such relations. Multiplying these
per-pair bounds shows that all remaining outside--outside first-layer components
together have at most
$p^{\binom{r_1-s}{2}(s_{\xi+2}-b_{\xi+2})}$ possible assignments.

The core-involving first-layer components have at most
$p^{(\binom{r_1}{2}-\binom{r_1-s}{2})s_{\xi+2}}$ choices.  The selected
components of the relations of source weight $2\le i\le c-\xi-1$
have at most
\[
 p^{s\sum_{i=2}^{c-\xi-1}r_i s_{i+\xi+1}}
\]
choices; for $i=2$ the exact number of selected source-weight-two
relations is
$\sum_{k=1}^{s}(r_2-d_{k-1})\le sr_2$.  Multiplying these three bounds
gives the stated exponent.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:filtered-fibre}
Work in a fixed Sims fibre and fix one graded Lie bracket with breadth
sequence $\mathbf b=(b_i)_{i=2}^{c}$. The number of possible
assignments of all positive-excess components of the selected
relations among valid completions inducing this fixed bracket is at
most
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:deeper-commutator-count}
p^{\sum_{\xi=1}^{c-2}\left(
      \binom{r_1}{2}s_{\xi+2}
      +s\sum_{i=2}^{c-\xi-1}r_i s_{i+\xi+1}
      -\binom{r_1-s}{2}b_{\xi+2}\right)}.
\end{equation}
Write $m_{\mathrm{deep}}=\sum_{i=2}^c s_i$ and $T_{\mathrm{core}}=\sum_{i=2}^{c-2}r_i\sum_{t=i+2}^{c}s_t$.
The bound in~\eqref{p12:eq:deeper-commutator-count} can also be written as
\[
 p^{\binom{r_1}{2}(m_{\mathrm{deep}}-s_2)
    +sT_{\mathrm{core}}
    -\binom{r_1-s}{2}\sum_{i=3}^{c-1}b_i}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Apply \cref{p12:prop:one-excess} successively for
$1\le\xi\le c-2$, each time conditional on all smaller positive
excesses. Multiplication of these conditional bounds gives the
exponent in
\eqref{p12:eq:deeper-commutator-count}.  Using $b_c=0$, the identities
\[
 \sum_{\xi=1}^{c-2}s_{\xi+2}=m_{\mathrm{deep}}-s_2,
 \qquad
 \sum_{\xi=1}^{c-2}b_{\xi+2}=\sum_{i=3}^{c-1}b_i,\qquad \sum_{\xi=1}^{c-2}\sum_{i=2}^{c-\xi-1}r_i s_{i+\xi+1}
 =\sum_{i=2}^{c-2}r_i\sum_{t=i+2}^{c}s_t
 =T_{\mathrm{core}}
\]
give the second exponent and prove the corollary.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
For each fixed graded bracket,
\cref{p12:prop:filtered-fibre} gives the same uniform bound
\eqref{p12:eq:deeper-commutator-count} for its positive-excess data.
Summing this bound over the brackets counted in
\eqref{p12:eq:lie-bracket-count} therefore multiplies the two bounds.  The
resulting base-$p$ exponent is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}s b_i(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)
   +\binom{r_1}{2}s_2-\binom{r_1-s}{2}b_2\\
 &\qquad+\binom{r_1}{2}(m_{\mathrm{deep}}-s_2)+sT_{\mathrm{core}}
   -\binom{r_1-s}{2}\sum_{i=3}^{c-1}b_i\\
 =&\binom{r_1}{2}m_{\mathrm{deep}}+sT_{\mathrm{core}}
   +\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}b_i
    \left(s(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)-\binom{r_1-s}{2}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{p12:cor:normalized-relation-bound}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{p12:prop:total-relation-bound}, the
base-$p$ logarithm of the number of valid completions with the
fixed breadth sequence is at most
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:normalized-relation-bound}
\begin{split}
 &\left(\binom{r_1}{2}-r_2\right)m_{\mathrm{deep}}+sT_{\mathrm{core}}\\
 &\qquad+\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}b_i
 \left(s(r_i+s_{i+1}-b_i+1)-\binom{r_1-s}{2}\right).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For each $j\in[r_2]$, the fixed Sims data include the defining
identity $[g_{1,f(j)},g_{1,k}]=g_{2,j}$, where
$d_{k-1}<j\le d_k$.  These are $r_2$ distinct core--core pairs:
the function $f$ is injective within each block, and different
blocks have different second indices $k$.  Their components in
$L_2$ are fixed, and all their deeper components are zero.

In the proof of \cref{p12:prop:count_leading_maps}, these pairs were
included among the freely counted core-involving pairs.  Omitting
them subtracts $r_2s_2$ from the graded exponent.  When $c=2$, the
same omission applies directly to the count of
$L_1\times L_1\to L_2$.  At each positive excess $\xi$, the
core-involving first-layer count in the proof of
\cref{p12:prop:one-excess} similarly improves by $r_2s_{\xi+2}$.
All these slots are disjoint from the outside--outside slots to
which the breadth saving is applied.  Thus both the graded and
positive-excess proofs remain valid, with total saving
\[
 r_2s_2+\sum_{\xi=1}^{c-2}r_2s_{\xi+2}
 =r_2m_{\mathrm{deep}}.
\]
Subtracting this from \eqref{p12:eq:total-relation-bound} proves the
claim.  This is an omission of fixed entries in the counting
argument, not a division by a presentation multiplicity.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:power-ledger}
Fix the relative-order exponents $a(i,v)$ of a Sims presentation.
The base-$p$ logarithm $P$ of the number of possible power-word
arrays is at most
\begin{align}\label{p12:eq:power-ledger}
 P&\le\sum_{i=1}^{c}\left[
       r_i\sum_{j>i}s_j+
       \sum_{v=1}^{r_i}(r_i-v)(a(i,v)-1)\right]\notag\\
  &\le\sum_{i=1}^{c}\left[
       r_i\sum_{j>i}s_j+(r_i-1)(s_i-r_i)\right].
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:power-ledger-simple}
 P\le r_1m_{\mathrm{deep}}+r_1\delta
       +m_{\mathrm{deep}}(e+m_{\ge3})+m_{\ge3}^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The power relation for $g_{i,j}$ has a right side involving earlier
generators in its own layer and arbitrary coordinates in deeper
layers.  The latter have at most $p^{\sum_{k>i}s_k}$ choices.
Modulo $pL_i$, the images of the chosen $r_i$ generators form a
basis.  Reducing the power relation modulo $pL_i$ therefore shows
that each same-layer coefficient is divisible by $p$.  For $v<j$,
the coefficient of $g_{i,v}$ has at most $p^{a(i,v)-1}$ choices.
There are $r_i-v$ power relations in which this coefficient can
occur.  Multiplying these bounds proves the first line of
\eqref{p12:eq:power-ledger}.  For the second line, use
$r_i-v\le r_i-1$ and
$\sum_v(a(i,v)-1)=s_i-r_i$.

The first layer contributes at most
$r_1m_{\mathrm{deep}}+r_1\delta$.  The second contributes at most
\[
 r_2m_{\ge3}+(r_2-1)e
 \le m_{\mathrm{deep}}(m_{\ge3}+e).
\]
There are at most $m_{\ge3}$ power relations of weight at least
three, and each has at most $p^{m_{\ge3}}$ possible right sides.
Their total contribution is thus at most $m_{\ge3}^2$.
This proves~\eqref{p12:eq:power-ledger-simple}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:second-layer-defect}
For every prime $p$, we have
\[
 e\le\binom{\delta}{2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Commutation induces an epimorphism of abelian groups
$\wedge^2L_1\twoheadrightarrow L_2$.  Write
$L_1\cong\bigoplus_{j=1}^{r_1}\mathbb Z/p^{\alpha_j}\mathbb Z$,
where $\alpha_j\ge1$, and put
$k_a=|\{j:\alpha_j\ge a\}|$ for $a\ge2$.  Then
\[
 \delta=\sum_{j=1}^{r_1}(\alpha_j-1)
        =\sum_{a\ge2}k_a.
\]
The epimorphism on exterior squares induces an epimorphism on their
$p$-multiples.  Since the exterior square of $L_1$ is the direct
sum, over pairs $j<k$, of cyclic groups of order
$p^{\min\{\alpha_j,\alpha_k\}}$, we obtain
\[
 e=\log_p|pL_2|
 \le\log_p|p(\wedge^2L_1)|
 =\sum_{a\ge2}\binom{k_a}{2}
 \le\binom{\sum_{a\ge2}k_a}{2}
 =\binom{\delta}{2}.
\]
This argument uses no restriction on the characteristic.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:saturated-optimisation}
Use the notation above for a fixed Sims fibre and a feasible
breadth sequence.  If $s^2\le2s_2+3s$, then
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:refined-saturated-optimization}
 \begin{split}
 &\frac12r_1^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}+\mathcal X
   +3m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}+\frac12m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}\\
 &\hspace{15mm}\le
   \frac{2}{27}(r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}})^3
   +O(r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}}).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The implied constant is absolute and independent of the prime.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The exact deficit from the cubic maximum is
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:cubic-deficit}
 \begin{split}
 D_{\mathrm{cub}}
 &:=\frac{2}{27}(r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}})^3
       -\frac12r_1^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}\\
 &=\frac{z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2(4r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}})}{54}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Dropping negative terms in~\eqref{p12:eq:X-breadth-total} and using
$T_{\mathrm{core}}\le m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2/2$,
$b_{\mathrm{tot}}\le m_{\mathrm{deep}}$, and
$s=O(\sqrt{m_{\mathrm{deep}}})$ gives
$\mathcal X\le O(m_{\mathrm{deep}}^{5/2})$.
Outside the range
\[
 m_{\mathrm{deep}}\le r_1\le3m_{\mathrm{deep}},
\]
the right side of~\eqref{p12:eq:cubic-deficit} is at least a positive
absolute multiple of $(r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}})^3$.  For sufficiently large
$r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}}$, it therefore absorbs the preceding upper bound
for $\mathcal X$ and the terms
$3m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}+m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}/2$, whose
absolute values are $O((r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}})^2)$.  Bounded
$r_1+m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ is covered by the final absolute constant.

We may henceforth assume $m_{\mathrm{deep}}\le r_1\le3m_{\mathrm{deep}}$.
Then $|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|\le m_{\mathrm{deep}}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:comparable-cubic-deficit}
 D_{\mathrm{cub}}\ge\frac5{54}m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2.
\end{equation}
If $m_{\ge3}=0$, then $T_{\mathrm{core}}=b_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mathcal X=0$,
and completing the square gives
\[
 \frac12m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}
 \le\frac5{54}m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2
       +\frac{27}{40}m_{\mathrm{deep}}
 \le D_{\mathrm{cub}}+O(m_{\mathrm{deep}}).
\]
Thus we may assume $m_{\ge3}>0$.  Then $c\ge3$ and $s_3>0$.
Since $s_3\le sb_2$ and $b_2$ is an integer, we have $b_2\ge1$.

Put
\[
 T_{\max}=\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2-s_2^2}{2},
 \qquad
 S_{\mathrm{net}}=\binom{r_1-s}{2}-s(2m_{\mathrm{deep}}+1).
\]
Since $r_1\ge m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ and $s=O(\sqrt{m_{\mathrm{deep}}})$, for all
sufficiently large $m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ we have, uniformly in the feasible $s$,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:net-saving-lower}
 S_{\mathrm{net}}
 \ge\frac12m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2-O(s m_{\mathrm{deep}}+m_{\mathrm{deep}})
 \ge\frac14m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2.
\end{equation}
We may assume this, since bounded $m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ in the present range
also bounds $r_1$.  Equation~\eqref{p12:eq:X-breadth-total} gives
the following two bounds, discarding the $b_2$ saving only in the first:
\begin{align}
 \mathcal X&\le
 (s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}})b_{\mathrm{tot}},
 \label{p12:eq:X-linear-breadth}\\
 \mathcal X&\le
 s\min\{T_{\max},s m_{\mathrm{deep}}(b_{\mathrm{tot}}-b_2)\}
       -S_{\mathrm{net}}b_{\mathrm{tot}}.
 \label{p12:eq:X-piecewise-breadth}
\end{align}
For fixed $b_2$, the latter right side, as a function of
$b_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge b_2$, is linear on either side of
$b_2+T_{\max}/(s m_{\mathrm{deep}})$.  Since $S_{\mathrm{net}}>0$,
it is maximized at $b_2$ or at this breakpoint.  Thus, writing
$x_+=\max\{x,0\}$, we obtain
\begin{align}\label{p12:eq:X-max}
 \mathcal X&\le
 \frac{T_{\max}}{s m_{\mathrm{deep}}}
       (s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}})_+
       -S_{\mathrm{net}}b_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{m_{\ge3}}s
       (s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}})_+
       -S_{\mathrm{net}}b_2.
\end{align}
The last inequality follows from
$T_{\max}=m_{\ge3}(2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-m_{\ge3})/2
\le m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}$.

Substituting $r_1=2m_{\mathrm{deep}}+z_{\mathrm{bal}}$ and using
\eqref{p12:eq:saturation}, we have
\begin{align}\label{p12:eq:balance-expand}
 s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}}
 &\le-2m_{\mathrm{deep}}(m_{\ge3}+z_{\mathrm{bal}})
       +7s m_{\mathrm{deep}}
       -\frac12(z_{\mathrm{bal}}-s)^2\notag\\
 &\qquad+m_{\mathrm{deep}}+\frac{z_{\mathrm{bal}}}{2}+\frac s2\notag\\
 &\le-2m_{\mathrm{deep}}(m_{\ge3}+z_{\mathrm{bal}})+9s m_{\mathrm{deep}}.
\end{align}
Here the last inequality uses $|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|\le m_{\mathrm{deep}}$,
$s\ge2$, and $m_{\mathrm{deep}}\ge1$.  Substitution into
\eqref{p12:eq:X-max}, followed by maximization of a quadratic in
$m_{\ge3}$, gives
\begin{align}\label{p12:eq:X-balance}
 \mathcal X
 &\le\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}}s m_{\ge3}
       (-2m_{\ge3}-2z_{\mathrm{bal}}+9s)_+
       -S_{\mathrm{net}}b_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}}{8s}(-2z_{\mathrm{bal}}+9s)_+^2
       -S_{\mathrm{net}}b_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2}{2s}
       +\frac92m_{\mathrm{deep}}|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|
       +\frac{81}{8}s m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}}b_2.
\end{align}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 1:
$m_{\ge3}\ge9(|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|+s)$.}
Equation~\eqref{p12:eq:balance-expand} gives
$s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}}\le-m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}$.
Using the lower bound on $b_{\mathrm{tot}}$ in
\eqref{p12:eq:breadth-total-le-deep}, we deduce from
\eqref{p12:eq:X-linear-breadth} that
\[
 \mathcal X+3m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}
 \le-\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}^2}s
       +3m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}\le0.
\]
Finally, completing the square gives
\[
 \frac12m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}
 \le\frac5{54}m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2
       +\frac{27}{40}m_{\mathrm{deep}}
 \le D_{\mathrm{cub}}+O(m_{\mathrm{deep}}).
\]
This proves the required bound in this case.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 2:
$m_{\ge3}<9(|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|+s)$.}
Equation~\eqref{p12:eq:X-balance} now gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:small-deeper-layer-bound}
 \begin{split}
 &\mathcal X+3m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}
          +\frac12m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}\\
 &\qquad\le\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2}{2s}
          +32m_{\mathrm{deep}}|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|
          +\frac{297}{8}s m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}}b_2.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
If $s\ge11$, the first term is at most
$5m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2/108$.  Completing the square in
the second term yields
\[
 32m_{\mathrm{deep}}|z_{\mathrm{bal}}|
 \le\frac5{108}m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}^2
       +\frac{27648}{5}m_{\mathrm{deep}}.
\]
The two square terms are absorbed by
\eqref{p12:eq:comparable-cubic-deficit}.  Since $b_2\ge1$,
\eqref{p12:eq:net-saving-lower} bounds the remaining terms by
\[
 \frac{27648}{5}m_{\mathrm{deep}}+\frac{297}{8}s m_{\mathrm{deep}}
       -\frac14m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2\le0
\]
for all sufficiently large $m_{\mathrm{deep}}$, using
$s=O(\sqrt{m_{\mathrm{deep}}})$.  This proves the required bound when $s\ge11$.

It remains to treat $2\le s\le10$.  Uniformly for these values,
when $m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ is sufficiently large and $r_1\ge m_{\mathrm{deep}}$,
\[
 s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}-S_{\mathrm{net}}
 =s^2m_{\mathrm{deep}}+s(2m_{\mathrm{deep}}+1)-\binom{r_1-s}{2}
 \le-\frac14m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2.
\]
Equations~\eqref{p12:eq:X-linear-breadth} and
\eqref{p12:eq:breadth-total-le-deep} consequently give
\[
 \mathcal X+3m_{\mathrm{deep}}m_{\ge3}
 \le\left(-\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}^2}{4s}+3m_{\mathrm{deep}}\right)m_{\ge3}
 \le0
\]
for all sufficiently large $m_{\mathrm{deep}}$.  The same completion of
the square as in Case~1 absorbs
$m_{\mathrm{deep}}z_{\mathrm{bal}}/2$ into $D_{\mathrm{cub}}$, up to
$O(m_{\mathrm{deep}})$.  Bounded $m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ again bounds $r_1$ in the
range under consideration and is absorbed by the absolute constant.
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For each feasible choice of the remaining presentation parameters,
\eqref{p12:eq:joint-relation-power} and
\cref{p12:lem:saturated-optimisation} give
\[
 \mathcal E\le\frac{2}{27}(m-\delta)^3
        +O(m)+2m_{\mathrm{deep}}e+r_1\delta.
\]
First use $e,\delta,m_{\mathrm{deep}},r_1\le m$ to obtain an absolute
constant $C_0$ such that
\[
 \mathcal E\le\frac{2}{27}(m-\delta)^3+C_0m^2.
\]
For $0\le\delta\le m$,
\[
 m^3-(m-\delta)^3
 =\delta(3m^2-3m\delta+\delta^2)\ge\delta m^2.
\]
Thus, after fixing an absolute threshold
$\delta_0>27C_0/2$, all choices with $\delta\ge\delta_0$
satisfy $\mathcal E\le2m^3/27$.

For $\delta<\delta_0$, \cref{p12:lem:second-layer-defect} gives
$e\le\binom{\delta}{2}=O(1)$ with an absolute constant.
Consequently $2m_{\mathrm{deep}}e+r_1\delta=O(m)$, and the refined
estimate above yields
\[
 \mathcal E\le\frac{2}{27}(m-\delta)^3+O(m)
 \le\frac{2}{27}m^3+O(m).
\]
All commutator and power-word choices have now been counted.  The
remaining numerical, relative-order, core-flag, defining-index,
and breadth-sequence choices contribute only $p^{O(m\log m)}$
by \cref{p12:prop:parameter-ledger}.  Summing over them gives the
exponent $2m^3/27+O(m\log m)$.
No alternating-map counting factor or further quadratic allowance
is used in this saturated count.  This proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:sims-hollowing-dictionary}
Let $\beta:\wedge^2X\to W$ be a surjective alternating map over
$\mathbb F_q$, and let $\mathcal A_\beta=\beta^*(W^*)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item For every subspace $U\le X$, one has
 \[
  \beta(\wedge^2U)=W
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \operatorname{res}^{\mathcal A_\beta}_U\text{ is injective}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \mathcal A_\beta\text{ is faithful on }U.
 \]
 \item For $0\le h<\dim X$,
 \[
  \mathcal A_\beta\text{ is $h$-hollowing}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  s(\beta)>h.
 \]
 \item For $1\le s\leq \dim X$, one has $s(\beta)=s$ precisely when
 $\mathcal A_\beta$ is $(s-1)$-hollowing and $s$-faithful.
                                                               
                                                                
     
                    
     
                                                   
                                                       
                                                       
                                                                     
                                                                    
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For \textup{(i)}, the kernel of $\operatorname{res}^{\mathcal A_\beta}_U$ consists of the
forms $\beta^*(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in
 \operatorname{Ann}_{W^*}\bigl(\beta(\wedge^2U)\bigr)$.
This annihilator is zero exactly when
$\beta(\wedge^2U)=W$.  Part \textup{(ii)} follows immediately:
$h$-hollowing says that the restriction map is noninjective for
every $h$-space, which by \textup{(i)} says that no $h$-space
generates $W$.  Part \textup{(iii)} is now exactly
\eqref{p12:eq:exact-linear-Sims-rank}, translated by \textup{(i)} and
\textup{(ii)}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:isotropic-exact}
Let $X$ be an $R$-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-space, let
$A\in\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ have rank $2a$, and let $0\le h\le R$.  Let
$r_0=R-2a$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:isotropic-exact}
 I_h(A)=
 \sum_{\ell=\max\{0,h-r_0\}}^{\min\{h,a\}}
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{r_0}{h-\ell}_{q}\cdot
 q^{\ell(r_0-h+\ell)}\cdot
 \prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}
 \frac{q^{2a-2i}-1}{q^{\ell-i}-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $K=\operatorname{rad} A$, so $\dim K=r_0$.  Choose a complementary subspace
$Y$ such that $X=K\oplus Y$.
The restriction of $A$ to $Y$ is nondegenerate: if $y\in Y$ is
orthogonal to $Y$, then it is also orthogonal to $K$, since $K$ is
the radical, and hence $y\in K\cap Y=0$.  Thus $Y$ is a
$2a$-dimensional symplectic space.  Let $p:X\to Y$ be the projection
along $K$.

Fix an isotropic $h$-space $H\le X$. Let $J=H\cap K$ and $L=p(H)$. Put $\ell=\dim L=h-\dim J$.
The space $L$ is isotropic in $Y$: removing the $K$-components of
two vectors does not change their value under $A$.

We reconstruct $H$ in three elementary choices.  First choose
$J$, an $(h-\ell)$-space in $K$.  This gives $\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{r_0}{h-\ell}_{q}$ possibilities.  Second choose $L$, an isotropic $\ell$-space in the
$2a$-dimensional symplectic space $Y$.  The standard symplectic
count (see~\cite[Lemma~1(a)]{KiermaierSchmidtWassermann} and
\cite[Section~8, Exercise~8.1(ii)]{Taylor}) gives
\[
 \prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}
 \frac{q^{2a-2i}-1}{q^{\ell-i}-1}
\]
possibilities.

It remains to count the spaces $H$ having these fixed $J$ and $L$.
For every linear map
\[
 f:L\longrightarrow K/J,
\]
choose a basis of $L$, choose in $K$ a representative of the coset
$f(u)$ for each basis vector $u$, and extend these choices linearly
to a map $\widetilde f:L\to K$.  Define
\[
 H_f=J+\{u+\widetilde f(u):u\in L\}.
\]
Changing $\widetilde f$ by a map from $L$ to $J$ does not change
$H_f$, so $H_f$ depends only on $f$.  Conversely, a space $H$ with
$H\cap K=J$ and $p(H)=L$ determines such an $f$: for $u\in L$,
choose $u+k\in H$ and set $f(u)=k+J$.  This is well-defined because
two choices of $k$ differ by an element of $H\cap K=J$.  Therefore
$f\mapsto H_f$ is a bijection.

There are consequently
\[
 q^{\dim L\,\dim(K/J)}
 =q^{\ell(r_0-h+\ell)}
\]
possible spaces $H$.  Every $H_f$ is isotropic, since $K$ is the
radical and hence, for $u,v\in L$,
\[
 A\bigl(u+\widetilde f(u),v+\widetilde f(v)\bigr)=A(u,v)=0.
\]
Multiplying the three counts and
summing over the feasible values of $\ell$ proves
\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-exact}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:isotropic-uniform}
Let $X$ be an $R$-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-space and
let $A\in\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ have rank $2a$, where $q\ge2$ is a prime power and $0\le a\le\lfloor R/2\rfloor$.  Then
for $0\le h\le R$, the size $I_h(A)$ of the $h$-dimensional isotropic locus of $A$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:isotropic-uniform}
 \frac{I_h(A)}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{h}_{q}}
 \le \frac43\,\pi_\infty(2)^{-4}q^{-\kappa_h(a)}.
\end{equation}
               
    
                                         
    
                                                                   
In particular, if
$a\ge h-1$, then we have
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:gamma-bound}
 \frac{I_h(A)}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{h}_{q}}
 \le \gamma_q q^{-\binom h2},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align}
 \gamma_q^-&=
 \sum_{j\ge1}q^{-3j(j-1)/2}
 \cdot
 \frac{\prod_{u=j}^{\infty}(1-q^{-2u})}
      {\pi_j(q)},\label{p12:eq:gamma-minus}\\
 \gamma_q^+&=
 1+\sum_{j\ge1}q^{-j(3j+1)/2}\cdot\frac1{\pi_j(q)},
 \label{p12:eq:gamma-plus}\\
 \gamma_q&=\max\{\gamma_q^-,\gamma_q^+\}.\label{p12:eq:gamma}
\end{align}
