These constants satisfy $\gamma_2<1.72$, $\gamma_q<1.563$ and $\frac{\gamma_q}{q-1}<\frac{391}{500}=0.782$ for $q\geq 3$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
If $h=0$ or $h=1$, every $h$-space is isotropic.  The first assertion
is then immediate from \eqref{p12:eq:kappa-definition} and
$\frac43\pi_\infty(2)^{-4}>1$, while
\eqref{p12:eq:gamma-bound} follows from $\gamma_q\ge1$.  For the remainder of the proof, we assume
$h\ge2$. For brevity throughout this proof, write $\pi_n=\pi_n(q)$.


From \cref{p12:lem:isotropic-exact}, let
\[
 T_{a,\ell}
 =\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{r_0}{j}_{q}\cdot
  q^{\ell(r_0-j)}\cdot
  \prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}
  \frac{q^{2a-2i}-1}{q^{\ell-i}-1}
\]
be the summand in
\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-exact} whose image in the symplectic quotient has
dimension $\ell$, where we substitute
$j=h-\ell$ and $r_0=R-2a$.

We first separate the powers of $q$ from the finite products.  The
Gaussian factor is
\[
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{r_0}{j}_{q}=\frac{\pi_{r_0}}{\pi_j\pi_{r_0-j}}\cdot q^{j(r_0-j)}.
\]
For the symplectic factor, extracting the leading power of $q$ from
the numerator gives the exponent
$2a\ell-\ell(\ell-1)$, whereas the denominator gives
$\ell(\ell+1)/2$. Indeed,
$\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}2i=\ell(\ell-1)$ and
$\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}k=\ell(\ell+1)/2$.  Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-1}
 \frac{q^{2a-2i}-1}{q^{\ell-i}-1}
 &=\frac{\prod_{u=a-\ell+1}^{a}(1-q^{-2u})}{\pi_\ell}
   \cdot q^{(2a\ell-\ell(\ell-1))-\ell(\ell+1)/2}\\
 &=\frac{\prod_{u=a-\ell+1}^{a}(1-q^{-2u})}{\pi_\ell}
   \cdot q^{\ell(4a-3\ell+1)/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]


Since $j+\ell=h$, multiplication of the three factors yields
\[
 T_{a,\ell}
 =\frac{\pi_{r_0}}
       {\pi_j\pi_{r_0-j}\pi_\ell}
  \prod_{u=a-\ell+1}^{a}(1-q^{-2u})\cdot q^{E_{a,\ell}},
 \qquad\text{where}~
 E_{a,\ell}
 =h(r_0-j)+\frac{\ell(4a-3\ell+1)}2.
\]
On the other hand, the ambient Grassmannian has size $\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{h}_{q}
 =\frac{\pi_R}{\pi_h\pi_{R-h}}\cdot q^{h(R-h)}$. Therefore, the exponent of $q$ in
$q^{\binom h2}T_{a,\ell}/\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{h}_{q}$ is
 $\binom h2+E_{a,\ell}-h(R-h)$.
Using $R=r_0+2a$ and $h=j+\ell$, we have 
\[
\begin{split}
 2(\binom h2+E_{a,\ell}-h(R-h))&=h(h-1)+2h(r_0-j)+\ell(4a-3\ell+1)-2h(R-h)\\
 &=3h^2-h-2hj-4ah+4a\ell-3\ell^2+\ell\\
 &=j^2+4j\ell-j-4aj\\
 &=-j(4a-h-3\ell+1)=-j(4a-4h+3j+1).
\end{split}
\]
Combining this exponent calculation with the finite products gives
the exact normalised identity
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:isotropic-normalised-term}
 \frac{T_{a,\ell}}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{h}_{q}}
 =\frac{\pi_{r_0}\pi_h\pi_{R-h}}
 {\pi_j\pi_{r_0-j}\pi_\ell\pi_R}
 \prod_{u=a-\ell+1}^{a}(1-q^{-2u})\cdot q^{-(\binom{h}{2}+j(4a-4h+3j+1)/2)}.
\end{equation}

Thus the loss relative to the ambient Grassmannian exponent
$h(R-h)$ is
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:isotropic-full-loss}
 L(a,j)=\binom h2+\frac{j(4a-4h+3j+1)}2.
\end{equation}

Recall that we are summing $\ell$ from $\max\{0,h-r_0\}$ to $\min\{h,a\}$. Substituting $j=h-\ell$ gives the range 
\[
 \max\{0,h-a\}\le j\le\min\{h,r_0\}.
\]
If $h>r_0+a$, this interval is empty.  Hence there is no isotropic $h$-space and
$I_h(A)=0$, so the desired upper bound is automatic. 

Assume now that $h\leq r_0+a$.  Note that
\[
 L(a,j+1)-L(a,j)=3j+2a-2h+2.
\]
If $a\le h-1$, the left endpoint is $j=h-a$.  At this point the
first difference is $h-a+2>0$, and it increases with $j$.
Consequently, $L(a,j)$ is increasing throughout the feasible range,
so its minimum is attained at $j=h-a$.  Substitution in
\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-full-loss} gives
\[
 L(a,h-a)=\frac{a(2h-a-1)}2.
\]
If $a\ge h$, the left endpoint is $j=0$, and the first difference is $2a-2h+2>0$.
Thus the minimum is
\[
 L(a,0)=\binom h2.
\]
These two values are exactly $\kappa_h(a)$, so every feasible
summand has loss at least $\kappa_h(a)$.  We now sum the losses more
carefully.  The finite-product factor in
\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-normalised-term} is at most
$\pi_\infty(2)^{-4}$.

If $a\le h-1$, put $j_0=h-a$.  For every $m\ge0$ for which
$j_0+m$ is feasible, the first-difference formula gives
\[
 L(a,j_0+m)-\kappa_h(a)\ge3m.
\]
If $a\ge h$, the left endpoint is $j_0=0$, and similarly
\[
 L(a,m)-\kappa_h(a)\ge2m.
\]
Consequently, in both cases,
\[
 \sum_{j\text{ feasible}}q^{-L(a,j)}
 \le q^{-\kappa_h(a)}\sum_{m\ge0}q^{-2m}
 \le \frac43q^{-\kappa_h(a)}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-normalised-term} proves
\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-uniform}. 
                                                                         
                                                         

\medskip

We now obtain a sharper constant in the high-rank regime $a\ge h-1$, where the exponent loss has saturated at $\binom h2$. We separate the threshold rank $a=h-1$ from the higher ranks $a\ge h$.
\paragraph{Rank $a=h-1$.}
Here the feasible range begins at $j=1$.  Formula
\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-normalised-term} becomes
\[
 \frac1{\pi_j}
 \left(
 \frac{\pi_{R-2h+2}}{\pi_{R-2h+2-j}}
 \frac{\pi_h}{\pi_{h-j}}
 \frac{\pi_{R-h}}{\pi_R}
 \prod_{u=j}^{h-1}(1-q^{-2u})
 \right)\cdot q^{-3j(j-1)/2}.
\]
We claim that the parenthesised factor is at most $\prod_{u=j}^{\infty}(1-q^{-2u})$.
It is
enough to show
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:finite-product-comparison}
 \frac{\pi_{R-2h+2}}{\pi_{R-2h+2-j}}
 \frac{\pi_h}{\pi_{h-j}}
 \frac{\pi_{R-h}}{\pi_R}
 \le \prod_{u=h}^{\infty}(1-q^{-2u}).
\end{equation}
Since $a=h-1$, the radical has dimension
$r_0=R-2h+2$. Also note that $j\le r_0$.  
Using $\log(1-q^{-n})=-\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{q^{-mn}}m$, the logarithm of the left-hand side
of~\eqref{p12:eq:finite-product-comparison} is
\[
 -\sum_{m\ge1}\frac1m\left(
   \sum_{n=r_0-j+1}^{r_0}q^{-mn}
   +\sum_{n=h-j+1}^{h}q^{-mn}
   -\sum_{n=R-h+1}^{R}q^{-mn}
 \right),
\]
whereas the logarithm of the right-hand side is
\[
 -\sum_{m\ge1}\frac1m\sum_{u=h}^{\infty}q^{-2um}.
\]
For every integer $m\ge1$, put $x=q^{-m}\le1/2$. We have
\[
 \sum_{n=r_0-j+1}^{r_0}x^n
 \ge jx^{r_0}
 \ge h x^{r_0+h-1}
 \ge \sum_{n=R-h+1}^{R}x^n~~\text{and}~~
 \sum_{n=h-j+1}^{h}x^n\ge x^h
 \ge \frac{x^{2h}}{1-x^2}
 =\sum_{u=h}^{\infty}x^{2u}
\]
because $h x^{h-1}\le1$ for $x\le1/2$ and $h\ge2$. Thus, for every $m\ge1$,
\[
 \sum_{n=r_0-j+1}^{r_0}q^{-mn}
 +\sum_{n=h-j+1}^{h}q^{-mn}
 -\sum_{n=R-h+1}^{R}q^{-mn}
 \ge \sum_{u=h}^{\infty}q^{-2um}.
\]
This proves~\eqref{p12:eq:finite-product-comparison}. Extending the
feasible sum to all $j\ge1$ then proves the bound by $\gamma_q^-$. 

\paragraph{Ranks $a\ge h$.}
Here the feasible range begins at $j=0$, and $\ell=h-j$.
Formula~\eqref{p12:eq:isotropic-normalised-term} shows that the
contribution of the $j$th summand to
$q^{\binom h2}I_h(A)/\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{R}{h}_{q}$ is
\[
 \frac1{\pi_j}
 \left(
  \frac{\pi_{R-2a}}{\pi_{R-2a-j}}
  \frac{\pi_h}{\pi_{h-j}}
  \frac{\pi_{R-h}}{\pi_R}
  \prod_{u=a-h+j+1}^{a}(1-q^{-2u})
 \right)
 \cdot q^{-j(4a-4h+3j+1)/2}.
\]
We claim that the parenthesised factor is at most one.  Note that
$r_0=R-2a$.  Since $j\le r_0$, its first ratio is
\[
 \frac{\pi_{r_0}}{\pi_{r_0-j}}
 =\prod_{n=r_0-j+1}^{r_0}(1-q^{-n})\le1.
\]
It remains to compare the other numerator factors with the $h$
denominator factors in $\pi_R/\pi_{R-h}$.  Note that
\[
 \frac{\pi_h}{\pi_{h-j}}
 \prod_{u=a-h+j+1}^{a}(1-q^{-2u})
 =\prod_{t=0}^{j-1}(1-q^{-(h-j+1+t)})
  \prod_{t=0}^{h-j-1}(1-q^{-2(a-h+j+1+t)}),
\]
whereas
\[
 \frac{\pi_R}{\pi_{R-h}}
 =\prod_{t=0}^{j-1}(1-q^{-(R-h+1+t)})
  \prod_{t=0}^{h-j-1}(1-q^{-(R-h+j+1+t)}).
\]
For the first pair of blocks, since $R\ge2a\geq 2h$, we have
\[
 h-j+1+t\le R-h+1+t,
 \qquad 0\le t<j.
\]
For the second pair, we have
\[
 2(a-h+j+1+t)\le R-h+j+1+t,
 \qquad 0\le t<h-j,
\]
because the right-hand side minus the left-hand side is
$r_0+h-j-1-t\ge0$.  Since $1-q^{-n}$ increases with $n$, each
numerator factor is at most the corresponding denominator factor.
Thus the parenthesised factor is at most one, as claimed.

Finally, $a\ge h$ gives
\[
 \frac{j(4a-4h+3j+1)}2\ge\frac{j(3j+1)}2.
\]
Consequently, the $j$th normalized contribution is at most
\[
 \frac1{\pi_j}\cdot q^{-j(3j+1)/2}.
\]
This also includes $j=0$, with the usual convention that an empty
product is one.  Extending the feasible sum to every $j\ge0$ proves
the bound by $\gamma_q^+$.

\paragraph{Explicit numerical estimates.}  For $q=2$, the
$j=1$ term of \eqref{p12:eq:gamma-minus} is less than
\[
 2(1-2^{-2})(1-2^{-4})(1-2^{-6})<1.4.
\]
The $j=2$ term is less than
\[
 \frac13(1-2^{-4})(1-2^{-6})<0.308.
\]
By \eqref{p12:eq:pi-infinity-two-lower} and \eqref{p12:eq:uniform-pi},
$\pi_j(2)\ge\pi_\infty(2)>1/4$.  Thus the tail $j\ge3$ is less than
\[
 4\sum_{j\ge3}2^{-3j(j-1)/2}<0.008.
\]
Therefore $\gamma_2^-<1.716$.  Similarly,
\[
 \gamma_2^+
 \le1+\frac12+4\sum_{j\ge2}2^{-j(3j+1)/2}<1.533.
\]
Hence $\gamma_2<1.72$.

For $q\ge3$ we give a completely explicit estimate, since this
is the only numerical input in the boundary argument.  The $j=1$ and
$j=2$ terms of $\gamma_q^-$ are bounded by
\[
 \frac1{1-q^{-1}}\le\frac32,
 \qquad
 \frac{q^{-3}}{(1-q^{-1})(1-q^{-2})}\le\frac1{16}.
\]
For every $j\ge3$ the numerator in \eqref{p12:eq:gamma-minus} is at most
one, whereas
\[
 \pi_j(q)
 \ge 1-\sum_{i\ge1}q^{-i}\ge\frac12.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum_{j\ge3}
 q^{-3j(j-1)/2}
 \cdot
 \frac{\prod_{u=j}^{\infty}(1-q^{-2u})}
      {\pi_j(q)}
 \le2\sum_{j\ge3}3^{-3j(j-1)/2}<\frac1{9000}.
\]
Thus
\[
 \gamma_q^-<\frac32+\frac1{16}+\frac1{9000}<1.563.
\]
Similarly, the $j=1$ term of $\gamma_q^+$ is at most $1/6$, and
\[
 \gamma_q^+
 <1+\frac16+2\sum_{j\ge2}3^{-j(3j+1)/2}<1.169.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \gamma_q<1.563,
 \qquad
 \frac{\gamma_q}{q-1}
 <\frac{1.563}{2}<\frac{391}{500}=0.782
 \qquad(q\ge3).
\]
This proves the stated bounds.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:hollowing-min-dim}
Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-space, let
$0\le h<\dim X$, and let $\mathcal A\le\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ be $h$-hollowing.  Then
$\dim\mathcal A\ge h$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
From $\mathcal A$, define the dual alternating map $\beta_{\mathcal A}:\wedge^2X\longrightarrow\mathcal A^*$ by $\beta_{\mathcal A}(x\wedge y)(A)=A(x,y)$ for any $A\in\mathcal A$. 
The dual map $\beta_{\mathcal A}^*:\mathcal A\to\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ is just the inclusion of
$\mathcal A$ into $\operatorname{Alt}(X)$.  It is injective, so $\beta_{\mathcal A}$ is
surjective.  By \cref{p12:prop:sims-hollowing-dictionary}, we have $h<s(\beta_{\mathcal A})$.
The original Sims rank bound \cite[Proposition~5.2]{BNV} then gives
\[
 h<s(\beta_{\mathcal A})\le\dim\mathcal A^*+1=\dim\mathcal A+1.
  \]
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:exponent-away}
Let $X$ be an $R$-dimensional
$\mathbb F_q$-space, and let
$\mathcal H_q(R,M,h)$ be the set of $M$-dimensional
$h$-hollowing subspaces of $\operatorname{Alt}(X)$, where
$1\le h<R$ and $h\le M\le\binom h2$.  Assume either that $q\ge3$, or
that $q=2$ and $M\le\binom h2-1$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:exponent-away}
 \log_q|\mathcal H_q(R,M,h)|
 \le (M-h)\binom R2+O(R^2+M^2).
\end{equation}
Here $\log_q0=-\infty$, and the implied constant is absolute.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The range $h\le M\le\binom h2$ is nonempty only when $h\ge3$.
                      
    
                           
                           
     
                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
    
                               
                             
    
                                                                                                                          
Recall that an $h$-hollowing $M$-space $\mathcal A\le\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:covering-property}
\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)=\bigcup_{0\ne A\in\mathcal A}\mathcal Z_h(A),
\qquad
\mathcal Z_h(A)=\{H\in\operatorname{Gr}(h,X):A|_{H\times H}=0\}.
\end{equation}
\cref{p12:lem:isotropic-uniform} shows that if $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2a$, then
\[
\frac{|\mathcal Z_h(A)|}{|\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)|}
\le q^{-\kappa_h(a)+O(1)}.
\]
Since $\kappa_h(a)$ is nondecreasing in $a$, forms of higher rank have uniformly smaller isotropic loci, up to the point where the exponent loss saturates at $\binom h2$. Consequently, once the combined contribution of the high-rank forms is shown to be small, the low-rank forms must cover a positive proportion of $\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$. This leads to a better upper bound on $\mathcal H_q(R,M,h)$ if we can isolate sufficiently many low-rank basis elements in $\mathcal A$ through the above discussion.
                                                                     
                                                                
                                                                     
                                                                       
                                                                    
                                                                       
            
                                                                  
                                             

                                                              
                                                                      
                                                                     
                                                                  
                                                                      
                            
                                                                
                                          

Fix an $h$-hollowing $M$-space $\mathcal A\le \operatorname{Alt}(X)$.  For
$1\le a\le h-2$, let
\[
 \mathcal L_a(\mathcal A)=\mathrm{span}\{A\in\mathcal A:\operatorname{rank} A\le 2a\},
 \qquad
 k_a=\dim\mathcal L_a(\mathcal A).
\]
For nonzero $A\in\mathcal L_a(\mathcal A)$, write $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2r$.  Then $r\ge1$, so
$\kappa_h(r)\ge\kappa_h(1)=h-1$.  Hence
\cref{p12:lem:isotropic-uniform} gives
\[
 \frac{|\mathcal Z_h(A)|}{|\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)|}\le q^{-h+O(1)}.
\]
There are fewer than $q^{k_a}$ such forms, so their isotropic loci
cover at most $q^{k_a-h+O(1)}$ of the Grassmannian. 

On the other hand, every element of $\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal L_a(\mathcal A)$ has rank at least $2a+2$.
There are fewer than $q^M/(q-1)$ projective directions in $\mathcal A$.~\footnote{We count projective directions here since $\mathcal Z_h(A)=\mathcal Z_h(\lambda A)$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb F_q^\times$.}
                                                                  
Thus, by the first estimate in
\cref{p12:lem:isotropic-uniform}, the directions outside
$\mathcal L_a(\mathcal A)$ cover at most
\[
 \frac{1}{q-1}\cdot q^{M-\kappa_h(a+1)+O(1)}
\]
of the Grassmannian.  The covering property
\eqref{p12:eq:covering-property} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:incidence-split}
 1\le q^{k_a-h+O(1)}
 +\frac{1}{q-1}\cdot q^{M-\kappa_h(a+1)+O(1)}.
\end{equation}

We now choose the cutoff $a$ based on $h$ and $M$. Fix a sufficiently large absolute
constant $C$ such that replacing $M-\kappa_h(a+1)$ by $-C$ in the second term of~\eqref{p12:eq:incidence-split} makes the second term less than $1/2$. If $\binom h2-M\ge C$, choose the least $a$ such that $\kappa_h(a+1)-M\ge C$.
Such an $a\le h-2$ exists because
$\kappa_h(h-1)=\binom h2$. In this setting, 
\[
 \frac{1}{2}\le q^{k_a-h+O(1)}~~\Rightarrow~~k_a\ge h-O(1).
\]

If instead $\binom h2-M<C$, choose $a=h-2$ and put
$\ell=\binom h2-M$.  The directions outside
$\mathcal L_{h-2}(\mathcal A)$ have rank at least $2h-2$, so the estimate
\eqref{p12:eq:gamma-bound} shows that they cover at most
\[
 \frac{\gamma_q}{q-1}q^{-\ell}
\]
of $\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$.  If $q\ge3$, this is less than
$391/500<43/50$.  If $q=2$, the hypothesis gives $\ell\ge1$, so it
is at most $\gamma_2/2<43/50$.  Hence the low-rank directions cover
more than $7/50$, and the first-group estimate gives again
\[
 k_{h-2}\ge h-O(1).
\]
                                                                   
                                                           
                                                                       
                                          

Note that the cutoff of $a$ chosen above satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:cutoff-cost}
 ha=O(M).
\end{equation}
Indeed, in the first case, the minimal choice of $a$ gives either
$a=1$, or
\[
 \kappa_h(a)<M+C.
\]
If $a\le h/2$, then
$\kappa_h(a)=a(2h-a-1)/2=\Omega(ha)$.  If $a>h/2$, then
$M=\Omega(h^2)$, and again $ha=O(M)$.  In the second case,
$a=h-2$ and $M>\binom h2-C$, so the same conclusion holds.  The
bounded values of $h$ are absorbed into the implied constant.

It remains to count the low-rank choices.  Put
$\rho=\min\{a,\lfloor R/2\rfloor\}$.  By
\cref{p12:lem:universal-field}, the number of alternating forms on $X$
of rank at most $2a$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:rank-variety}
 q^{\rho(2R-2\rho-1)+O(1)}=q^{O(aR)}.
\end{equation}
When $a>R/2$, this also includes the trivial count of all alternating
forms on $X$.

There is an absolute constant $C_0$ such that
$k_a\ge h-C_0$.  Put $d=\min\{h,k_a\}$, so
$h-C_0\le d\le h$.  Every space $\mathcal A$ has an ordered basis whose
first $d$ members are independent rank-$\le2a$ forms from
$\mathcal L_a(\mathcal A)$.  For an upper bound, choose these first $d$ forms from
the rank-$\le2a$ variety and choose the remaining $M-d$ forms freely
from $\operatorname{Alt}(X)$, allowing dependent choices.  Counting these ordered
lists only enlarges the number of possible spaces.  Therefore
\[
\begin{split}
 \log_q|\mathcal H_q(R,M,h)|
 &\le d\,O(aR)+(M-d)\binom R2\\
 &\le (M-h)\binom R2+O(haR+R^2)\\
 &\le (M-h)\binom R2+O(MR+R^2),
\end{split}
\]
where the second inequality holds since $haR=O(MR)$. Moreover, since $MR\le\frac{R^2+M^2}{2}$, this proves \eqref{p12:eq:exponent-away}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:minimal-reduction}
Let $X$ be an $R$-dimensional $\mathbb F_2$-space, let $3\le h<R$, and put
$M=\binom h2$.  Let $\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{nonmin}}$ be the family
of $M$-dimensional $h$-hollowing subspaces of $\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ that are not
minimally $h$-hollowing.  Then
\[
 \log_2|\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{nonmin}}|
 \le (M-h)\binom R2+O(R^2+M^2).
\]
The implied constants are absolute.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Every $\mathcal A\in\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{nonmin}}$ contains a proper
minimally $h$-hollowing subspace $\mathcal B$.  Put $t=\dim\mathcal B$.  By
\cref{p12:lem:hollowing-min-dim},
\[
 h\le t<M=\binom h2.
\]
For each fixed $t$, \cref{p12:prop:exponent-away} shows that the number of
possible $\mathcal B$ is at most
\[
 2^{(t-h)\binom R2+O(R^2+t^2)}
 \le
 2^{(t-h)\binom R2+O(R^2+M^2)}.
\]
For a fixed $\mathcal B$, the number of $M$-dimensional subspaces of
$\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ containing $\mathcal B$ is
\[
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{\binom R2-t}{M-t}_{2}
 \le \pi_\infty(2)^{-1}
 2^{(M-t)(\binom R2-M)}
 \le 2^{(M-t)\binom R2+2}.
\]
Multiplying these estimates and summing over $h\le t<M$ gives
\[
\begin{split}
 |\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{nonmin}}|
 &\le
 \sum_{t=h}^{M-1}
 2^{(t-h)\binom R2+O(R^2+M^2)}
 \cdot 2^{(M-t)\binom R2+2}\\
 &\le
 2^{(M-h)\binom R2+O(R^2+M^2)}.
\end{split}
\]
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:private-span}
Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-space, and let
$\mathcal B\le\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ be minimally $h$-hollowing.  For $H\in\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$, define 
\[
 \mathcal B_H:=\{A\in\mathcal B:A|_{H\times H}=0\}.
\]
Then those spaces $\mathcal B_H$ for which $\dim\mathcal B_H=1$ span $\mathcal B$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal B'$ be their span and suppose that $\mathcal B'$ is a proper subspace of 
$\mathcal B$.  Choose a hyperplane $\mathcal C$ of $\mathcal B$ which contains $\mathcal B'$. 

Consider $H\in\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$.  If $\dim\mathcal B_H=1$, then $\mathcal B_H\leq\mathcal B'\leq\mathcal C$ by the definition of $\mathcal B'$. If $\dim\mathcal B_H\ge2$, since $\mathcal C$ is a hyperplane in $\mathcal B$, it has codimension $1$ and thus
\[
 \dim(\mathcal C\cap\mathcal B_H)
 \ge 1.
\]
In either case $\mathcal C\cap\mathcal B_H$ contains a nonzero matrix for any $H\in\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$.  Hence $\mathcal C$
is $h$-hollowing, contradicting the minimal $h$-hollowing property
of $\mathcal B$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:private-rank}
Let $X$ be an $R$-dimensional $\mathbb F_2$-space, let
$\mathcal B\le\operatorname{Alt}(X)$ be minimally $h$-hollowing with
$\dim\mathcal B=\binom h2$, and let $H\in\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$ be such that
$\mathcal B_H=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{A\}$ for some nonzero $A\in\mathcal B$.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{rank} A\le \frac{10-\sqrt{10}}9 \cdot h^2+O(h),
\]
where the implied constant is absolute.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:endpoint-exponent}
There is an absolute integer $h_0$ such that the following holds.  Let
$X$ be an $R$-dimensional $\mathbb F_2$-space, let $h_0\le h<R$, and put
\[
 M=\binom h2,
 \qquad
 \kappa=\frac45,
 \qquad
 a_*=\min\left\{
       \left\lfloor\frac{\kappa h^2}{2}\right\rfloor,
       \left\lfloor\frac R2\right\rfloor
      \right\}.
\]
Let $\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{min}}$ be the family of $M$-dimensional
minimally $h$-hollowing subspaces of $\operatorname{Alt}(X)$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:endpoint-exponent}
 \log_2|\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{min}}|
 \le
 (M-h)\binom R2
 +h a_*(2R-2a_*-1)
 +O(hR+h^4).
\end{equation}
The implied constants are absolute.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Assume \cref{p12:prop:private-rank}. 
Since $\frac{10-\sqrt{10}}9<\kappa=4/5$, we may choose an absolute $h_0\ge3$ such that
\cref{p12:prop:private-rank} gives
\[
 \operatorname{rank} A\le\kappa h^2
\]
for every unique hollowing form $A$ arising from
\cref{p12:lem:private-span}.  Since these forms span $\mathcal B$, we may choose
$h$ linearly independent ones.  Their ranks are at most $2a_*$.

By \cref{p12:lem:universal-field}, the number of alternating forms on $X$
of rank at most $2a_*$ is at most
$2^{a_*(2R-2a_*-1)+O(1)}$.  Choose an ordered $h$-tuple of unique
hollowing forms from this set, and then choose the remaining $M-h$
ordered basis forms arbitrarily from the $\binom R2$-dimensional
space $\operatorname{Alt}(X)$.  Hence
\[
 \log_2|\mathfrak A_M^{\mathrm{min}}|
 \le
 (M-h)\binom R2
 +h a_*(2R-2a_*-1)+O(h).
\]
This proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:rank-bound-private-span}
For every $A\in\mathcal B_H$, let $J=H\cap\operatorname{rad} A$ and choose $H_1\le H$ such that $H=H_1\oplus J$. Let $d=\dim H-\dim J$. Define
\[
 H^{\perp_A}=\{x\in\mathbb F_2^R:{x}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah=0\text{ for every }h\in H\},
\]
and choose $X_0\le H^{\perp_A}$ such that
\[
 H^{\perp_A}=\operatorname{rad} A\oplus H_1\oplus X_0.
\]
Then there exist a $d$-dimensional complement $Y$ of $H^{\perp_A}$ in
$\mathbb F_2^R$ and bases adapted to
\[
 \mathbb F_2^R=\operatorname{rad} A\oplus H_1\oplus X_0\oplus Y
\]
for which
\[
 A=
 \bordermatrix{
          &\operatorname{rad} A&H_1&X_0&Y\cr
  \operatorname{rad} A  &0&0&0&0\cr
  H_1     &0&0&0&I_d\cr
  X_0     &0&0&B_0&D\cr
  Y       &0&I_d&{D}^{\mathrm{t}}&E\cr
 },
\]
where $B_0$ is the coefficient matrix of $A|_{X_0\times X_0}$ and is invertible, $D\in\mathbb F_2^{\dim X_0\times d}$ and $E\in\mathbb F_2^{d\times d}$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:rank-A-X0}
 \operatorname{rank} A=2d+\dim X_0\le 2\dim H+\dim X_0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Since $J\le\operatorname{rad} A$ and $H=H_1\oplus J$, we have $\operatorname{rad} A+H=\operatorname{rad} A\oplus H_1$,
and hence $H^{\perp_A}=\operatorname{rad} A\oplus H_1\oplus X_0$.
 
The restriction of $A$ to $X_0$ is nondegenerate.  Indeed, suppose
$u\in X_0$ satisfies
\[
 {u}^{\mathrm{t}}Av=0\qquad\text{for every }v\in X_0.
\]
Since $u\in H^{\perp_A}$, we also have ${u}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah'=0$ for every $h'\in H_1\leq H$.
Moreover, ${u}^{\mathrm{t}}Ar=0$ for every $r\in\operatorname{rad} A$.  Every
$w\in H^{\perp_A}$ can be written as $w=r+h'+v$ with
$r\in\operatorname{rad} A$, $h'\in H_1$, and $v\in X_0$.  Therefore
\[
 {u}^{\mathrm{t}}Aw={u}^{\mathrm{t}}Ar+{u}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah'+{u}^{\mathrm{t}}Av=0.
\]
Thus $u\in(H^{\perp_A})^{\perp_A}$.  Since it is straightforward to verify that $(H^{\perp_A})^{\perp_A}=\operatorname{rad} A\oplus H_1$,
we have $u\in (\operatorname{rad} A\oplus H_1)\cap X_0$. The direct-sum choice of $X_0$ gives
$u=0$.  Therefore $B_0$ is invertible.

Consider the linear map $T:\mathbb F_2^R\longrightarrow H^*$ defined by mapping $x$ to $T(x):~H\to\mathbb F_2$, where $T(x)(h)={x}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah$ for any $h\in H$.
Its kernel is precisely $H^{\perp_A}$. The transpose map of $T$ is ${T}^{\mathrm{t}}:H\longrightarrow(\mathbb F_2^R)^*$, defined by mapping $h$ to ${T}^{\mathrm{t}}(h):\mathbb F_2^R\to\mathbb F_2$, where ${T}^{\mathrm{t}}(h)(x)={h}^{\mathrm{t}}{A}^{\mathrm{t}}x$ for any $x\in\mathbb F_2^R$. Since $A$ is alternating, ${A}^{\mathrm{t}}=A$ over $\mathbb F_2$. Thus, the kernel of ${T}^{\mathrm{t}}$ is $J=H\cap\operatorname{rad} A$.
Hence
\[
 \operatorname{codim}_{\mathbb F_2^R}H^{\perp_A}
 =\operatorname{rank} T =\operatorname{rank} {T}^{\mathrm{t}}
 =\dim H-\dim J=d.
\]
Choose a $d$-dimensional complement $Y$ of $H^{\perp_A}$ in $\mathbb F_2^R$.  The
pairing between $H_1$ and $Y$ is nondegenerate.  Indeed, if $y\in Y$
is orthogonal to $H_1$, then ${y}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah'=0$ for any $h'\in H_1$.
Since $J\le\operatorname{rad} A$, we also have ${y}^{\mathrm{t}}Ar=0$ for any $r\in J$.
Every $h\in H=H_1\oplus J$ can be written as $h=h'+r$, and hence
\[
 {y}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah={y}^{\mathrm{t}}Ah'+{y}^{\mathrm{t}}Ar=0.
\]
Thus $y\in H^{\perp_A}$.  Since $Y\cap H^{\perp_A}=0$, we have $y=0$.
As $\dim H_1=\dim Y=d$, the pairing is nondegenerate, and we may
choose dual bases for which its coefficient matrix is $I_d$.

Choose bases of $\operatorname{rad} A,H_1,X_0,Y$ in this order.  We may write 
\[
 A=
 \bordermatrix{
          &\operatorname{rad} A&H_1&X_0&Y\cr
  \operatorname{rad} A  &0&0&0&0\cr
  H_1     &0&0&0&I_d\cr
  X_0     &0&0&B_0&D\cr
  Y       &0&I_d&{D}^{\mathrm{t}}&E\cr
 },
\]
where $B_0$ is the coefficient matrix of $A|_{X_0\times X_0}$ and is invertible, $D\in\mathbb F_2^{\dim X_0\times d}$ is responsible for the pairing between $X_0$ and $Y$ and $E\in\mathbb F_2^{d\times d}$ is the coefficient matrix of $A|_{Y\times Y}$. 

Applying Gaussian elimination to the block form then gives
\[
 \operatorname{rank} A
 =2d+\dim X_0
 \le2\dim H+\dim X_0,
\]
which proves the result.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\cref{p12:lem:rank-bound-private-span} also holds over an arbitrary field. In this case, we replace the two lower-left blocks $I_d$ and ${D}^{\mathrm{t}}$ by $-I_d$ and $-{D}^{\mathrm{t}}$, respectively, and the proof proceeds similarly.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:private-row-basis}
Let $\mathcal B$ be a minimally $h$-hollowing alternating matrix space in $\mathbb F_2^{R\times R}$ of
dimension $M=\binom h2$.  Fix an $H\in\operatorname{Gr}(h,X)$ satisfying
$\mathcal B_H=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{A\}$.
Let $A=A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_M$ be a basis of $\mathcal B$. Then there exists an ordered basis $z_1,\ldots,z_h$ of $H$, such that the rows
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\mathbf r(z_i,z_j), &&1\le i<j\le h-2,\\
 &\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1}),\quad\mathbf r(z_i,z_h),
     &&1\le i\le h-2,
 \end{aligned}
\]
form a basis of
\[
 V_0=\{(c_1,\ldots,c_M)\in\mathbb F_2^{1\times M}:c_1=0\}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal B_H=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{A\}$, the right kernel of
$\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H}$ is spanned by $(1,0,\ldots,0)$, and hence
$\operatorname{rank}\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H}=M-1$.  Thus the left kernel is
one-dimensional.  For any ordered basis $z_1,\ldots,z_h$ of
$H$, there exists a unique nonzero solution $(\tau_{ij})_{1\le i<j\le h}$ satisfying
\[
 \sum_{1\le i<j\le h}\tau_{ij}\mathbf r(z_i,z_j)=0.
\]
After reordering the $z_i$, we may assume that $\tau_{h-1,h}=1$.
If the first $M-1$ rows were dependent, their relation would give
a second element of the left kernel whose $(h-1,h)$-coordinate is
zero, contradicting the uniqueness of $(\tau_{ij})$.  Hence, the first $M-1$ rows are linearly independent.  Since
$A=A_1$ vanishes on $H\times H$, these $M-1$ linearly independent rows lie in $V_0$ and thus also form a basis of $V_0$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:perturbed-test-spaces}
Let $H=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{z_1,\dots,z_h\}$ with the ordered basis obtained from~\cref{p12:lem:private-row-basis}. Let $X_0\le H^{\perp_A}$ be the complement of $\operatorname{rad} A+H$ in $H^{\perp_A}$. For $u,v\in X_0$, define $H_{u,v}
 =K+\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{z_{h-1}+u\}
  +\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{z_h+v\}$.
Then the sum is direct and $\dim H_{u,v}=h$. 

Moreover, let $A=A_1,\ldots,A_M$ be the basis of $\mathcal B$ fixed in
\cref{p12:lem:private-row-basis}. With respect to the displayed ordered basis, the first $M-1$ rows of
$\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H_{u,v}}$ lie in $V_0$, while the remaining row has
first coordinate $b(u,v)={u}^{\mathrm{t}}Av$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We first verify the direct sum. Suppose that
\[
 k+a(z_{h-1}+u)+c(z_h+v)=0
\]
for some $k\in K$ and $a,c\in\mathbb F_2$.  Then
\[
 k+az_{h-1}+cz_h=au+cv.
\]
The left-hand side belongs to $H$, whereas the right-hand side belongs
to $X_0$.  Since $X_0\cap H=0$, both sides are zero.  The fact that
$z_1,\ldots,z_h$ is a basis of $H$ now gives $k=0$ and $a=c=0$.
Thus the displayed sum is direct, and
$\dim H_{u,v}=(h-2)+1+1=h$.

For the ``Moreover'' part, note that 
the first $M-1$ rows of $\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H_{u,v}}$ are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\mathbf r(z_i,z_j)\in W<V_0, &&1\le i<j\le h-2,\\
 &\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1}+u),\quad\mathbf r(z_i,z_h+v),
     &&1\le i\le h-2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first $\binom{h-2}{2}$ rows already lie in $V_0$. For $1\le i\le h-2$, since $A=A_1$ is alternating over $\mathbb F_2$, $A$ vanishes on $H$ and $u,v\in X_0\leq H^{\perp_A}$, we have
\[
 {z_i}^{\mathrm{t}}A(z_{h-1}+u)={u}^{\mathrm{t}}Az_i=0,
 \qquad
 {z_i}^{\mathrm{t}}A(z_h+v)={v}^{\mathrm{t}}Az_i=0.
\]
Thus all these rows lie in $V_0$.  The remaining row $\mathbf r(z_{h-1}+u,z_h+v)$ has first
coordinate
\[
 {(z_{h-1}+u)}^{\mathrm{t}}A(z_h+v)={u}^{\mathrm{t}}Av=b(u,v),
\]
because $A|_{H\times H}=0$ and $u,v\in H^{\perp_A}$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:private-coefficient-maps}
Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{A=A_1,\dots,A_M\}$, $H=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{z_1,\dots,z_h\}$ and $\mathcal B_H=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{A\}$ be defined as above. Let $X_0\le H^{\perp_A}$ be the complement of $\operatorname{rad} A+H$ in $H^{\perp_A}$.
For every $u\in X_0$ and $1\le i, j\le h-2$, there are unique
$w_j(u)\in W$ and unique coefficients
$P(u)_{ij},Q(u)_{ij}\in\mathbb F_2$ such that
\[
 \mathbf r(z_j,u)
 =w_j(u)
  +\sum_{i=1}^{h-2}P(u)_{ij}\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1})
  +\sum_{i=1}^{h-2}Q(u)_{ij}\mathbf r(z_i,z_h).
\]
Writing $P(u)=(P(u)_{ij})$ and $Q(u)=(Q(u)_{ij})$, the maps
$P,Q:X_0\to\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}$ are linear and satisfy $P(0)=Q(0)=0$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Since $u\in H^{\perp_A}$ and $z_j\in H$, and $A$ is alternating over
$\mathbb F_2$, we have ${z_j}^{\mathrm{t}}Au={u}^{\mathrm{t}}Az_j=0$, and hence
$\mathbf r(z_j,u)\in V_0$.  By
\cref{p12:lem:private-row-basis}, every vector of $V_0$ has a unique
expansion in the displayed basis.  This gives $w_j(u)$ and the
coefficients $P(u)_{ij},Q(u)_{ij}$.  Bilinearity of $\mathbf r$ and
uniqueness of the basis coefficients show that $P$ and $Q$ are
linear and satisfy $P(0)=Q(0)=0$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:private-determinant}
Let $P,Q:X_0\to\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}$ be the coefficient maps
defined in~\cref{p12:lem:private-coefficient-maps}.
For $u,v\in X_0$ such that $b(u,v)=1$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:compatible-minor}
 F(u,v)=
 \det\begin{pmatrix}
 I+P(u)&P(v)\\
 Q(u)&I+Q(v)
 \end{pmatrix}=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Fix $u,v\in X_0$ such that $b(u,v)=1$.  By
\cref{p12:lem:perturbed-test-spaces}, $H_{u,v}$ is an $h$-dimensional
subspace. Meanwhile, the first $M-1$ rows of $\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H_{u,v}}$ lie in $V_0$ and the last row has first coordinate $1$.

Since $\mathcal B$ is $h$-hollowing, there is a nonzero vector
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_M)\in\mathbb F_2^M$ such that
$\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H_{u,v}}{a}^{\mathrm{t}}=0$.  Thus the square matrix
$\mathcal R_{\mathcal B,H_{u,v}}$ is singular, and its rows satisfy a
nontrivial linear dependence.  The first $M-1$ rows lie in $V_0$,
whereas the last row has first coordinate one.  Comparing first
coordinates shows that the coefficient of the last row is zero.
Hence the first $M-1$ rows are linearly dependent.  Equivalently, there
are coefficients $\{\alpha_{ij}\}$, $\{\beta_i\}$, and $\{\gamma_i\}$,
not all zero, such that
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:linear-dependence-row}
 \sum_{1\le i<j\le h-2}\alpha_{ij}\mathbf r(z_i,z_j)
 +\sum_{i=1}^{h-2}\beta_i\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1}+u)
 +\sum_{i=1}^{h-2}\gamma_i\mathbf r(z_i,z_h+v)=0.
\end{equation}
Note that the coefficients $\beta_i,\gamma_i$ cannot all be zero, since the rows
$\mathbf r(z_i,z_j)$ are linearly independent by
\cref{p12:lem:private-row-basis}.  We now compute the coordinates of the
other two families of rows. Since
\[
\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1}+u)=\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1})+\mathbf r(z_i,u)~~\text{and}~~\mathbf r(z_i,z_h+v)=\mathbf r(z_i,z_h)+\mathbf r(z_i,v),
\]
substituting the expressions of $\mathbf r(z_i,u)$ and
$\mathbf r(z_i,v)$ in~\cref{p12:lem:private-coefficient-maps} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1}+u)
  &=w_i(u)
    +\sum_{j=1}^{h-2}\bigl(\delta_{ji}+P(u)_{ji}\bigr)
       \mathbf r(z_j,z_{h-1})
    +\sum_{j=1}^{h-2}Q(u)_{ji}\mathbf r(z_j,z_h),~~\text{and}\\
 \mathbf r(z_i,z_h+v)
  &=w_i(v)
    +\sum_{j=1}^{h-2}P(v)_{ji}\mathbf r(z_j,z_{h-1})
    +\sum_{j=1}^{h-2}\bigl(\delta_{ji}+Q(v)_{ji}\bigr)
       \mathbf r(z_j,z_h),
 \end{aligned}
\]
where $\delta_{ji}$ is the Kronecker delta and the vectors $w_i(u)$ and
$w_i(v)$ belong to $W$ and involve only the basis vectors
$\mathbf r(z_j,z_\ell)$ with $1\le j<\ell\le h-2$.  By
\cref{p12:lem:private-row-basis}, these basis vectors together with
\[
 \mathbf r(z_j,z_{h-1}),\quad\mathbf r(z_j,z_h),
 \qquad 1\le j\le h-2,
\]
are linearly independent. Substitute the above equations for $\mathbf r(z_i,z_{h-1}+u)$ and $\mathbf r(z_i,z_h+v)$ into~\eqref{p12:eq:linear-dependence-row}. For each $1\le j\le h-2$, the coefficients of
$\mathbf r(z_j,z_{h-1})$ and $\mathbf r(z_j,z_h)$ become
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{h-2}\bigl(\delta_{ji}+P(u)_{ji}\bigr)\beta_i
 +\sum_{i=1}^{h-2}P(v)_{ji}\gamma_i~~\mathrm{and}~~ \sum_{i=1}^{h-2}Q(u)_{ji}\beta_i
 +\sum_{i=1}^{h-2}\bigl(\delta_{ji}+Q(v)_{ji}\bigr)\gamma_i
\]
respectively.
These coefficients must be zero by linear independence.
Writing
\[
 \beta={(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_{h-2})}^{\mathrm{t}},
 \qquad
 \gamma={(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{h-2})}^{\mathrm{t}},
\]
these equations are equivalent to
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 I+P(u)&P(v)\\
 Q(u)&I+Q(v)
 \end{pmatrix}
 \binom{\beta}{\gamma}=0.
\]
Since $(\beta,\gamma)\ne0$ when $b(u,v)=1$, the block matrix is singular, and hence
$F(u,v)=0$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:RM-support}
Let $n,d\ge0$.  If a nonzero polynomial $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb F_2$ has degree at most $d$, then
\[
 |\operatorname{supp} f|\ge2^{n-d}.
\]
If, in addition, $f(0)=1$, then $\operatorname{codim}\mathrm{span}(\operatorname{supp} f)\le d$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
If $d\ge n$, the first assertion follows immediately from
$|\operatorname{supp} f|\ge1$.  If $0\le d\le n$, the evaluation vector of $f$ is a
nonzero codeword in the binary Reed--Muller code $\operatorname{RM}(d,n)$,
whose minimum distance is $2^{n-d}$; see
\cite{Reed,DelsarteGoethalsMacWilliams} and
\cite[Chapter~13]{MacWilliamsSloane}.

For the second assertion, let $S=\mathrm{span}(\operatorname{supp} f)$ and $c=\operatorname{codim} S$. 
After an invertible linear change of coordinates, which preserves the
algebraic degree and fixes the origin, we may assume that
\[
 S=\{x\in\mathbb F_2^n:x_1=\cdots=x_c=0\}.
\]
Thus $f(x)=0$ whenever at least one of $x_1,\ldots,x_c$ is equal to
$1$.  In the Boolean polynomial ring
\[
 \mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(x_1^2-x_1,\ldots,x_n^2-x_n),
\]
the factor $1+x_i$ is the indicator of the condition $x_i=0$.
Define
\[
 g(x_{c+1},\ldots,x_n)
 =f(0,\ldots,0,x_{c+1},\ldots,x_n).
\]
It follows that, as functions on $\mathbb F_2^n$,
\[
 f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
 =(1+x_1)\cdots(1+x_c)g(x_{c+1},\ldots,x_n).
\]
Indeed, when $x_1=\cdots=x_c=0$, the product of the first $c$
factors is $1$ and the right-hand side equals $f(x)$.  If some
$x_i=1$, then the product and $f(x)$ are both zero.  Finally,
$f(0)=1$ gives $g(0)=1$, so $g$ has constant term $1$.  The displayed
product therefore contains the monomial $x_1\cdots x_c$ with
coefficient $1$.  Hence $\deg f\ge c$, and the assumption
$\deg f\le d$ gives $\operatorname{codim}\mathrm{span}(\operatorname{supp} f)=c\le d$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:fibre-kernel}
For every $u\in S_0$, the linear map $R_u:X_0\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times (h-2)}$ defined in~\eqref{p12:eq:R_uv}
satisfies $\dim X_0\leq \dim R_u(X_0)+2(h-2)$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Fixing $u\in S_0$, let $U=\{w\in S_0:G_w=G_u\}$, where $G_u=Q(u)(I+P(u))^{-1}$. We first use~\cref{p12:lem:RM-support} to lower bound $|U|$. Note that $R_u(w)=Q(w)-G_uP(w)$. Meanwhile, since $w\in S_0$, $I+P(w)$ is invertible. The condition $G_w=G_u$ then gives
\[
  Q(w)(I+P(w))^{-1}=G_u~~\Leftrightarrow~~Q(w)=G_u(I+P(w))~~\Leftrightarrow~~R_u(w)=G_u.
\]
Thus, 
\[
 U=\{w\in R_u^{-1}(G_u):\det(I+P(w))=1\}.
\]
The affine space $R_u^{-1}(G_u)$ contains $u$. Indeed,
\[
  R_u(u)=Q(u)-G_uP(u)=Q(u)-G_u(I+P(u))+G_u=G_u,
\]
where the second equality uses the fact that $G_u(I+P(u))=Q(u)$.
Since $R_u^{-1}(G_u)$ is nonempty, it is a translate of $\ker R_u$
and therefore has dimension $\dim\ker R_u$.


 The polynomial $w\mapsto\det(I+P(w))$ has degree at
most $h-2$ and takes the value $1$ at $u$.  Its restriction to this
affine space is therefore nonzero.  Hence \cref{p12:lem:RM-support} gives
$|U|\ge2^{\dim\ker R_u-(h-2)}$.

We next upper bound $|U|$. Note that for any $w\in U$, we have $R_w(v)=R_u(v)$ for any $v\in X_0$. Thus, if $v\in \ker R_u$, then $\det(I+R_w(v))=\det I=1$, so
\eqref{p12:eq:support-orthogonality} gives $b(w,v)=0$.  Hence, for every
$w\in U$, the functional $b(w,-)$ vanishes on $\ker R_u$ and induces a
well-defined linear functional
\[
 \lambda_w:R_u(X_0)\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2,
 \qquad
 \lambda_w(R_u(v))=b(w,v).
\]

Apply the second assertion of \cref{p12:lem:RM-support} to the polynomial
$M\mapsto\det(I+M)$ on $R_u(X_0)$.  It has degree at most $h-2$ and takes
the value $1$ at $M=0$, so
\[
 L=\mathrm{span}\{M\in R_u(X_0):\det(I+M)=1\}
\]
has codimension at most $h-2$ in $R_u(X_0)$.  
On the other hand, every $\lambda_w$ belongs to the annihilator
\[
 L^\circ=\{\lambda\in R_u(X_0)^*: \lambda(M)=0
          \text{ for every }M\in L\}.
\]
Indeed, for any $M=R_u(v)$ satisfying $\det(I+M)=1$, since $R_u(v)=R_w(v)$ for any $v\in X_0$, we have $\det(I+R_w(v))=1$. By~\eqref{p12:eq:support-orthogonality}, $b(w,v)=0$. Thus,
\[
 \lambda_w(M)=\lambda_w(R_u(v))=b(w,v)=0.
\]
Since $\dim L^\circ=\operatorname{codim}_{R_u(X_0)}L\le h-2$,
the space $L^\circ$ contains at most $2^{h-2}$ functionals.

The map $w\mapsto\lambda_w$ is injective on $U$.  Indeed, if
$\lambda_w=\lambda_{w'}$, then $b(w+w',v)=0$ for every $v\in X_0$,
and the nondegeneracy of $b$ gives $w=w'$.  Therefore $|U|\le2^{h-2}$.
Together with $|U|\ge2^{\dim\ker R_u-(h-2)}$, this gives $\dim\ker R_u\le2(h-2)$. 
By rank--nullity,
\[
 \dim R_u(X_0)=\dim X_0-\dim\ker R_u\ge \dim X_0-2(h-2).
\]
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:GL-Fourier}
For $k\geq1$, let $1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}$ be the indicator function of
$\operatorname{GL}_k(2)\subseteq\mathbb F_2^{k\times k}$.  Put $\langle C,A\rangle=\operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}A)$
and define the unnormalised Fourier transform of $1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}$ as
\[
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)=
 \sum_{A\in \mathbb F_2^{k\times k}}1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}(A)(-1)^{\langle C,A\rangle}.
\]
If $\operatorname{rank} C=r$, then
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:GL-Fourier}
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)=
 (-1)^r2^{k(k-r)+\binom r2}
 \pi_{k-r}(2).
\end{equation}
In particular, $|\widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)|$ is nonincreasing as a function of
$r$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
For a subspace $U\le\mathbb F_2^k$, the M\"obius function of the subspace
lattice is $\mu(0,U)=(-1)^{\dim U}2^{\binom{\dim U}{2}}$.
Therefore
\[
 1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}(A)
 =1_{\ker A=0}
 =\sum_{U\le\ker A}\mu(0,U).
\]
Substitution into the Fourier sum gives
\[
\widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)=
 \sum_{U\le\mathbb F_2^k}\mu(0,U)
 \sum_{A:\,AU=0}(-1)^{\langle C,A\rangle}.
\]
For the inner sum, let $d=\dim U\leq k$. Write $a_i,c_i\in\mathbb F_2^k$
for the transposes of the $i$th rows of $A,C$, respectively.  The
condition $AU=0$ is equivalent to $a_i\in U^\perp$ for every $i$, and
\[
 \langle C,A\rangle
 =\operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}A)
 =\sum_{i=1}^k {c_i}^{\mathrm{t}}a_i.
\]
Thus the character $A\mapsto(-1)^{\langle C,A\rangle}$ is trivial on
the space $\{A:AU=0\}$ if and only if $c_i\in(U^\perp)^\perp=U$ for every $i$. 
This condition is equivalent to the row space of $C$ being
contained in $U$.  In this case every summand is $1$, so the inner
sum equals $2^{k(k-d)}$.

On the other hand, if the row space of $C$ is not contained in $U$, choose $i$ with
$c_i\notin U$.  Then there is $b\in U^\perp$ such that
${c_i}^{\mathrm{t}}b=1$.  Let $B$ be the matrix whose $i$th row is
${b}^{\mathrm{t}}$ and whose other rows are zero.  Then $BU=0$ and
$\langle C,B\rangle=1$.  Translation by $B$ permutes the matrices
satisfying $AU=0$ and changes the sign of every summand:
\[
 (-1)^{\langle C,A+B\rangle}
 =-(-1)^{\langle C,A\rangle}.
\]
The terms therefore cancel in pairs, and the inner character sum is zero. Thus,
\[
\widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)=
 \sum_{\substack{U\le\mathbb F_2^k\\
                  \operatorname{row}(C)\le U}}
 \mu(0,U)\,2^{k(k-\dim U)}.
\]

Now suppose that $\operatorname{rank} C=r$.  For each $r\le d\le k$, the number of
$d$-dimensional subspaces $U$ containing $\operatorname{row}(C)$
is $\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{k-r}{d-r}_{2}$.
Grouping the above sum according to $d=\dim U$ and substituting
the formula for $\mu(0,U)$ gives
\[
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)=
 \sum_{d=r}^{k}
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{k-r}{d-r}_{2}
 (-1)^d2^{\binom d2}2^{k(k-d)}.
\]
Writing $d=r+j$ and $n=k-r$ gives
\[
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_k(2)}}(C)=
 (-1)^r2^{k(k-r)+\binom r2}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n}
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{j}_{2}(-1)^j2^{\binom j2}2^{-nj}=(-1)^r2^{k(k-r)+\binom r2}\pi_{k-r}(2),
\]
where the last equality uses the Gaussian binomial theorem
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{n}\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{j}_{2}(-1)^j2^{\binom j2}x^j
 =\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1-2^ix)
\]
with $x=2^{-n}$.  

The ratio of the
absolute values at ranks $r+1$ and $r$ is $\frac1{2^{k-r}-1}\le1$, so these absolute values are nonincreasing.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:trace-representation}
For every $u\in S_0$, the rule
\[
 \lambda_u:R_u(X_0)\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2,
 \qquad \lambda_u(R_u(v))=b(u,v),
\]
defines a linear functional.  Define
\[
 \mathcal C_u=\left\{C\in\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}:
 \operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}M)=\lambda_u(M)
 \text{ for every }M\in R_u(X_0)\right\}.
\]
Then $\mathcal C_u$ is a nonempty affine space of dimension $(h-2)^2-\dim R_u(X_0)$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
If $v\in\ker R_u$, then $\det(I+R_u(v))=\det I=1$.
By \eqref{p12:eq:support-orthogonality}, this implies $b(u,v)=0$.
Consequently, if $R_u(v)=R_u(v')$, then $v-v'\in\ker R_u$ and
$b(u,v)=b(u,v')$.  Thus $\lambda_u$ is well defined, and its linearity
follows from the linearity of $R_u$ and $b(u,-)$.

Consider the linear map
\[
 \mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}\longrightarrow R_u(X_0)^*,
 \qquad
 C\longmapsto\bigl(M\mapsto\operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}M)\bigr).
\]
This map is surjective.  Indeed, choose a basis of $R_u(X_0)$ and
extend it to a basis of $\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}$.  Any linear
functional on $R_u(X_0)$ can then be extended to the full matrix space
by assigning the value zero to the additional basis matrices.

Every such extension is represented by the trace pairing.  To see
this, first note that the trace pairing on the full matrix space is
nondegenerate.  If $C=(c_{ij})\ne0$, choose an entry with $c_{ij}=1$ and let $E_{ij}$
be the matrix with its only nonzero entry in position $(i,j)$.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}E_{ij})=c_{ij}=1.
\]
Thus the map from the full matrix space to its dual induced by the
trace pairing is injective and, since the two spaces have the same
dimension, is an isomorphism. This proves the claimed surjectivity.~\footnote{The extension of a linear functional
from a subspace and its representation by a nondegenerate bilinear
form are standard finite-dimensional duality results; see
\cite[Section~3.5, Exercise~12, and Section~10.1]{HoffmanKunze}.}

Applying surjectivity to $\lambda_u$ gives a matrix $C_0\in\mathcal C_u$.
Moreover,
\[
 \mathcal C_u=C_0+
 \left\{C\in\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}:
 \operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}M)=0
 \text{ for every }M\in R_u(X_0)\right\}.
\]
Hence $\mathcal C_u$ is an affine space whose translation space is the kernel
of the displayed surjective map.  Its image has dimension
$\dim R_u(X_0)^*=\dim R_u(X_0)$, so rank--nullity gives
\[
 \dim\mathcal C_u=(h-2)^2-\dim R_u(X_0).
\]
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:affine-singular}
For every $0\ne u\in S_0$, let $\lambda_u$ and $\mathcal C_u$ be as in
\cref{p12:lem:trace-representation}. Let $\rho_u=\min\{\operatorname{rank} C:~C\in\mathcal C_u\}$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:affine-singular}
 \dim R_u(X_0)
 \le (h-2)^2+(h-2)+1-(h-2)\rho_u+\binom{\rho_u}{2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Since $u\ne0$ and $b$ is nondegenerate, there is $v\in X_0$ such
that $b(u,v)=1$.  Hence $\lambda_u(R_u(v))=1$, so $\lambda_u$ is
nonzero.  Thus $0\notin\mathcal C_u$, which gives $\rho_u\ge1$.  Since
$\mathcal C_u$ is nonempty and consists of $(h-2)\times(h-2)$ matrices, we
also have $\rho_u\le h-2$.

Let $T_u=\ker\lambda_u=\{M\in R_u(X_0):\lambda_u(M)=0\}$.  Since $\lambda_u$ is nonzero, its image is
$\mathbb F_2$. Thus,
\[
 \dim T_u=\dim R_u(X_0)-1.
\]
The Boolean polynomial $M\mapsto\det(I+M)$ restricted to $T_u$ has
degree at most $h-2$ and takes the value $1$ at zero.  Let
\[
 N_0=|\{M\in T_u:I+M\in\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)\}|.
\]
Then \cref{p12:lem:RM-support} gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:N0-lower}
 N_0\ge
 2^{\dim R_u(X_0)-(h-2)-1}.
\end{equation}

Note that we can write $N_0$ as the indicator sum $N_0=\sum_{M\in T_u}1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}(I+M)$.
Recall from \eqref{p12:eq:Riccati-constraint} that, for $M\in R_u(X_0)$, $\lambda_u(M)=1$ implies $\det(I+M)=0$.
Thus, the coset $\{M\in R_u(X_0):\lambda_u(M)=1\}$ contains no
$M$ for which $I+M$ is invertible. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:character-sum-N0}
\begin{split}
&\sum_{M\in R_u(X_0)}1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}(I+M)(-1)^{\lambda_u(M)}\\
=&
 \sum_{\substack{M\in R_u(X_0)\\ \lambda_u(M)=0}}
 1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}(I+M)
 -
 \sum_{\substack{M\in R_u(X_0)\\ \lambda_u(M)=1}}
 1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}(I+M)\\
 =&\sum_{M\in T_u}
 1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}(I+M)\\
 =& N_0.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
With the unnormalized Fourier transform in \cref{p12:lem:GL-Fourier},
Fourier inversion gives, for every $M\in\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}$,
\[
\begin{split}
 1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}(I+M)
 &=2^{-(h-2)^2}\sum_{C\in \mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}}
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}}(C)
 (-1)^{\operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}(I+M))}\\
&=2^{-(h-2)^2}\sum_{C\in \mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}}
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}}(C)(-1)^{\operatorname{tr} C}
 (-1)^{\operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}M)}.
\end{split}
\]
Substitute this into the character-sum expression for $N_0$ as in~\eqref{p12:eq:character-sum-N0}.
Interchanging the sums gives
\[
 N_0=2^{-(h-2)^2}\sum_{C\in \mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}}
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}}(C)(-1)^{\operatorname{tr} C}
 \sum_{M\in R_u(X_0)}
 (-1)^{\operatorname{tr}({C}^{\mathrm{t}}M)+\lambda_u(M)}.
\]
Note that the inner character sum is $2^{\dim R_u(X_0)}$ precisely when
$C\in\mathcal C_u$, and vanishes otherwise.  Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:N0-fourier-exact}
 N_0=
 2^{\dim R_u(X_0)-(h-2)^2}
 \sum_{C\in\mathcal C_u}
 \widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}}(C)(-1)^{\operatorname{tr} C}.
\end{equation}
By \cref{p12:lem:trace-representation}, $|\mathcal C_u|=2^{(h-2)^2-\dim R_u(X_0)}$.
Applying the triangle inequality to
\eqref{p12:eq:N0-fourier-exact} gives
\[
 N_0\le
 \max_{C\in\mathcal C_u}
 \bigl|\widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}}(C)\bigr|.
\]
By the explicit formula and rank monotonicity in
\cref{p12:lem:GL-Fourier}, the largest absolute Fourier coefficient in the maximum
therefore occurs at rank $\rho_u$.  Using also
$\pi_{h-2-\rho_u}(2)\le1$, we obtain
\[
 N_0\le
 \max_{C\in\mathcal C_u}
 \bigl|\widehat{1_{\operatorname{GL}_{h-2}(2)}}(C)\bigr|
 =2^{(h-2)(h-2-\rho_u)+\binom{\rho_u}{2}}
   \pi_{h-2-\rho_u}(2)
 \le
 2^{(h-2)(h-2-\rho_u)+\binom{\rho_u}{2}}.
\]
Comparing this with \eqref{p12:eq:N0-lower} proves
\eqref{p12:eq:affine-singular}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Recall that~\cref{p12:lem:rank-bound-private-span} shows that $\operatorname{rank} A\leq 2h+\dim X_0$, where $X_0$ is the complement of $H+\operatorname{rad} A$ in $H^{\perp_A}$. If $\dim X_0\le h-2$, then
\eqref{p12:eq:rank-A-X0} immediately gives
\[
 \operatorname{rank} A\le2h+\dim X_0\le2h+(h-2)=O(h).
\]

Suppose from now on that $\dim X_0\ge h-1$. Then \eqref{p12:eq:S0-lower} gives
$|S_0|\ge 2^{\dim X_0-(h-2)}\ge2$. Since $P(0)=0$, we have $\det(I+P(0))=1$, so $0\in S_0$ and hence $S_0\setminus\{0\}$ is nonempty.
Transferring the hollowing property of $\mathcal B$ to determinant constraints on the evaluation matrix of $\mathcal B$, we then use a low-degree polynomial argument to prove $\dim X_0\leq \dim R_u(X_0)+2(h-2)$ (\cref{p12:lem:fibre-kernel}) for any nonzero $u\in S_0$. The Fourier-analysis argument then shows that for any nonzero $u\in S_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:X0-rho-one}
   \dim X_0\leq \dim R_u(X_0)+2(h-2)
 \le (h-2)^2+3(h-2)+1-(h-2)\rho_u+\binom{\rho_u}{2},
\end{equation}
where $\rho_u$ is the minimal rank of matrices in the affine space $\mathcal C_u$ (\cref{p12:lem:affine-singular}). 

We now discuss possible choices of $\rho_u$ and derive the stated bound for $\operatorname{rank} A$. For each $0\neq u\in S_0=\{u\in X_0:\det(I+P(u))=1\}$,
                               
    
                                  
    
                                            
                                                  
                                            
                                                           
                                           
                                           
                                      
                
choose one minimum-rank representative $C_u\in\mathcal C_u$. Since $\lambda_u\ne0$, we have $0\notin\mathcal C_u$, and hence
$1\leq\rho_u=\operatorname{rank} C_u\leq h-2$. 

Recall that $G_u=Q(u)(I+P(u))^{-1}$ and $R_u(v)=Q(v)-G_uP(v)$. Let 
$D_u={G_u}^{\mathrm{t}}C_u$.  By~\cref{p12:lem:trace-representation},
\[
 b(u,v)=\operatorname{tr}({C_u}^{\mathrm{t}}(Q(v)-G_uP(v)))=\operatorname{tr}({C_u}^{\mathrm{t}}Q(v))-\operatorname{tr}({D_u}^{\mathrm{t}}P(v)).
\]
Note that the map
\[
 S_0\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow
 \mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)}\times\mathbb F_2^{(h-2)\times(h-2)},
 \qquad u\longmapsto(C_u,D_u),
\]
is injective.  Indeed, suppose that
$(C_u,D_u)=(C_{u'},D_{u'})$.  Then, for every $v\in X_0$,
\[
\begin{split}
 b(u,v)
 &=\operatorname{tr}({C_u}^{\mathrm{t}}Q(v))-\operatorname{tr}({D_u}^{\mathrm{t}}P(v))\\
 &=\operatorname{tr}({C_{u'}}^{\mathrm{t}}Q(v))-\operatorname{tr}({D_{u'}}^{\mathrm{t}}P(v))
 =b(u',v).
\end{split}
\]
Thus $b(u-u',v)=0$ for every $v\in X_0$.  Since $b$ is
nondegenerate on $X_0$, we have $u-u'=0$, and hence $u=u'$.

Recall that the number of rank-at-most-$\rho$ matrices $C$ is
$2^{\rho(2(h-2)-\rho)+O(h)}$. For a fixed $C$ of rank at most $\rho$,
there are at most $2^{(h-2)\rho}$ matrices $D$ whose row space is
contained in the row space of $C$. Thus,
\[
|\{(C,D):~\operatorname{rank} C\le\rho\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{row}(D)\leq
\operatorname{row}(C)\}|\leq 2^{\rho(3(h-2)-\rho)+O(h)}.
\]
Since $D_u={G_u}^{\mathrm{t}}C_u$, every pair $(C_u,D_u)$ is counted in
this set.

Partition $S_0\setminus\{0\}$ into the $h-2$
possible exact ranks.  Some class has at least
\[
 \frac{|S_0|-1}{h-2}
 \ge\frac{2^{\dim X_0-(h-2)}-1}{h-2}
 \ge\frac{2^{\dim X_0-(h-2)-1}}{h-2}
\]
elements.  If its common rank is $\rho$, injectivity of
$u\mapsto(C_u,D_u)$ and the preceding pair count give
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:X0-rho-two}
 \dim X_0\le\rho(3(h-2)-\rho)+O(h).
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{p12:eq:X0-rho-one} and \eqref{p12:eq:X0-rho-two}, and putting
$x=\rho/(h-2)$, gives
\[
 \frac{\dim X_0}{(h-2)^2}
 \le
 \min\left\{3x-x^2,1-x+\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}+O(h^{-1}).
\]
For $0\le x\le1$, the first function in the minimum is increasing and
the second is decreasing. Hence the maximum of this minimum is attained
at their intersection $x_0=\frac{4-\sqrt{10}}3$, with value
$\frac{10-\sqrt{10}}9$.
Thus we have
\[
 \operatorname{rank} A\le2h+\dim X_0\le \frac{10-\sqrt{10}}9\cdot h^2+O(h).
\]
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:endpoint-absorption}
Let $m,R,h$ be integers satisfying
\[
 m\ge2,\qquad h\ge1,\qquad R\ge0,\quad\text{and}\quad
 R+\binom h2\le m.
\]
Denote $w=m-R-\binom h2$
and suppose $0\le\theta\le4/5$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:endpoint-full-exponent}
\begin{split}
 &\frac12R^2(m-R-h)
 +\left(\frac12h^3-h^2\right)w
 +\frac h2w^2
 +\theta h^3R-\frac{\theta^2}{2}h^5\\
 &\hspace{20mm}\le \frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac{11}{1602}hm^2+O(m^2),
\end{split}
\end{equation}
with an absolute implied constant.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Let $E$ denote the left-hand side of
\eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-full-exponent}.  Substituting
$w=m-R-\binom h2$ and expanding gives
\[
 E=\frac12R^2(m-R)
 +\frac h2(m-\theta h^2)(m+\theta h^2-2R)+\frac{h^2}{2}(R-m)
 -\frac{h^3}{8}(h-1)(h-3).
\]
Note that
\[
 \frac12R^2(m-R)
 =\frac{2}{27}m^3
  -\frac12\left(R+\frac m3\right)
   \left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)^2.
\]
For the remaining terms, write
$R=(R-2m/3)+2m/3$ and expand.  This gives
\begin{align*}
 &\frac h2(m-\theta h^2)(m+\theta h^2-2R)
 +\frac{h^2}{2}(R-m)
 -\frac{h^3}{8}(h-1)(h-3)\\
 ={}&-h\left(m-\frac h2-\theta h^2\right)
       \left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)-\frac h{24}\left(
       4(m-2\theta h^2)^2+(3-4\theta^2)h^4
      \right)
 -\frac16h^2m+\frac12h^4-\frac38h^3.
\end{align*}
Adding these two identities yields
\begin{align*}
 E={}&\frac{2}{27}m^3\\
 &+\underbrace{
   -\frac12\left(R+\frac m3\right)
       \left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)^2-h\left(m-\frac h2-\theta h^2\right)
       \left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)
  }_{\text{$R$-dependent group}}\\
 &+\underbrace{
  -\frac h{24}\left(
       4(m-2\theta h^2)^2+(3-4\theta^2)h^4
      \right)
  }_{\text{$\theta$-square group}}\\
 &+\underbrace{
  -\frac16h^2m+\frac12h^4-\frac38h^3
  }_{\text{lower-order remainder}}.
\end{align*}
We retain the negative contribution of the ``$\theta$-square group''.
Completing the square in $h^2$ gives
\begin{align*}
 &4(m-2\theta h^2)^2+(3-4\theta^2)h^4\\
 &\quad=(12\theta^2+3)
 \left(h^2-\frac{8\theta m}{12\theta^2+3}\right)^2
 +\frac{4(3-4\theta^2)}{12\theta^2+3}m^2
 \ge\frac{44}{267}m^2.
\end{align*}
For the last inequality, use
$3-4\theta^2\ge11/25$ and $12\theta^2+3\le267/25$.
Thus the ``$\theta$-square group'' is at most
$-11hm^2/1602$.  The ``lower-order remainder'' is at most
$\frac12h^4$ since $h,m\geq0$.

We now deal with the ``$R$-dependent group''.
First note that $h\leq m$: this follows from $m\geq2$ when $h\leq2$, and from
$h\leq\binom h2\leq m$ when $h\geq3$.  Since
$h(h-1)\leq2m$, it follows that
$h^2\leq2m+h\leq3m$.
Note that \[
\left|h\left(m-\frac h2-\theta h^2\right)\right|\leq h(m+\frac h2+\theta h^2)
\leq h\left(m+\frac{13}{10}h^2\right)
\leq\frac{49}{10}hm<5hm,
\]
where we use $h/2\leq h^2/2$, $h^2\leq3m$, and $0\leq \theta\leq4/5$. Since $R+m/3\ge m/3$, the ``$R$-dependent group'' term
\[
  -\frac12\left(R+\frac m3\right)
       \left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)^2-h\left(m-\frac h2-\theta h^2\right)
       \left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)
\]
is upper bounded by
\begin{align*}
 -\frac m6\left(R-\frac{2m}{3}\right)^2
 +5hm\left|R-\frac{2m}{3}\right|.
\end{align*}
The right-hand side equals
\[
 -\frac m6\left(\left|R-\frac{2m}{3}\right|-15h\right)^2
 +\frac{75}{2}h^2m,
\]
so it is at most $\frac{75}{2}h^2m$.

Combining these estimates, we obtain that
\begin{align*}
 E&\le\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac{11}{1602}hm^2
       +\frac{75}{2}h^2m+\frac12h^4\\
  &\le\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac{11}{1602}hm^2+117m^2,
\end{align*}
where the second inequality again uses $h^2\leq3m$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{p12:lem:bounded-second-rank}
For every fixed integer $K\ge1$, the number of isomorphism classes
of nonabelian groups $G$ of order $p^m$ with $r_2\le K$ is at most
\[
 p^{\frac{2}{27}\frac{K}{K+1}m^3+O_K(m^2)},
\]
uniformly in the prime $p$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Fix $r_2\le K$.  By the Sims rank inequality,
$s\le r_2+1\le K+1$.  Retain
$m_{\mathrm{deep}}=\sum_{i=2}^c s_i$,
$b_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i=2}^{c-1}b_i$ and
$\delta=s_1-r_1$ from Section~\ref{p12:sec:saturated-optimisation}.
The general fixed-breadth bound in
\cref{p12:prop:total-relation-bound} has no saturation assumption.
Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of valid commutator data in a fixed fibre
with a fixed breadth sequence.
Since $T_{\mathrm{core}}\le m^2/2$, $b_{\mathrm{tot}}\le m$, and
$\binom{r_1-s}{2}=r_1^2/2+O_K(m)$, it gives the bound
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:bounded-second-rank-relations}
 \log_p|\mathcal P|
 \le\frac12r_1^2(m_{\mathrm{deep}}-b_{\mathrm{tot}})+O_K(m^2).
\end{equation}
Indeed, all positive terms in \eqref{p12:eq:total-relation-bound}
apart from $\binom{r_1}{2}m_{\mathrm{deep}}$ are $O_K(m^2)$.

By \eqref{p12:eq:e-breadth}, $s_{i+1}\le s b_i$, and hence
\[
 b_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge\frac{m_{\mathrm{deep}}-s_2}{s}.
\]
Each invariant-factor exponent of $L_1$ is at most $\delta+1$, so
$\exp(L_1)\le p^{\delta+1}$.  The epimorphism
$\bigwedge^2L_1\twoheadrightarrow L_2$ implies
$\exp(L_2)\le p^{\delta+1}$.  Since $d(L_2)=r_2$, this gives
$s_2\le r_2(\delta+1)$.  Using also
$m_{\mathrm{deep}}=m-r_1-\delta$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 m_{\mathrm{deep}}-b_{\mathrm{tot}}
 &\le\min\left\{m-r_1-\delta,
 \frac{(s-1)(m-r_1)+(r_2-s+1)\delta+r_2}{s}\right\}\\
 &\le\frac{r_2}{r_2+1}(m-r_1+1).
\end{align*}
To see the last inequality, the first affine function of $\delta$
is decreasing, and the second is nondecreasing since $r_2\ge s-1$.
They agree at $\delta=(m-r_1-r_2)/(r_2+1)\ge0$, where their
common value is $r_2(m-r_1+1)/(r_2+1)$.  Their minimum cannot
exceed this common value.

Substituting in \eqref{p12:eq:bounded-second-rank-relations} gives
\[
 \log_p|\mathcal P|
 \le\frac{r_2}{r_2+1}\frac12r_1^2(m-r_1)+O_K(m^2)
 \le\frac{2}{27}\frac{r_2}{r_2+1}m^3+O_K(m^2).
\]
The coarse power and auxiliary-parameter count in
\cref{p12:prop:parameter-ledger} costs only another $O(m^2)$ in the
exponent, including the sum over the numerical data and breadth
sequences.  Maximizing over $1\le r_2\le K$ proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
By \cref{p12:lem:hollowing-min-dim}, every dual image occurring here
satisfies $s-1\le r_2$.  In particular, the parameters used below
lie in the ranges of the corresponding matrix-space propositions.
Put $h=s-1$.

First consider any case in which the full leading-map count satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:ordinary-map-bound}
 N_p(r_1,r_2,s)\le(r_2-s+1)\binom{r_1}{2}+O(m^2).
\end{equation}
The same calculation applies to a subfamily whenever its logarithmic
count satisfies the right-hand side of \eqref{p12:eq:ordinary-map-bound}.
After inserting this estimate in \eqref{p12:eq:book-master}, the cubic
part, divided by $m^3$, is
\[
 B(x,y,z,u)=
 \frac{x^2}{2}(y+z-u)
 +(uy-u^2/2)z+uz^2/2,
\]
where
\[
 x=\frac{r_1}{m},\qquad y=\frac{r_2}{m},\qquad
 z=\frac{m-r_1-r_2}{m},\qquad u=\frac{s-1}{m},
\]
so $x+y+z=1$ and $0\le u\le\min\{x,y\}$.
We strengthen the cubic comparison in \cite[Lemma~A.1]{BNV} by
retaining its deficit.  Direct expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:ordinary-cubic-deficit}
 \frac2{27}-B(x,y,z,u)
 =\frac12\left(x-\frac23\right)^2\left(x+\frac13\right)
  +\frac u2(2x-1+y^2+uz).
\end{equation}
For $x\ge7/12$, the right-hand side is at least $u/12$.
For $1/2\le x\le7/12$, its second term is nonnegative, while
the first is at least
\[
 \frac2{27}-\frac12\left(\frac7{12}\right)^2\frac5{12}
 =\frac{11}{3456}.
\]
For $x\le1/2$, use the factorization
\[
 B(x,y,z,u)
 =\frac{1-x-u}{2}\bigl(x^2+u(1-x)\bigr)
  -\frac{uy(y-u)}{2}.
\]
Here $1-x-u\ge0$, $y\ge u$, and
\[
 x^2+u(1-x)-\frac{x+u}{2}
 =\left(x-\frac12\right)(x-u)\le0.
\]
Consequently,
$B(x,y,z,u)\le(x+u)(1-x-u)/4\le1/16$ in this range.
Since $u\le1$, these three ranges give
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:ordinary-group-deficit}
 m^3 B(x,y,z,u)
 \le\frac2{27}m^3-\frac{11}{3456}hm^2.
\end{equation}
Thus the ordinary map bound gives the presentation exponent
$2m^3/27-11hm^2/3456+O(m^2)$, with an absolute implied constant.

We now distinguish the three cases.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 1: away from the binary endpoint.}
Assume that $p\ge3$, or that $p=2$ and
$r_2\le\binom{s-1}{2}-1$.  By
\eqref{p12:eq:Np-hollowing-correspondence}, we apply \cref{p12:prop:exponent-away} with $(q,R,M,h)=(p,r_1,r_2,s-1)$.
The number of possible dual images is at most
\[
 p^{(r_2-s+1)\binom{r_1}{2}+O(r_1^2+r_2^2)}.
\]
For each image, the factor $|\operatorname{GL}_{r_2}(p)|\le p^{r_2^2}$ counts the
choices of $\beta^*:W^*\to\mathcal A$.  Since
$r_1^2+r_2^2=O(m^2)$, this proves
\eqref{p12:eq:ordinary-map-bound}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 2: the nonminimal binary endpoint.}
Suppose that $p=2$, $r_2=\binom{s-1}{2}$, and the dual image $\mathcal A$
is not minimally $(s-1)$-hollowing.  Apply
\cref{p12:lem:minimal-reduction} with
$(R,M,h)=(r_1,r_2,s-1)$.  By
\eqref{p12:eq:Np-hollowing-correspondence}, its space count and the factor
$|\operatorname{GL}_{r_2}(2)|\le2^{r_2^2}$ show that the maps in this subfamily have
base-$2$ logarithmic count at most
\[
 (r_2-s+1)\binom{r_1}{2}+O(r_1^2+r_2^2).
\]
Thus the ordinary map-bound calculation applies to this case as well.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 3: the minimal binary endpoint.}
Suppose that $p=2$, $r_2=\binom{s-1}{2}$, and $\mathcal A$ is minimally
$(s-1)$-hollowing.  Let $R=r_1$, $M=r_2=\binom h2$ and $h=s-1$.
If $h<h_0$, then $r_2\le\binom{h_0}{2}$ is bounded, and we use
\cref{p12:lem:bounded-second-rank} at the end of the proof.

It remains to assume $h\ge h_0$.  Denote
\[
 \kappa=\frac45,
 \qquad
 w=m-R-\binom{h}{2},
 \qquad
 a_*=\min\left\{
       \left\lfloor\frac{\kappa h^2}{2}\right\rfloor,
       \left\lfloor\frac R2\right\rfloor
      \right\},
 \qquad
 \theta=\frac{2a_*}{h^2}\le\kappa.
\]
By \cref{p12:prop:endpoint-exponent} and
\eqref{p12:eq:Np-hollowing-correspondence}, the logarithmic count of the
leading maps is at most
\[
 (M-h)\binom R2
 +h a_*(2R-2a_*-1)
 +O(hR+h^4),
\]
where the factor $|\operatorname{GL}_M(\mathbb F_2)|\le2^{M^2}$ is absorbed by $O(h^4)$.
Under the substitutions
\[
 r_1=R,\qquad r_2=M=\binom h2,\qquad s-1=h,
 \qquad m-r_1-r_2=w,
\]
the master estimate~\eqref{p12:eq:book-master} and the preceding
leading-map bound give
\begin{align*}
 \log_2|\mathcal P|
 \leq{}&(M-h)\binom R2+h a_*(2R-2a_*-1)\\
 &+\binom R2w
  +\left(hM-\frac{h^2}{2}\right)w
  +\frac h2w^2+O(m^2+hR+h^4).
\end{align*}
By the definition $\theta=2a_*/h^2$, the rank-variety term is exactly
\[
 h a_*(2R-2a_*-1)
 =\theta h^3R-\frac{\theta^2}{2}h^5-\frac\theta2h^3.
\]
Also, since $w=m-R-M=m-R-\binom h2$,
\begin{align*}
 \bigl((M-h)+w\bigr)\binom R2
 &= (m-R-h)\frac{R(R-1)}2=\frac12R^2(m-R-h)-\frac12R(m-R-h),\\
 hM-\frac{h^2}{2}
 &=\frac{h^2(h-1)}2-\frac{h^2}{2}
  =\frac12h^3-h^2.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \log_2|\mathcal P|
 \leq{}&\frac12R^2(m-R-h)
 +\left(\frac12h^3-h^2\right)w
 +\frac h2w^2+\theta h^3R-\frac{\theta^2}{2}h^5\\
 &-\frac12R(m-R-h)-\frac\theta2h^3
 +O(m^2+hR+h^4).
\end{align*}
The first line on the right-hand side is exactly the left-hand
side of~\eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-full-exponent}.  The hypotheses of
\cref{p12:lem:endpoint-absorption} hold, so this line is at most
$2m^3/27-11hm^2/1602+O(m^2)$.  Moreover, since $R+M\le m$, we have
$R\le m$ and $h^2=O(m)$.  Thus the two explicit correction terms and
the error term on the last line are all $O(m^2)$.  Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{p12:eq:endpoint-group-deficit}
 \log_2|\mathcal P|\le\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac{11}{1602}hm^2+O(m^2).
\end{equation}

These cases exhaust the nonsaturated range.  Fix $A>0$.
The ordinary and endpoint estimates, including the coarse quadratic
parameter count of \cref{p12:prop:parameter-ledger}, have absolute
error constants independent of $p$.  Choose an integer $H\ge h_0$
so large that the negative $hm^2$ terms in
\eqref{p12:eq:ordinary-group-deficit} and
\eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-group-deficit} absorb these errors and leave
at least $(A+2)m^2$ of saving whenever $h\ge H$.

If $h<H$, then $r_2\le\binom{H-1}{2}$ is bounded.
With $K=\max\{1,\binom{H-1}{2}\}$,
\cref{p12:lem:bounded-second-rank} gives the fixed cubic deficit
$2m^3/(27(K+1))$.  For sufficiently large $m$, this absorbs its
$O_K(m^2)$ error and leaves at least $(A+2)m^2$ of saving as well.
Finally, summing over the numerical data, the three cases and the
two ranges of $h$ costs at most $O(m\log m)$ in the exponent,
which is covered by the spare $2m^2$ for sufficiently large $m$.
All thresholds are independent of $p$.  This proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{p12:prop:parameter-ledger}
For groups of order $p^m$, uniformly for all primes $p$, the
following bounds hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
 \item After the normalized commutator data of
 \cref{p12:cor:normalized-relation-bound} and the power words of
 \cref{p12:lem:power-ledger} have been counted, all remaining numerical,
 abelian, indexing, breadth and summation choices in the saturated
 argument contribute at most $p^{O(m\log m)}$ possibilities.

 \item If the power words are instead counted by the crude bound,
 the numerical, abelian, power, indexing and summation choices
 contribute at most $p^{O(m^2)}$ possibilities, in either regime.
 In the nonsaturated argument, all residual matrix-space errors
 used in the proof of \cref{p12:cor:nonsaturated-group} are also
 $O(m^2)$ in the base-$p$ logarithm.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
We list the choices.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item The class and the sequence $(s_1,\ldots,s_c)$ form an ordered
 partition of $m$, giving at most $2^{m-1}$ choices.  For each
 $1\le i\le c$,
 the isomorphism type of the abelian group $L_i$ is a partition of
 $s_i$; using the elementary bound on partition numbers, the product
 over all layers is at most $2^m$.

 \item For each $1\le i\le c$, the positive relative-order exponents
 $a(i,1),\ldots,a(i,r_i)$ form an ordered composition of $s_i$.
 Across all layers these compositions have at most $2^{m-1}$ choices,
 and their lengths determine the ranks $r_i$, exactly as in the proof
 of \cite[Theorem~5.7]{BNV}.  Ordering and relabelling the generators
 used in the Sims normal form, choosing the $s$ core positions, the chain
 $(d_1,\ldots,d_s)$, and the auxiliary coordinate choices made in
 item~\textup{(c)} of Section~\ref{p12:sec:sims-counting-strategy} cost at
 most $m^{O(m)}$ choices.
 This includes the auxiliary function $f$ and the defining-commutator
 indices; they are counted here as coordinate choices, not as
 additional commutator values.
 Any same-layer coefficients not specified by the exponents are
 included in the power-word count in~\textup{(iii)}.
 The count runs over fixed formal generators, so a choice of basis
 of each abstract layer creates no further factor: its additive
 relations are specified by those power coefficients.
 \Cref{p12:cor:normalized-relation-bound} is applied with one fixed
 feasible breadth sequence.  Since $0\le b_i\le s_{i+1}$ for
 $2\le i\le c-1$, the number
 of such sequences is at most
 \[
  \prod_{i=2}^{c-1}(s_{i+1}+1)
  \le 2^{\sum_{j=3}^{c}s_j}
  \le 2^m\le p^m.
 \]
 For all $p$, the preceding ordering and indexing factors are
 $p^{O(m\log m)}$.

 \item In the saturated argument, all power words, including their
 same-layer coefficients, have already been counted by
 \cref{p12:lem:power-ledger} and combined with the normalized commutator
 count in Section~\ref{p12:sec:saturated-optimisation}.  They therefore
 contribute no further factor to part~\textup{(a)}.  The full power
 words remain fixed when the comparison results of
 Section~\ref{p12:sec:filtered-HW} are applied; counting those fixed
 fibres afterward does not change their hypotheses.

 For the nonsaturated argument, the original bound remains
 available.  There are at most $\sum_{i=1}^{c}r_i\le m$ power
 relations.  Each right-hand side is a Sims normal-form word in a
 subgroup of order at most $p^m$, so there are at most $p^{m^2}$
 power-word arrays in total.  This is the quadratic-size allowance
 already isolated in the classical Sims count; it is not added to
 the refined power count.

 \item The image subgroups used to count the core bracket maps
 $L_i\times C_{\mathrm{core}}\to L_{i+1}$, $2\le i\le c-1$, are included in
 the Lie-bracket estimate~\eqref{p12:eq:lie-bracket-count}, including the
 $+1$ in the subgroup estimate.
 Thus they create no additional ledger factor.  In particular, the
 resulting term $s b_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is retained in $\mathcal X$ in the
 saturated optimization, rather than absorbed into an $O(m^2)$
 allowance.  Choices of the integers $b_i$ themselves were included
 in~\textup{(ii)}.

 \item The following matrix-space factors occur only in the
 nonsaturated argument.  Away from the binary endpoint, that
 argument counts the full $(s-1)$-hollowing dual space directly; no
 minimal-core extension is used.  Changes of basis in the target are
 already counted by the factor $|\operatorname{GL}_{r_2}(p)|$ in
 \eqref{p12:eq:Np-hollowing-correspondence}.  At the binary
 endpoint, the proper-core branch additionally uses the Gaussian
 superspace exponent $(r_2-t)\binom{r_1}{2}$ from
 \cref{p12:lem:minimal-reduction}.  The residual finite-product and basis
 errors from these steps contribute $O(r_2^2)$ to the base-$p$
 logarithm.  The incidence error $O((r_1+r_2)^2)$ is at most $O(m^2)$.
 None of these factors is used in the saturated count.

 \item Again only in the nonsaturated argument, at the binary
 endpoint with $s-1\ge h_0$, substitute the local matrix parameters
 $(R,h)=(r_1,s-1)$ in \eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-exponent}.  Its error is
 $O((s-1)r_1+(s-1)^4)$.  Since
 $\binom{s-1}{2}\le m$ and $r_1\le m$, one has
 $(s-1)^2=O(m)$, so this is $O(m^2)$.  The residual overhead from
 ordering the chosen unique hollowing forms and changing bases in
 the endpoint matrix space is covered by the same $O((s-1)^4)$ term.
 The choice of the forms themselves is counted by the main
 rank-variety term in \eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-exponent}.
 The bounded-$s$ range is handled by the fixed cubic deficit in
 Section~\ref{p12:sec:endpoint-absorption}, which also absorbs the
 quadratic ledger.

 \item In the nonsaturated optimization, replacing binomial
 coefficients by their quadratic leading terms costs at most
 $O(m^2)$.  This allowance is not used in the saturated optimization:
 the defining-commutator saving and the linear term in
 $\binom{r_1}{2}$ are retained before the refined power count is added.
 Finally, summing over the numerical patterns and indexing choices
 in~\textup{(i)}--\textup{(ii)} costs $p^{O(m\log m)}$.  This gives
 the final $O(m\log m)$ upper error in the saturated regime and is
 absorbed by the quadratic saving in the nonsaturated regime.
\end{enumerate}
Every group under consideration has at least one presentation of the counted form.
Counting invalid arrays or counting a group more than once only
increases the upper bound, so no division by presentation
multiplicity is required.  Every displayed estimate above is uniform
in $p$: partition counts are independent of $p$, Gaussian and general
linear counts are bounded by \cref{p12:lem:universal-field}, and
$m^{O(m)}\le p^{O(m\log m)}$ because $p\ge2$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{p12:thm:uniform-upper}
There is an absolute constant $C$ such that, for every prime $p$
and every integer $m\ge1$,
\[
 f(p^m)\le p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+Cm\log m}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Part~\textup{(a)} of the preceding proposition supplies the remaining
factor in the proof of \cref{p12:cor:saturated-groups}.  Its logarithm
is $O(m\log m)$; together with the $O(m)$ error for fixed
presentation parameters, this gives a saturated count of at most
$p^{2m^3/27+O(m\log m)}$.  In the nonsaturated argument,
part~\textup{(b)} is precisely the quadratic allowance absorbed in
Section~\ref{p12:sec:endpoint-absorption}: for large $h=s-1$ the
negative $hm^2$ term covers it, and for bounded $h$ the fixed cubic
deficit covers it.  Thus \cref{p12:cor:nonsaturated-group} already
includes these parameter choices, with no additional quadratic
cost to be added afterward.

Every nonabelian group lies in exactly one of these two regimes.
By \cref{p12:cor:saturated-groups}, there is an absolute constant
$C_s\ge0$ such that the saturated count is at most
$p^{2m^3/27+C_s m\log m}$.
Apply \cref{p12:cor:nonsaturated-group} with $A=1$ to bound the
nonsaturated count by $p^{2m^3/27-m^2}$ for all sufficiently
large $m$, with a threshold independent of $p$.
The number of abelian groups of order $p^m$ is at most $p^m$.
Thus, for all sufficiently large $m$, uniformly in $p$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 f(p^m)
 &\le p^m+p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+C_s m\log m}
           +p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-m^2}\\
 &\le 3p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3+C_s m\log m}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since $p\ge2$, the factor $3$ is absorbed by increasing $C_s$
by an absolute constant.

For the finitely many remaining integers $m\ge2$, use the
coarse power-commutator count
\[
 f(p^m)\le p^{m(m+\binom m2)}\le p^{m^3}.
\]
Indeed, every group of order $p^m$ has a power-commutator
presentation on $m$ generators of relative order $p$.
There are $m$ power relations and $\binom m2$ commutator relations,
and each right-hand side has at most $p^m$ normal-form choices.
Since $m\log m>0$ for $m\ge2$, a further absolute increase of
$C$ covers these bounded exponents, uniformly in $p$.
Finally, $f(p)=1$ handles $m=1$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{p3:thm:linear}
There is an absolute constant $C$ such that, for every prime $p$
and every integer $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:sharp}
 p^{Q(m)}\le f(p^m)\le p^{Q(m)+Cm}.
\end{equation}
Thus $\log_p f(p^m)=2m^3/27-4m^2/9+O(m)$ uniformly in $p$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{p3:cor:adjacent}
For every fixed integer $d\ge1$,
\[
 \log_p\frac{f(p^{m-d})}{f(p^m)}
 \le-\frac{2d}{9}m^2+O_d(m)\qquad(m>d),
\]
uniformly in $p$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{p3:lem:eta}
In the saturated range, for every fixed $\eta\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:opt}
 \frac12r^2D+\mathcal X+3Dt+\eta Dz
 \le\frac{2}{27}(r+D)^3+O_\eta(r+D),\qquad z=r-2D.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Put $n=r+D$. The exact cubic deficit is
\[
 \Delta:=\frac{2}{27} n^3-\tfrac12r^2D
 =\frac{z^2(4r+D)}{54}.
\]
Saturation gives $s^2\le2(D-t)+3s$, hence $s=O(\sqrt D)$.
Dropping negative terms in \eqref{p3:eq:roughX} gives
$\mathcal X=O(D^{5/2})$ as an upper bound. Outside $D\le r\le3D$,
the deficit is at least an absolute positive multiple of $n^3$,
which absorbs this bound and the $O_\eta(n^2)$ remaining terms.
Bounded $n$ is included in the final constant.

We may therefore assume $D\le r\le3D$, so $|z|\le D$ and
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:Delta}
 \Delta\ge\frac5{54}Dz^2.
\end{equation}
If $t=0$, then $\mathcal X=0$ and completion of the square gives
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:square}
 \eta Dz\le\frac5{54}Dz^2+\frac{27\eta^2}{10}D.
\end{equation}
Assume $t>0$, so $b_2\ge1$. Set
\[
 S=\binom{r-s}{2}-s(2D+1),\qquad
 T_{\max}=\frac{D^2-(D-t)^2}{2}\le Dt.
\]
For sufficiently large $D$, uniformly in feasible $s$, we have
$S\ge D^2/4$. From \eqref{p3:eq:breadth} we obtain
\begin{align}
 \mathcal X&\le(s^2D-S)B,\label{p3:eq:linearB}\\
 \mathcal X&\le s\min\{T_{\max},sD(B-b_2)\}-SB.
 \label{p3:eq:piecewiseB}
\end{align}
As a function of $B\ge b_2$, the latter upper bound is linear
on either side of $b_2+T_{\max}/(sD)$. Maximizing at an endpoint
or at this breakpoint yields, with $v_+=\max\{v,0\}$,
\[
 \mathcal X\le\frac{t}{s}(s^2D-S)_+-Sb_2.
\]
Expanding at $r=2D+z$ and using saturation gives
\begin{align*}
 s^2D-S
 &\le-2D(t+z)+7sD-\tfrac12(z-s)^2+D+z/2+s/2\\
 &\le-2D(t+z)+9sD.
\end{align*}
It follows, by maximizing a quadratic in $t$, that
\begin{align}\label{p3:eq:Xbalance}
 \mathcal X&\le\frac{D}{s}t(-2t-2z+9s)_+-Sb_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{D}{8s}(-2z+9s)_+^2-Sb_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{Dz^2}{2s}+\frac92D|z|+\frac{81}{8}sD-Sb_2.
\end{align}

If $t\ge9(|z|+s)$, then $s^2D-S\le-Dt$, so
\eqref{p3:eq:linearB} and $B\ge t/s$ imply
\[
 \mathcal X+3Dt\le-Dt^2/s+3Dt\le0.
\]
Equation~\eqref{p3:eq:square} finishes this case.
If $t<9(|z|+s)$, then \eqref{p3:eq:Xbalance} gives
\[
 \mathcal X+3Dt+\eta Dz
 \le\frac{Dz^2}{2s}
   +\left(\frac{63}{2}+|\eta|\right)D|z|
   +\frac{297}{8}sD-Sb_2.
\]
When $s\ge11$, the first term is at most $5Dz^2/108$.
Writing $A_\eta=63/2+|\eta|$, we also have
\[
 A_\eta D|z|\le\frac5{108}Dz^2+\frac{27A_\eta^2}{5}D.
\]
The two square terms are absorbed by \eqref{p3:eq:Delta}.
The remaining expression is at most
\[
 \frac{27A_\eta^2}{5}D+\frac{297}{8}sD-\frac14D^2,
\]
which is nonpositive for sufficiently large $D$, since
$s=O(\sqrt D)$.
Finally, for $2\le s\le10$ and large $D$ we have
$s^2D-S\le-D^2/4$, whence
\[
 \mathcal X+3Dt\le\left(-\frac{D^2}{4s}+3D\right)t\le0.
\]
Again use \eqref{p3:eq:square}. All excluded bounded values are
absorbed by $O_\eta(n)$, proving the lemma.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{p3:lem:core}
In the saturated range, $K\cap C=0$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
If $0\ne v\in K\cap C$, then $\beta|_{C\times C}$ factors
through an alternating map on $C/\langle v\rangle$. Its image
