would have dimension at most $\binom{s-1}{2}$, contrary to
\eqref{p3:eq:saturation} and the spanning property of the core.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{p3:lem:bases}
For bounded $\delta$, the core and the derived generators can be
fixed while varying a space of outside generators of dimension
$u\ge r-s-\delta$. The resulting complete arrays number at least
\[
 c_*p^{u^2-ud},\qquad
 c_*:=\prod_{i\ge1}(1-2^{-i})>0,
\]
for each fixed group. The numerical parameters and the breadths
are preserved; the full power words are allowed to vary.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Decompose the abelianization as $P/P_2=B_0\oplus E_0$, where
$B_0$ is the sum of cyclic factors of order at least $p^2$ and
$E_0$ is elementary abelian. The rank of $B_0$ is at most
$\delta$. Let $E_1$ span the $E_0$-components of the core
elements; its dimension is at most $s$. Choose a complement
$U$ to $E_1$ in $E_0$, so $u:=\dim U\ge r-\delta-s$.

Complete the core to a minimal generating set of $B_0\oplus E_1$
and append a basis of $U$. Core independence modulo $p$ ensures
this completion exists. Fix actual lifts of the nonmoving
generators, including all derived generators defined from core
words. Vary only the basis of $U$ by $\operatorname{GL}(u,p)$, choosing one
tuple of actual lifts for each basis. The appended generators all
have relative order $p$ in the abelianization. All defining
commutators and core flags remain unchanged, as do the higher
layer structures and their core breadth maps.

If two choices give the same complete selected array, their
core--outside leading commutator coefficients agree. For each
moving generator the difference of its two images in $V$ belongs
to $K$. Thus an array has at most $p^{ud}$ preimages among these
basis choices. Since $|\operatorname{GL}(u,p)|\ge c_*p^{u^2}$, the assertion
follows. No assertion of a free automorphism action is needed.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{p3:lem:kernel}
The number of possible $K$ of dimension $d$ is at most
$c_*^{-1}p^{d(r-d)}$. For each prescribed $K$ disjoint from $C$,
the equations $\beta(K,C)=0$ save $sdM$ scalar parameters in the
raw graded count. The other conditional bounds remain applicable.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
The subspace count is the usual Gaussian-binomial bound. Choose
a complement $V=C\oplus U_0$. Since $K\cap C=0$, projection
identifies $K$ with a $d$-subspace $U_1\le U_0$, with $K$ the
graph of a linear map $U_1\to C$. After fixing core--core values,
the equations prescribe the restriction to $U_1$ of the map
\[
 U_0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(C,W),
 \qquad v\longmapsto\beta(v,-)|_C.
\]
This amounts to exactly $sdM$ independent affine scalar conditions on
the freely counted core--outside coordinates. Reduction
$L_2\to L_2/pL_2=W$ has constant fibre size $p^{s_2-M}$, so
the saving holds also for nonelementary $L_2$.

The defining core--core slots and the breadth-restricted
outside--outside slots are disjoint from these coordinates.
The higher completion bounds hold uniformly for each fixed
graded bracket, so they are unchanged. Counting maps for which
the centralizer contains the prescribed $K$ may overcount
the stratum where its dimension is exactly $d$, which is harmless.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{p3:prop:preliminary}
Uniformly in the prime $p$,
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:preliminary-sharp}
 \log_p f(p^m)\le Q(m)+O(m^{3/2}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
\emph{Large defects and the nonsaturated range.}
Since $m^3-(m-\delta)^3\ge\delta m^2$, the coarse estimate
\eqref{p3:eq:coarse} discards all $\delta$ exceeding a fixed
threshold with any desired fixed quadratic margin. For example,
choose an absolute integer $\delta_0$ with
\[
 \frac{2\delta_0}{27}>C_0+\frac49+2.
\]
The remaining $\delta$ and $e\le\binom\delta2$ are bounded.
The nonsaturated estimate likewise has an arbitrarily large
fixed quadratic saving. Abelian groups number at most $p^m$,
so their contribution is negligible.

\emph{The exceptional small-core range.}
Suppose $sM<2r$. Saturation implies
$s\binom{s-1}{2}<2m$, hence
\[
 s=O(m^{1/3}),\qquad M=O(m^{2/3}).
\]
Dropping the negative term in \eqref{p3:eq:roughX} gives
$\mathcal X\le O(m^{7/3})$. If $r<m/12$ or $D<m/12$, the main term
$r^2D/2$ has a fixed cubic deficit from $2m^3/27$, since
$r+D\le m$. This absorbs that correction and all quadratic
terms in \eqref{p3:eq:raw}.

Otherwise $r,D\ge m/12$, and $t=D-M-e\ge m/24$ for large $m$.
In that case
\[
 s(2D+1)-\binom{r-s}{2}\le-cm^2
\]
for an absolute $c>0$. Using $B\ge t/s$ in
\eqref{p3:eq:roughX} yields
\[
 \mathcal X\le O(m^{7/3})-cm^2t/s\le-c'm^{8/3}
\]
for some absolute $c'>0$ and sufficiently large $m$.
This range therefore also has any prescribed fixed quadratic
deficit, including the cost of the parameter ledger.

\emph{Source normalization and the quadratic term.}
We may now assume $sM\ge2r$. Since $u\le r$, the coefficient
of $d$ in \eqref{p3:eq:normalizedraw} is nonpositive. Bounded
$\delta$ and $s=O(\sqrt m)$ give
$u^2=r^2+O(m^{3/2})$, so the exponent is at most
\[
 \mathcal E-r^2+O(m^{3/2}).
\]
Put $n=r+D=m-\delta$. The exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:identity}
 -r^2=-\frac49n^2-\frac43Dz-\frac59z^2
\end{equation}
combines with \eqref{p3:eq:raw} to bound the exponent by
\[
 \left(\tfrac12r^2D+\mathcal X+3Dt-\tfrac56Dz\right)
 -\frac49n^2-\frac59z^2+O(m^{3/2}).
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:eta} with $\eta=-5/6$ and discard the
negative square. For every fixed bounded $\delta$ this gives
\[
 Q(m-\delta)+O(m^{3/2})\le Q(m)+O(m^{3/2}),
\]
because $Q$ is increasing for sufficiently large arguments.
The $m^{O(m)}$ numerical patterns cost only $O(m\log m)$
in the logarithm. Increasing the absolute constant covers
the bounded values of $m$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{p3:lem:lower-bound}
For every prime $p$ and every integer $m\ge1$,
\[
 f(p^m)\ge p^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Let $r$ be a positive integer and set $\nu=r(r+1)/2$.
There is a group $U_r$ of order $p^{r+\nu}$ with generators
$x_1,\ldots,x_r$ and an elementary abelian central Frattini
subgroup of dimension $\nu$, freely spanned by
\[
 z_i=x_i^p\quad(1\le i\le r),\qquad
 w_{ij}=[x_i,x_j]\quad(1\le i<j\le r).
\]
Here is an explicit construction, including characteristic two.
On $\mathbb F_p^r\times\mathbb F_p^\nu$ define multiplication by
\[
 (a,z)(b,w)=(a+b,z+w+c(a,b)),
\]
where addition is in the displayed vector spaces, and, using
integer representatives $0\le a_i,b_i<p$,
\[
 c(a,b)=\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{a_i+b_i}{p}\right\rfloor z_i
       +\sum_{i<j}a_i b_j w_{ij}.
\]
The carry terms are the usual cyclic-group cocycles and the
other terms are bilinear cocycles. Thus the operation is
associative. The basis lifts $x_i=(e_i,0)$ have the stated
powers and commutators. Their powers and commutators span
all the central coordinate space, so that this space is
exactly $\Phi(U_r)$. The construction also proves the
independence of the displayed generators of $\Phi(U_r)$.

Equivalently, $U_r$ has the presentation with these central
$p$-torsion elements, $x_i^p=z_i$ and
$[x_i,x_j]=w_{ij}$. Collection bounds the order of that
presentation by $p^{r+\nu}$, and the model above attains it.
It follows in particular that every $r$-tuple in a finite $p$-group
whose Frattini subgroup is central elementary abelian
induces a homomorphism from $U_r$.

For $0\le D\le\nu$, quotient by a codimension-$D$ subspace
$K\le\Phi(U_r)$. The quotient has order $p^{r+D}$ and
Frattini rank $r$. If two such quotients are isomorphic,
lift the images of their $r$ generators to $U_r$. The
presentation gives an endomorphism of $U_r$ inducing the
isomorphism. Its images generate the Frattini quotient,
so the Burnside basis theorem makes it surjective, hence
an automorphism. Consequently quotient isomorphism types
are the orbits of $\operatorname{Aut}(U_r)$ on these subspaces.

The kernel of $\operatorname{Aut}(U_r)\to\operatorname{GL}(r,p)$ fixes $\Phi(U_r)$
pointwise: it replaces each $x_i$ by $x_i v_i$ with
$v_i\in\Phi(U_r)$, leaving all $x_i^p$ and $[x_i,x_j]$
unchanged. Therefore each orbit has size at most
$|\operatorname{GL}(r,p)|\le p^{r^2}$. The Gaussian-binomial count gives
at least $p^{D(\nu-D)}$ codimension-$D$ subspaces, and hence
\[
 f(p^{r+D})\ge
 p^{D(\nu-D)-r^2}
 =p^{\frac12r^2D+\frac12rD-D^2-r^2}.
\]
Take $r=\lfloor2m/3\rfloor$ and $D=m-r$. For $m\ge2$,
$D\le\nu$. Let $E=\tfrac12r^2D+\tfrac12rD-D^2-r^2$.
Writing $m=3q+\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon\in\{0,1,2\}$,
we obtain by direct substitution
\[
 E-\left(\tfrac{2}{27}m^3-\tfrac49m^2\right)
 =\begin{cases}
 0,&\varepsilon=0,\\
 q-17/27,&\varepsilon=1,\\
 (2/3)q+5/27,&\varepsilon=2.
 \end{cases}
\]
These quantities are nonnegative for $m\ge2$. The case $m=1$
is immediate from $f(p)=1$. This proves Higman's lower bound
\cite{Higman,BNV} uniformly in $p$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{p3:lem:positive-depth}
There is an absolute $\kappa>0$, with
the following property. For every fixed $\eta\in\mathbb R$, every
sufficiently large $n=r+D$, and every feasible saturated stratum
with $t>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:positive-depth}
 \frac12r^2D+\mathcal X+3Dt+\eta Dz
 \le\frac{2}{27} n^3-\kappa n^2.
\end{equation}
The threshold depends only on $\eta$, not on $p$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Let $\Delta=\frac{2}{27} n^3-r^2D/2=z^2(4r+D)/54$.
As in Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:eta}, outside $D\le r\le3D$ this has a
fixed cubic lower bound in $n$, whereas
$\mathcal X\le O(D^{5/2})$ and $3Dt+\eta Dz=O_\eta(n^2)$.
This proves \eqref{p3:eq:positive-depth} outside that range for large $n$.

Hence assume $D\le r\le3D$. Then $|z|\le D$,
$\Delta\ge5Dz^2/54$, and saturation gives $s=O(\sqrt D)$.
Since $t>0$, the breadth relations give $b_2\ge1$.
Put
\[
 S_1=\binom{r-s}{2}-s(5D+1),\qquad
 T_{\max}=\frac{D^2-(D-t)^2}{2}\le Dt.
\]
For large $D$, uniformly in all feasible $s$,
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:S1}
 S_1\ge D^2/4.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $r\ge D$ and $s=O(\sqrt D)$ give
$S_1\ge D^2/2-O(D^{3/2})$.

The definition of $\mathcal X$, \eqref{p3:eq:breadth}, and $t\le sB$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:absorbed-depth}
 Y:=\mathcal X+3Dt
 \le s\min\{T_{\max},sD(B-b_2)\}-S_1B.
\end{equation}
This absorbs the whole positive term $3Dt$ before maximizing.
Since $S_1>0$, maximizing the right side over $B\ge b_2$ at
the endpoint or breakpoint gives
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:depth-max}
 Y\le\frac{T_{\max}}{sD}(s^2D-S_1)_+-S_1b_2
 \le\frac{t}{s}(s^2D-S_1)_+-S_1b_2.
\end{equation}
Expanding $r=2D+z$ and using $s^2\le2(D-t)+3s$ gives
\begin{align*}
 s^2D-S_1
 &\le-2D(t+z)+10sD-\tfrac12(z-s)^2+D+z/2+s/2\\
 &\le-2D(t+z)+12sD.
\end{align*}
Substitute this into \eqref{p3:eq:depth-max} and maximize in $t$:
\begin{align}\label{p3:eq:depth-square}
 Y
 &\le\frac{D}{s}t(-2t-2z+12s)_+-S_1b_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{D}{8s}(-2z+12s)_+^2-S_1b_2\notag\\
 &\le\frac{Dz^2}{2s}+6D|z|+18sD-S_1b_2.
\end{align}
For $s\ge11$, the square term is at most $5Dz^2/108$.
Writing $A_\eta=6+|\eta|$, we have
\[
 A_\eta D|z|
 \le\frac5{108}Dz^2+\frac{27A_\eta^2}{5}D.
\]
Therefore
\[
 Y+\eta Dz-\Delta
 \le\frac{27A_\eta^2}{5}D+18sD-\frac14D^2
 \le-\frac18D^2
\]
for all sufficiently large $D$.

If $2\le s\le10$, then $s^2D-S_1\le-D^2/4$ for large $D$.
Dropping $b_2$ from the first term of \eqref{p3:eq:absorbed-depth}
gives $Y\le(s^2D-S_1)B\le-D^2/4$, since $B\ge b_2\ge1$.
Also $\eta Dz\le\Delta+(27\eta^2/10)D$.
Thus $Y+\eta Dz-\Delta\le-D^2/8$ eventually in this case too.

Finally, $n\le4D$, so the saving $D^2/8$ is at least
$n^2/128$. The smaller constant $\kappa=1/256$ works in all
ranges once $n$ is sufficiently large.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{p3:prop:frattini-concentration}
There is an absolute $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for all sufficiently
large $m$, uniformly in $p$,
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:complement-gap}
 f(p^m)-f_{\mathfrak H_p}(p^m)
 \le p^{Q(m)-\varepsilon m^2}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
 1\le\frac{f(p^m)}{f_{\mathfrak H_p}(p^m)}
 \le1+p^{-\varepsilon m^2}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Use the source-basis proof in Subsection~\ref{p3:sec:preliminary},
retaining its deficits before the last optimization.
The abelian contribution is at most $p^m$.
Nonsaturated strata, strata with $\delta\ge\delta_0$ for a
sufficiently large absolute $\delta_0$, and the exceptional
small-core range $sM<2r$ can each be discarded with any
prescribed fixed quadratic margin below $2m^3/27$.
Choose those margins larger than $4/9+1$, including the costs
of summing parameters. Their contribution is then negligible
relative to the right side of \eqref{p3:eq:complement-gap}.

For every remaining stratum, $\delta$ and $e$ are bounded,
$sM\ge2r$, and the source-basis and kernel estimates give an
upper exponent
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:normalized-for-gap}
 \mathcal E-r^2+O(m^{3/2}).
\end{equation}
This includes the $O(m\log m)$ presentation-parameter ledger.
Put $n=r+D=m-\delta$. Identity~\eqref{p3:eq:identity} gives
\[
 -r^2=-\frac49n^2-\frac43Dz-\frac59z^2.
\]
Consequently \eqref{p3:eq:raw} and \eqref{p3:eq:normalized-for-gap}
bound the exponent by
\begin{equation}\label{p3:eq:normalized-gap-identity}
 \left(\tfrac12r^2D+\mathcal X+3Dt-\tfrac56Dz\right)
 -\tfrac49n^2-\tfrac59z^2+O(m^{3/2}).
\end{equation}

If $1\le\delta<\delta_0$, apply Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:eta} with
$\eta=-5/6$ and discard the negative square. The result is
\[
 Q(m-\delta)+O(m^{3/2})
 =Q(m)-\frac{2\delta}{9}m^2+O(m^{3/2})
 \le Q(m)-\frac19m^2
\]
for sufficiently large $m$. The constants are uniform because
$\delta$ ranges over a fixed finite set.

We may now assume $\delta=0$, so $n=m$ and $e=0$.
If $t>0$, use Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:positive-depth} in
\eqref{p3:eq:normalized-gap-identity}; this gives
\[
 Q(m)-\frac{m^2}{256}+O(m^{3/2})
 \le Q(m)-\frac{m^2}{512}
\]
for large $m$. The finite combination of all discarded families
is at most $p^{Q(m)-m^2/1024}$ after increasing the threshold.

The only remaining nonabelian groups have $\delta=t=0$.
Then $P/P_2$ is elementary abelian, $P_3=1$, and $e=0$
makes $P_2$ elementary abelian. In particular
\[
 P^p\le P_2,\qquad
 \Phi(P)=P^pP_2=P_2\le Z(P),\qquad \Phi(P)^p=1.
\]
Thus every remaining group lies in $\mathfrak H_p$, proving
\eqref{p3:eq:complement-gap}.
The lower-bound construction in Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:lower-bound}
lies in $\mathfrak H_p$ and gives
$f_{\mathfrak H_p}(p^m)\ge p^{Q(m)}$.
Division proves the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Combine \eqref{p3:eq:complement-gap} and \eqref{p3:eq:BLQR}:
\[
 f(p^m)\le
 p^{Q(m)+C_{\!H}m}+p^{Q(m)-\varepsilon m^2}
 \le p^{Q(m)+(C_{\!H}+1)m}
\]
for sufficiently large $m$.
The lower bound is Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:lower-bound}.
The finitely many smaller exponents are absorbed by an absolute
increase of $C$, using the elementary uniform bound
$f(p^m)\le p^{O(m^3)}$ from power-commutator presentations.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{p3:prop:linear-necessary}
For every prime $p$ and all sufficiently large $m$,
\[
 \log_p f(p^m)\ge Q(m)+\frac29m-2.
\]
In particular, the remainder after $Q(m)$ cannot be $o(m)$.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
The quotient construction in Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:lower-bound} gives
the exponent
\[
 E(r,D)=\tfrac12r^2D+\tfrac12rD-D^2-r^2,\qquad r+D=m.
\]
Set $z=r-2D$, so $r=(2m+z)/3$ and $D=(m-z)/3$. Direct
expansion gives
\[
 E(r,D)-Q(m)
 =-\frac{z^2+5z}{18}m-\frac{z^3}{54}-\frac{5z^2}{18}.
\]
Choose $z=-3,-2,-1$ according as $m\equiv0,1,2\pmod3$.
These give integral $r,D$ with $0\le D\le r(r+1)/2$
for sufficiently large $m$, and yield respectively
\[
 E(r,D)-Q(m)=
 \begin{cases}
 m/3-2,&m\equiv0\pmod3,\\
 m/3-26/27,&m\equiv1\pmod3,\\
 2m/9-7/27,&m\equiv2\pmod3.
 \end{cases}
\]
Each is at least $2m/9-2$, as required.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{p4:thm:main}\label{p4:thm:class-2}
One has
\[
 \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{F_{2,2}(x)}{F(x)}=1.
\]
Thus almost all finite groups, counted up to isomorphism and ordered
by their cardinalities, are $2$-groups of nilpotency class $2$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{p4:lem:generators}
The group $Q$ has a generating tuple $q_1,\ldots,q_{h+1}$ in which
$q_1$ has odd prime order and
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:h}
 h\le\lfloor\log_2(|Q|/3)\rfloor\le v-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Choose $q_1$ by Cauchy's theorem. Successively adjoin an element
outside the subgroup already generated, until that subgroup is $Q$.
Each additional generator at least doubles the subgroup's order. If $h$
generators have been added, then $3\cdot2^h\le|Q|$. Finally,
$\lfloor\log_2(b/3)\rfloor\le\lfloor\log_2 b\rfloor-1$.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{p4:lem:frattini}
There is a surjection $\operatorname{Out}(N)\to A(N)$ whose kernel $T_N$ is a
$2$-group satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:frattini}
 |T_N|\le2^{r(n-r)},\qquad |\operatorname{Out}(N)|=a(N)|T_N|.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Let $J_N=\ker(\operatorname{Aut}(N)\to A(N))$. Fix an ordered basis of
$N/\Phi(N)$. There are exactly $|\Phi(N)|^r=2^{r(n-r)}$ ordered
tuples lifting it, and each tuple generates $N$ by the Burnside
basis theorem. The action of $J_N$ on these tuples is free, since
an automorphism fixing a generating tuple is the identity. Thus
$|J_N|$ divides $2^{r(n-r)}$. Inner automorphisms act trivially on
$N/\Phi(N)$, so $\operatorname{Inn}(N)\le J_N$. The desired kernel is
$T_N=J_N/\operatorname{Inn}(N)$.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{p4:lem:extensions}
For the tuple of Lemma~\ref{p4:lem:generators}, the number of
isomorphism types of extensions of $N$ by $Q$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:extension-cost}
 a(N)^{h+1}2^{h r(n-r)+n|Q|^2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Write $\ell$ for the odd prime order of $q_1$. For each element
$\alpha\in A(N)$ of order dividing $\ell$, there is at most one
$T_N$-conjugacy class of elements $y\in\operatorname{Out}(N)$ with $y^\ell=1$
and image $\alpha$. If $\alpha=1$, then $y=1$, since $T_N$ is a
$2$-group. Otherwise the inverse image of $\langle\alpha\rangle$
is an extension of the normal $2$-group $T_N$ by a cyclic group of
order $\ell$. Each such $y$ generates a complement to $T_N$.
By Schur--Zassenhaus conjugacy, these complements are conjugate by elements of $T_N$;
in each complement exactly one element maps to $\alpha$.

The image of $q_1$ therefore has at most $a(N)$ choices up to
conjugacy in $\operatorname{Out}(N)$. After fixing it, allow arbitrary images
for the remaining $h$ generators. Relations and further conjugacy
identifications can only reduce the count. Hence the number of
outer actions $Q\to\operatorname{Out}(N)$, up to conjugacy, is at most
\[
 a(N)|\operatorname{Out}(N)|^h\le a(N)^{h+1}2^{h r(n-r)}.
\]

Fix one outer action $\theta$. For each $q\in Q$, choose a lift
$\alpha_q\in\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ of $\theta(q)$. In any realizing extension,
modify each coset representative $t_q$ by an element of $N$ so
that its conjugation action is precisely $\alpha_q$. With
$\operatorname{Inn}(c)(x)=cxc^{-1}$, the factors
$c(q,w)=t_qt_wt_{qw}^{-1}$ satisfy
\[
 \alpha_q\alpha_w=\operatorname{Inn}(c(q,w))\alpha_{qw}.
\]
Thus each factor has at most $|Z(N)|$ choices. These factors and
the chosen actions determine multiplication on $N\times Q$;
associativity only imposes further restrictions. There are at
most $|Z(N)|^{|Q|^2}\le2^{n|Q|^2}$ factor systems. Every conjugator
in $\operatorname{Out}(N)$ lifts to an automorphism of $N$, so relabeling the
kernel identifies extensions with conjugate outer actions.
Multiplying the two bounds proves the result.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{p4:prop:fixedQ}
For each fixed $Q$ as above and the integer $h$ in
Lemma~\ref{p4:lem:generators},
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:gQ}
 g_Q(n)\le
 2^{\frac{2}{27}n^3+\frac{2h-4}{9}n^2+O_Q(n^{3/2})}
 \qquad(n\ge1).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
We insert the extension cost~\eqref{p4:eq:extension-cost} into the
presentation count of Section~\ref{p3:sec:normalization}. All parameters below describe the
kernel $N$, so its order exponent is $n$ and
$n=r+D+\delta$. Constants may depend on $Q$ (and hence on $h$).
The factor $2^{n|Q|^2}$ costs only $O_Q(n)$ in the logarithm and
will be included at the end.

\emph{Discarded ranges.}
The elementary bounds $a(N)\le2^{r^2}$ and $r(n-r)\le n^2/4$
give
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:crude-cost}
 a(N)^{h+1}2^{h r(n-r)}
 \le2^{(h+1+h/4)n^2}.
\end{equation}
The nonsaturated theorem of Part~\ref{p12:part:leading-maps} has an arbitrarily large
fixed quadratic saving. Choose that saving larger than the
coefficient in~\eqref{p4:eq:crude-cost} and
$|(2h-4)/9|+2$; this removes all nonsaturated kernels.
Abelian kernels number at most $2^n$, so their contribution is
$2^{O_Q(n^2)}$ and is also negligible on the cubic scale.

For saturated kernels, the coarse estimate~\eqref{p3:eq:coarse}
is $\mathcal E\le2(n-\delta)^3/27+C_0n^2$. Since
\[
 n^3-(n-\delta)^3\ge\delta n^2,
\]
choose a fixed integer $\delta_0$ such that
\[
 \frac{2\delta_0}{27}>
 C_0+h+1+h/4+|(2h-4)/9|+2.
\]
All $\delta\ge\delta_0$ can then be discarded, including their
extension costs and the $O(n\log n)$ parameter ledger. We may
assume $\delta<\delta_0$ and hence
$e\le\binom\delta2=O_Q(1)$.

There is one further range to discard: $sM<(h+3)r$.
Saturation~\eqref{p3:eq:saturation} implies
$s=O_Q(n^{1/3})$ and $M=O_Q(n^{2/3})$. Dropping negative terms
in~\eqref{p3:eq:roughX} gives $\mathcal X\le O_Q(n^{7/3})$.
If $r<n/12$ or $D<n/12$, then $r^2D/2$ has a fixed cubic
deficit from $2n^3/27$; this absorbs the preceding error and
all quadratic extension and power costs in~\eqref{p3:eq:raw}.
Otherwise $r,D\ge n/12$, and $t=D-M-e\ge n/24$ for large $n$.
In that case
\[
 s(2D+1)-\binom{r-s}{2}\le-c n^2
\]
for an absolute $c>0$ once $n$ is sufficiently large depending
on $Q$. Using $B\ge t/s$ in~\eqref{p3:eq:roughX} gives
\[
 \mathcal X\le O_Q(n^{7/3})-c n^2t/s\le-c_Q n^{8/3}
\]
for some $c_Q>0$ and large $n$. This again leaves any prescribed
fixed quadratic saving after the extension costs are included.

\emph{Source normalization with the extension cost retained.}
We are left with bounded $\delta$ and $sM\ge(h+3)r$.
Fix a core with span $C\le V=N/\Phi(N)$ and let
\[
 K=\{v\in V:\beta(v,C)=0\},\qquad d=\dim K.
\]
Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:core} gives $K\cap C=0$. An element of $A(N)$
fixing $C$ pointwise fixes $W$ pointwise, because the core
commutators span $W$. Its action $g$ on $V$ therefore satisfies
$(g-1)V\subseteq K$ and $(g-1)C=0$. There are at most
$2^{d(r-s)}$ such linear maps. The images of a basis of $C$
have at most $2^{sr}$ possibilities, so
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:autoimage}
 a(N)\le2^{sr+d(r-s)}.
\end{equation}

Apply Lemmas~\ref{p3:lem:bases} and~\ref{p3:lem:kernel} before
dividing by source multiplicity. They give a moving outside
space of dimension $u\ge r-s-\delta$, a multiplicity at least
$c_*2^{u^2-ud}$, a cost at most $c_*^{-1}2^{d(r-d)}$ for choosing
$K$, and a saving of $sdM$ in the raw exponent $\mathcal E$, where
$c_*=\prod_{i\ge1}(1-2^{-i})>0$. All power-word fibres are
included before this division. The extension cost is an
isomorphism invariant, and~\eqref{p4:eq:autoimage} bounds it for
every group represented by the fixed core stratum. Different
isomorphism classes cannot yield the same complete array.
Consequently the total contribution of this stratum, with
$a(N)^{h+1}2^{h r(n-r)}$ included, has logarithm at most
\begin{align}\label{p4:eq:normalized-extension}
 &\mathcal E-u^2+(h+1)sr+h r(n-r)\notag\\
 &\quad+d\bigl(r+u-d-sM+(h+1)(r-s)\bigr)+O(n\log n).
\end{align}
One may assign a single admissible core stratum to each group;
allowing more choices only increases the upper bound.

Since $u\le r$ and $sM\ge(h+3)r$, the coefficient multiplying
$d$ in~\eqref{p4:eq:normalized-extension} is nonpositive.
Bounded $\delta$ and saturation give
$u^2=r^2+O_Q(n^{3/2})$ and $sr=O(n^{3/2})$. Thus this expression
is at most
\[
 \mathcal E-r^2+h r(n-r)+O_Q(n^{3/2}).
\]
Put $n_0=r+D=n-\delta$ and $z=r-2D$. The identity
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:quadratic-identity}
 -r^2+hrD
 =\frac{2h-4}{9}n_0^2-\frac{h+4}{3}Dz
                  -\frac{2h+5}{9}z^2
\end{equation}
and~\eqref{p3:eq:raw} now give the upper bound
\begin{align*}
 &\left(\frac12r^2D+\mathcal X+3Dt-\frac{2h+5}{6}Dz\right)
 +\frac{2h-4}{9}n_0^2-\frac{2h+5}{9}z^2+O_Q(n^{3/2})\\
 &\hspace{8mm}\le
 \frac{2}{27}n_0^3+\frac{2h-4}{9}n_0^2+O_Q(n^{3/2}),
\end{align*}
using~\eqref{p3:eq:opt} with $\eta=-(2h+5)/6$. The terms
$2De+r\delta+hr\delta$ are $O_Q(n)$ here. The polynomial
$2y^3/27+(2h-4)y^2/9$ is increasing for sufficiently large $y$,
so $n_0\le n$ permits replacement by $n$. Finally, the parameter
ledger, the sum over $d,u$, and the factor $2^{n|Q|^2}$ contribute
only $O_Q(n\log n)$. The discarded ranges obey stronger bounds,
and finitely many small values of $n$ are absorbed by the implied
constant. This proves~\eqref{p4:eq:gQ}.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{p4:prop:cutoff}
For a fixed $Q$ with nontrivial odd part, the proportion of all groups
of order at most $x$ that admit a normal $2$-subgroup with quotient
$Q$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:margin}
 2^{-\frac29m^2+O_Q(m^{3/2})},\qquad m=\lfloor\log_2x\rfloor.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Such a group has order $b2^{n+j}$. Write
$u_b=\lfloor\log_2b\rfloor$, so $v=j+u_b$.
The inequalities $b\ge2^{u_b}$ and $b2^{n+j}\le x<2^{m+1}$
imply, by integrality, $n\le m-v$.
The polynomial in~\eqref{p4:eq:gQ} is increasing for sufficiently
large $n$, and its error is bounded by $O_Q(m^{3/2})$ throughout
this range. Bounded kernel orders contribute finitely many
groups. Evaluating at $n=m-v$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac{2}{27}(m-v)^3+\frac{2h-4}{9}(m-v)^2
 &=\frac{2}{27}m^3-
   \left(\frac49+\frac29(v-h)\right)m^2+O_Q(m)\\
 &\le\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac69m^2+O_Q(m),
\end{align*}
because $h\le v-1$. Summing the $O(m)$ possible kernel orders
adds only $O(\log m)$ to the exponent. By
Lemma~\ref{p3:lem:lower-bound},
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:denominator}
 F(x)\ge f(2^m)\ge2^{\frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac49m^2}.
\end{equation}
Division proves~\eqref{p4:eq:margin}. This includes the floor
in the cutoff and requires no adjacent-order comparison.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{p4:cor:boundedodd}
For every fixed $B_0$, the proportion of groups of order at most
$x$ whose odd part lies in $1<b\le B_0$ tends to zero.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
For $|G|=b2^k$, choose a Sylow $2$-subgroup $S$ and take its core
$N=\bigcap_{g\in G}S^g$. This is a normal $2$-subgroup, and the
coset action embeds $Q=G/N$ into $\operatorname{Sym}(b)$.
Moreover $|Q|=2^jb$ for some $j\ge0$. For bounded $b$ there are
only finitely many possible quotient isomorphism types, all of
nontrivial odd part. Apply Proposition~\ref{p4:prop:cutoff} to
each. No normality of the original Sylow subgroup is assumed.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{p4:prop:largeodd}
The proportion of groups of order at most $x$ whose orders have
odd part at least $2^{342}$ tends to zero.
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
Pyber's prescribed-Sylow theorem~\cite[p.~204]{Pyber} gives
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:pyber}
 f(n)\le n^{75\mu(n)+16}\prod_{p\mid n}f(p^{v_p(n)}),
 \qquad \mu(n)=\max_p v_p(n).
\end{equation}
The sharp uniform bound~\eqref{p3:eq:sharp} implies, in particular,
$f(p^a)\le p^{2a^3/27+Ca}$ with an absolute $C$.
Let $\ell=\log_2x$, write $n=2^ab\le x$ with $b$ odd, and put
$B=\log_2b$, $q=\log_2 3$. For
$w_p=v_p(n)\log_2p$, we have
\[
 \sum_{p\text{ odd}}v_p(n)^3\log_2p
 =\sum_{p\text{ odd}}\frac{w_p^3}{(\log_2p)^2}
 \le\frac{B^3}{q^2},\qquad
 \sum_p v_p(n)\log_2p\le\ell.
\]
Since $a\le\ell-B$ and $\mu(n)\le\ell$, equation~\eqref{p4:eq:pyber}
yields
\begin{equation}\label{p4:eq:large-odd-exponent}
 \log_2 f(n)\le
 \frac{2}{27}\left((\ell-B)^3+\frac{B^3}{q^2}\right)
 +75\ell^2+O(\ell).
\end{equation}
The function $(\ell-B)^3+B^3/q^2$ is convex on $[0,\ell]$.
For $342\le B\le\ell$, its maximum is therefore at an endpoint.
At $B=342$, multiplication by $2/27$ gives
$2\ell^3/27-76\ell^2+O(\ell)$; at $B=\ell$ the leading cubic
coefficient is $2/(27q^2)<2/27$. Consequently, after summing over at
most $x$ integer orders, we find that the number of groups under consideration
is at most
\[
 2^{\frac{2}{27}\ell^3-\ell^2+O(\ell)}.
\]
For $m=\lfloor\ell\rfloor$, the rounding loss in
\eqref{p4:eq:denominator} gives
\[
 \log_2 F(x)\ge\frac{2}{27}\ell^3-\frac23\ell^2-O(\ell).
\]
The required proportion is at most
$2^{-\ell^2/3+O(\ell)}$, which tends to zero.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{p4:cor:two-groups}
Almost all finite groups are $2$-groups.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{p4:prop:largeodd} removes the odd parts at least
$2^{342}$. Corollary~\ref{p4:cor:boundedodd} removes the remaining
finitely many odd parts greater than one.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
It remains to exclude $2$-groups of class different from two.
Set
\[
 H(y)=\frac{2}{27}y^3-\frac49y^2.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{p3:prop:frattini-concentration}, there are
constants $\varepsilon>0$ and $k_0$ such that, for $k\ge k_0$,
the number $e_k$ of groups of order $2^k$ whose Frattini subgroup
is not central elementary abelian satisfies
\[
 e_k\le2^{H(k)-\varepsilon k^2}.
\]
After increasing $k_0$ if necessary, we may assume that the polynomial
$H(y)-\varepsilon y^2$ is increasing for $y\ge k_0$.
For $m=\lfloor\log_2x\rfloor$, this gives
\[
 \sum_{0\le k\le m}e_k
 \le O(1)+(m+1)2^{H(m)-\varepsilon m^2}.
\]
Division by $F(x)\ge2^{H(m)}$ shows that these groups have
cumulative density zero. Every group with central elementary
abelian Frattini subgroup has class at most two, since its
commutator subgroup is contained in its Frattini subgroup.

There are at most $2^k$ abelian groups of order $2^k$, by the
partition count. Thus all abelian $2$-groups of order at most
$x$ number at most $\sum_{k=0}^m2^k<2^{m+1}$, also negligible
relative to $2^{H(m)}$. The remaining $2$-groups have class
exactly two. Combining this with
Corollary~\ref{p4:cor:two-groups} proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
